It is the summer between Mira's first and second years. They have to pass a written qualifying exam in three weeks, and a major component of that exam is a lit review on coastal climate adaptation. Mira has been reading constantly. Their notes are voluminous. Their advisor has been encouraging.

Mira sits down on a Sunday afternoon and writes 4,200 words. Each paragraph begins something like:

> _Hallegatte (2013) examined the costs of coastal flooding in 136 major coastal cities. He found that exposure to flood losses could grow rapidly under sea-level rise scenarios. Following this, Kim (2018) studied the case of Busan and found…_

Each paragraph is well-organized. Each cites the right authors. Each ends with a tidy summary of what each author found.

Their advisor reads it Monday morning and writes back: _"This is a list. Please write me a literature review."_

Mira stares at the email for an hour.

The diagnosis is one that almost every graduate student receives at some point in their first year. Mira has written what is technically called an **annotated bibliography in prose** : a parade of paragraphs, each devoted to one source, walking through what each author did. It is summary. It is not synthesis. The genre called "literature review" is a synthesis genre, and Mira has produced something that does not perform the genre's central job.

This chapter is about what that job is, and how to do it.


### 3.1 Vignette: What "Synthesis" Actually Looks Like

Let me show you the contrast directly. Here is a paragraph in Mira's first-draft style:

> _Hallegatte (2013) modeled flood risk in 136 large coastal cities under several sea-level rise scenarios and projected substantial annual losses. Tessler et al. (2015) analyzed delta cities and showed that subsidence could compound sea-level rise effects. Kim (2018) studied Busan and identified institutional fragmentation as a barrier to adaptation. Brown (2019) studied Miami and identified similar institutional issues._

It is competent. It is informative. It is a list.

Here is what a synthesis paragraph on the same material might look like:

> _Most quantitative work on coastal flood risk has focused on large coastal cities at the global scale (Hallegatte, 2013; Tessler et al., 2015), producing top-down projections that are useful for international policy but coarse for local decision-making. A parallel literature has examined single cities in depth, often surfacing institutional fragmentation as a recurring barrier to adaptation (Kim, 2018; Brown, 2019). What links these literatures — and what neither has fully addressed — is the question of how mid-sized cities, which lack the resources of megacities and the data of global samples, navigate adaptation under fiscal stress._

Both paragraphs cite the same four sources. The first walks through them; the second uses them to _tell a story about the field_. The second establishes that there are two strands of literature, characterizes each strand by its methodological choices and findings, and identifies a gap that the writer's own work will address. The citations are doing rhetorical work — what we called _positioning_ moves in Chapter 2.

This is the central distinction the literature review genre demands: **synthesis, not summary.** A literature review tells the reader the _shape_ of a field and the _gap_ the writer's contribution will occupy. It does this through citations that work as moves, not as decorations.

### 3.2 What Examiners and Reviewers Look For

A senior reader skimming a literature review asks several questions, often without realizing they are asking them:

**Has the writer mapped the field?** Can I tell, after reading, what the major positions or strands are? Are there acknowledged debates? Is there a sense of which work is foundational and which is recent?

**Has the writer evaluated the field?** Or are they just reporting? A good lit review doesn't merely list; it characterizes. It says _this strand is methodologically rigorous but small in scope_ ; _this strand is influential but increasingly questioned_ ; _this strand is fragmented but converging on a consensus._

**Has the writer identified a gap?** And is the gap _real_ — not manufactured, not trivial, not already filled? The gap is the bridge to the writer's own contribution. A lit review without a gap is half a review.

**Has the writer been fair to opposing views?** A lit review that only cites work congenial to the writer's argument is a red flag. Senior readers can usually name three or four obvious omissions in a poorly done lit review within minutes.

**Has the writer cited the right people?** Every field has a small set of works that any competent writer in that field would cite. Missing them signals one of two things: the writer is new to the field (forgivable but to be addressed quickly) or the writer hasn't read enough (less forgivable).

**Has the writer been recent?** A lit review that bottoms out in 2010 with no engagement with the last decade looks dated. Conversely, a lit review that only cites the last two years and ignores foundational work looks shallow.

These six questions are the implicit grading rubric for a lit review chapter, qualifying exam essay, or stand-alone review article. If you can answer yes to all six, you have a lit review. If you can't, you have something else — and you should know what it is so you can fix it.


### 3.3 The Four Moves of an Effective Literature Review

A literature review has its own four-move arc, parallel in some ways to the CARS introduction model we will see in Chapter 4 but adapted for a longer, denser, more structurally complex genre.


#### Move 1 — Situate

Tell the reader what conversation we are entering and why it matters. Establish the territory. This is not the place for "Climate change is one of the most important challenges of our time"; it is the place for _"Coastal cities face accelerating risk from sea-level rise; the policy and scholarly response has clustered around three approaches…"_

Situating typically takes one to three paragraphs. It names the field, the subfield, and the specific conversation. It does not define every term; it assumes a reader familiar with the broad topic.

#### Move 2 — Group

Organize the literature into strands, schools, debates, or methodological camps. _This_ is the move that distinguishes a synthesis from a list. You are imposing intellectual order on what would otherwise be a chronological recitation.

Grouping moves include:

* _By methodology:_ "The literature divides roughly into quantitative modeling work and qualitative case studies."
* _By position:_ "Two main interpretations have emerged: those who attribute outcomes to institutional capacity, and those who emphasize fiscal constraint."
* _By scale:_ "Existing studies cluster at three scales: global comparative, national case-study, and individual-city ethnographic."
* _By chronology of debate:_ "Early work in the 1990s emphasized X; this view was challenged in the 2000s; the current consensus is roughly Y."

You can combine grouping schemes. You can also signal where strands overlap or contradict. The point is: _the writer organizes the literature, and the organization is itself an analytical claim._


#### Move 3 — Evaluate

Within each strand, characterize the work. What does it get right? What does it leave unaddressed? What methodological choices does it make, and what do those choices buy and cost?

Evaluation does not mean attack. The conventions of academic politeness apply: you don't say "Smith's work is wrong"; you say "Smith's analysis offers important insights, but its case selection limits generalizability to high-resource settings." You can be sharp; you have to be measured.

Evaluation is where new graduate students most often hold back. They assume that everyone they cite is more authoritative than they are, so they dare not characterize the work. The result is summary masquerading as review. Senior readers are trained to spot this and to mark it down.


#### Move 4 — Locate the gap

Identify what is missing. Where does the existing literature fail to answer a question, fail to consider a population, fail to use a method, fail to integrate two strands? _That gap_ is where your contribution will sit.

The gap should be specific. _"More research is needed"_ is not a gap; it is a placeholder. _"While quantitative work has examined megacities and qualitative case studies have examined individual cities, comparative analysis at the mid-sized scale is largely absent — yet mid-sized cities house 30% of coastal populations and face distinctive constraints"_ is a gap. Specific, defensible, and pointing toward your work.

These four moves do not need to map one-to-one with sections of your lit review. They can interleave; you can iterate. The most important thing is that all four are _present_ , and a careful reader can identify each one. A lit review missing Move 2 is a list (Mira's first draft). A lit review missing Move 3 is summary. A lit review missing Move 4 is a survey, not a setup for a contribution.

#### Definition: Synthesis

In academic writing, **synthesis** means combining information from multiple sources to produce a new, integrated understanding that none of the sources individually provides.

In plain language: synthesis is what happens when 1+1+1 becomes more than 3. You read three studies; you don't just summarize each. You look across them and ask: _what does the combination tell me that no single study does?_ Maybe two studies use methods that, taken together, reveal a pattern neither study alone could see. Maybe one study contradicts another, and the contradiction is itself the interesting finding. Maybe all three together imply a missing piece. Synthesis is the production of that meta-finding.

Most graduate students arrive at lit-review writing with the skill of summary fully developed (they wrote summary throughout undergraduate education) and the skill of synthesis underdeveloped (because their undergraduate writing rarely required it). The lit review is the genre where this skill gap most painfully shows.


#### Common Misconception

A common misconception is that the lit review is _the place where you prove you have read everything_. New graduate students often try to demonstrate breadth by citing as many sources as possible, fearing that omitting any work would be a defect. The result is a bloated, exhausting document with no analytical spine.

Reviewers and examiners are not impressed by sheer citation count. They are impressed by _judgment_ : the writer's ability to identify the works that matter, organize them sensibly, characterize them fairly, and locate a gap. A well-organized 30-source lit review almost always beats a comprehensive 100-source list.

The fix: cite enough to establish the strands and the gap, then stop. If you have read 100 papers, your work is in _choosing which 30 to feature_ ; the other 70 informed your judgment but don't all need to appear.

### 3.4 The Six Moves Applied to Mira's Lit Review

Mira is now sitting with their advisor, who has marked up the failed first draft. Together they apply the six moves from Chapter 2 to plan a rewrite.

**Move 1 — Genre and venue.** This is a qualifying-exam lit review (genre), evaluated by the writer's three-person committee (venue). The committee includes a quantitative climate-policy modeler, a qualitative urban policy scholar, and a comparative public administration scholar. The writer must satisfy all three. (This already explains why a single-strand lit review will not work — Mira has three audiences with three different preferred literatures.)

**Move 2 — Structure.** A lit review is not always rigidly structured, but a useful default is: introduction (situate the conversation), 3–4 substantive sections (one per strand), a synthesis section (where strands are compared), and a section that locates the gap and previews the writer's own work.

**Move 3 — Calibration.** A qualifying exam lit review is calibrated to be _thorough but not exhaustive_ ; _evaluative but not combative_ ; _evidently aware of the field's debates without taking sides on settled questions_. Citation density is high (3–6 per page). Voice is third-person impersonal in the situate sections, can shift to first-person plural ("we observe") in the synthesis sections.

**Move 4 — Positioning.** Mira maps citations into roles: _Hallegatte, Tessler, Nicholls_ are foundational quantitative-modeling allies. _Kim, Brown, Aerts_ are case-study allies. _Bulkeley_ is a frequently cited theorist of urban climate governance — a definition source. _No clear antagonists_ — this is a young enough subfield that the debates are not crystallized into camps. The gap is at the _intersection_ of strands rather than at the _boundary_ of one strand.

**Move 5 — Anticipated reviewer.** Predictable objections: _"What about the work of [author X]?"_ — answered by deciding now which adjacent literatures to address and which to bracket. _"Aren't you overstating the gap?"_ — answered by characterizing existing work fairly and being precise about what the gap is. _"Is this lit review really setting up your dissertation, or are you just demonstrating reading?"_ — answered by ending with a clear forward statement: _"This review motivates the present study's focus on mid-sized cities…"_

**Move 6 — AI.** Mira uses AI to help generate alternative grouping schemes ("Suggest five different ways to organize this set of references"), to spot repetitive phrasing in the draft, and to play the role of a hostile reader. They do _not_ use AI to find or summarize sources they haven't read. They check every cited work against their own notes.

After this planning, Mira rewrites. The second draft is half as long and twice as good. The committee passes the chapter.

### 3.5 Templates and Examples

Here are five small templates that often help graduate writers move from list to synthesis.

**Template 1 — The two-strand opener:**

> _Two main strands characterize the literature on [topic]. The first, exemplified by [Author A; Author B], approaches the question through [method/lens]. The second, exemplified by [Author C; Author D], emphasizes [different method/lens]. The two strands have rarely engaged each other directly._

This template is useful when you can identify a clean methodological or conceptual divide. It immediately announces synthesis, because it is telling the reader the _organization_ of the field rather than the contents of individual papers.

**Template 2 — The convergence statement:**

> _Despite different methodological approaches, work in [field] has converged on the finding that [X] is shaped by [Y]. [Author A] showed this through [method 1]; [Author B] reached a similar conclusion using [method 2]; and recent work by [Author C] extended the finding to [new context]._

Useful when the literature is in genuine consensus on one point. Demonstrates synthesis by showing the writer has identified the convergence and named it.

**Template 3 — The genuine debate:**

> _A key debate in [field] concerns [question]. [Author A] argues [position 1], on the grounds that [reasoning]. In contrast, [Author B] maintains [position 2], pointing to [evidence]. The disagreement turns on [conceptual or empirical crux]._

Useful when the literature contains a real disagreement. Demonstrates synthesis by characterizing the disagreement clearly. Note: do not manufacture debates that don't exist; manufactured debates are easy for senior readers to detect and discrediting.

**Template 4 — The methodological gap:**

> _While [field] has been examined extensively through [method 1] and [method 2], the application of [method 3] has been limited. The few studies that have applied [method 3] (e.g., [Author A; Author B]) have produced suggestive findings but were limited by [scope/sample/data]. The present study applies [method 3] to [context] in order to [contribution]._

Useful when your contribution is methodological. Demonstrates synthesis by characterizing the existing methodological landscape and locating the gap.

**Template 5 — The population gap:**

> _Existing work on [phenomenon] has focused predominantly on [population A], with much smaller attention to [population B], despite the fact that [population B] [statistic establishing relevance]. The present study addresses this asymmetry by [contribution]._

Useful when your contribution is studying an under-represented population, region, or case. Demonstrates synthesis by characterizing where attention has gone and not gone.

These templates are scaffolds, not formulas. Use them to start, then revise into your own voice.

### 3.6 Common Pitfalls

**The annotated bibliography in prose.** Mira's first draft. Each paragraph one source. No grouping. No evaluation. No gap. Fix: regroup the literature by strand before drafting; never let a paragraph be devoted to one source unless that source genuinely deserves the attention.

**The chronological recitation.** The lit review walks through the literature in order of publication date. This produces a "first this, then this" structure that is rarely the most analytically illuminating order. Fix: organize by strand or theme, with chronology layered in only where it does work.

**The bloated comprehensive list.** A hundred citations, no judgment. Fix: name the strands, choose representative works for each, and stop.

**The advocacy lit review.** Only the works that support the writer's position are cited; opposing views are absent. Fix: identify the strongest counter-evidence and engage with it explicitly.

**The fake gap.** _"More research is needed."_ This sentence in your lit review is a sign that you have not done the analytical work of locating a real gap. Fix: be specific. What method, population, scale, or theoretical move is missing?

**The recency trap.** Only the last three years of literature are cited; the foundational work is missing. Fix: ensure the lit review reaches back to at least the foundational works in the strand.

**The decade gap.** Conversely, the lit review stops at 2015 and ignores the last decade. Fix: ensure recent work is engaged, especially work that complicates or updates older findings.


### 3.7 Scholar Profile: John Swales and the Reverse-Engineering of Academic Writing

John Swales is a British-American applied linguist whose work in the 1980s and 1990s effectively founded modern genre analysis of academic writing. He was bothered by a question that few people had thought to ask: _what, structurally, do academic introductions actually look like?_

Most writing advice up to that point had been prescriptive: _introductions should do X, Y, Z._ Swales wanted to know what they _did_ do. So he collected hundreds of published introductions across disciplines — biology, linguistics, education, engineering — and read them carefully, looking for recurring rhetorical patterns.

He found them. The pattern he identified, the **CARS model** (Create A Research Space), is the subject of Chapter 4. But the more general lesson of Swales's work is that academic writing has _describable structure_ — that the conventions are real and recurring, and they can be reverse-engineered from the published corpus.

A surprising fact: Swales developed the CARS model partly by analyzing introductions in non-English-language journals. The pattern recurs across linguistic boundaries, suggesting that some of academic writing's conventions are not narrowly Anglophone. The patterns are not universal — German academic introductions, for instance, often defer the gap until later — but they are widespread enough that Swales's framework remains the dominant model 35 years after he published _Genre Analysis_ (1990).

Swales's gift to graduate students was making the _implicit explicit_. Before Swales, "good academic writing" was something senior scholars recognized but couldn't articulate. After Swales, it became something anyone could be taught. The book you are reading owes him a deep debt.

### 3.8 Reader's Manuscript Audit Prompt

It is time to start Thread B. Take a current manuscript of your own — your dissertation lit review, a draft article's literature section, or a graded paper from a recent course — and perform the following audit:

**Count the synthesis vs. summary moves.** Read each paragraph and label it:

* **S** if the paragraph synthesizes — that is, it groups, evaluates, or locates a gap.
* **L** if the paragraph lists — that is, it summarizes one or two sources without performing a synthesis move.

Now compute the ratio. A strong literature review usually runs at least 60% S, often 80% or higher. A draft that is 70%+ L is an annotated bibliography in prose, regardless of how well-written each paragraph is.

For each L paragraph, ask: _What synthesis move could this paragraph perform instead?_ Sometimes the answer is to merge two L paragraphs into one S paragraph. Sometimes the answer is that the L paragraph is doing necessary background work and can be radically shortened. Sometimes the answer is to delete the paragraph entirely.

Save your annotated draft. We will return to this manuscript across the chapters of Part II, building up a portfolio of revised sections by the time you reach Chapter 18.


### 3.9 Exercises


#### Concept Check

**Q1.** In one sentence each, distinguish _summary_ from _synthesis_ as the chapter has used these terms.

Hint

The Definition box in §3.3 names synthesis directly; summary is contrasted throughout §3.1 and §3.3.

**Answer:** _Summary_ is restating what individual sources say, one source at a time; _synthesis_ is combining information from multiple sources to produce a new, integrated understanding (groupings, evaluations, debates, gaps) that none of the sources individually provides.

**Q2.** Name the four moves of an effective literature review.

**Answer:** (1) Situate — establish the conversation and its importance. (2) Group — organize the literature into strands, schools, or debates. (3) Evaluate — characterize each strand's contributions and limits. (4) Locate the gap — identify what is missing that the writer's work will address.

**Q3.** What are the six implicit questions a senior reader asks while skimming a literature review?

**Answer:** Has the writer (1) mapped the field, (2) evaluated it, (3) identified a real gap, (4) been fair to opposing views, (5) cited the right people, and (6) been recent (engaging the last decade as well as foundational work)?

**Q4.** Why does the chapter argue that the _annotated bibliography in prose_ is the most common failure mode for first lit reviews?

**Answer:** Because graduate students arrive at lit-review writing with summary skills well-developed (used throughout undergraduate education) and synthesis skills underdeveloped. Without explicit teaching, the default is to walk through sources one paragraph at a time, which is summary; the genre demands grouping, evaluation, and gap-location, which is synthesis. The default mode is technically competent but does not perform the genre's central job.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Take Mira's first-draft paragraph from §3.1 ("Hallegatte (2013) modeled flood risk…") and rewrite it as a synthesis paragraph using one of the templates from §3.5. Identify which template you used and why.

Hint

The four sources cited (Hallegatte, Tessler, Kim, Brown) split into a quantitative-modeling strand (Hallegatte, Tessler) and a case-study strand (Kim, Brown). Templates 1 (two-strand opener) and 4 (methodological gap) are good fits.

**Answer:** A successful response will (a) consolidate the four sources into a single synthesis paragraph that names two strands (quantitative modeling vs. case study) and (b) say which template was used. Example using Template 1: _"Two main strands characterize the literature on coastal city flood risk. The first, exemplified by Hallegatte (2013) and Tessler et al. (2015), approaches the question through quantitative global modeling, projecting losses across many cities under varying scenarios. The second, exemplified by Kim (2018) and Brown (2019), uses single-city case studies to identify institutional barriers to adaptation. The two strands have rarely engaged each other directly — yet the institutional factors the case studies identify likely shape the loss outcomes the quantitative work models."_

**Q2.** Read the literature review section of any paper in your field. For each paragraph, label it **S** (synthesis) or **L** (list/summary), as in §3.8. Compute the ratio. In a 200-word commentary, identify the strongest synthesis paragraph and the weakest, and explain what makes each what it is. (This is the manuscript audit prompt applied to someone else's paper before you apply it to your own.)

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful response identifies the S/L pattern accurately and characterizes specific strengths and weaknesses. Common findings: (1) lit reviews in shorter papers (high-impact journals with strict word limits) tend to be high-S because the constraint forces synthesis; (2) lit reviews in dissertation chapters tend to be lower-S because the unrestricted length tempts the writer to include everything; (3) the strongest synthesis paragraphs typically perform Move 2 (grouping) explicitly, often with sentences like "The literature divides into…" or "Two main approaches have emerged…"; the weakest paragraphs walk through sources one at a time without analytical organization.

**Q3.** Identify a _real_ debate in your field — one where two camps have published in genuine disagreement. Write a 200-word paragraph that uses Template 3 (the genuine debate) to characterize the disagreement. Cite at least two works on each side. (This connects to Move 4 from Chapter 2: positioning through citation, with antagonist-naming.)

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful response will name an actual disagreement (not a manufactured one) and characterize each side fairly, using citations to mark camps. The exercise teaches the diagnostic eye: many young writers struggle to name real debates because they have absorbed the mistaken impression that academic writing is mostly consensus. In most active subfields there are several real debates; locating them is part of becoming a competent member of the field.

**Sample Response (Mira on a real debate in coastal adaptation):** _"A genuine disagreement runs through the coastal adaptation literature on the question of whether managed retreat is a viable adaptation strategy for low- and middle-income coastal cities. One camp, exemplified by Hino, Field, and Mach (2017) and Siders (2019), argues that managed retreat — the planned withdrawal of populations and infrastructure from increasingly hazardous coastlines — is an essential and underused tool, and that political resistance has crowded out a strategy that the evidence supports. The opposing camp, exemplified by Adger et al. (2011) and Pelling and Garschagen (2019), argues that managed retreat in low- and middle-income contexts is often incompatible with property rights, livelihood structures, and political feasibility, and that emphasizing it diverts attention from in-place adaptation that better fits the contexts. The debate is real: both camps have published substantively, both engage each other's evidence, and the disagreement turns on (a) the political-economy assumptions each camp imports from its case base and (b) what counts as 'success' for adaptation policy. The dissertation's mid-sized-city findings sit between the two camps, suggesting that fiscal sequencing dynamics — not retreat-versus-stay-in-place — drive most of the within-city variation we observe."_

**Q4.** Compare the literature review section of two papers in your field — one on a relatively new topic (under five years of literature) and one on an established topic (decades of literature). How does the synthesis structure differ? Where is the gap easier to locate, and where is it harder? Write 250 words.

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A typical successful response notes that lit reviews on new topics are often shorter and rely on (a) connecting the new topic to adjacent established literatures and (b) framing the absence of work as itself the gap. Lit reviews on established topics rely on (a) characterizing the strands and debates that have accumulated and (b) locating the gap as a specific underexplored dimension. The exercise teaches that "the gap" is not a fixed kind of object — it can be a missing population, a missing method, a missing scale, an unresolved debate, or a synthesis between two strands that have not engaged each other (Mira's case).

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The chapter argues that "the writer organizes the literature, and the organization is itself an analytical claim" (§3.3). But a more skeptical reader might say: any organization is an interpretation, and interpretations can be biased toward the writer's own contribution. How should a writer balance the analytical work of grouping with the risk of grouping in self-serving ways? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** This question gets at a real tension in academic writing. Every grouping scheme privileges some lines of work and obscures others. A writer whose contribution is methodological will tend to group by methodology, making the methodological gap visible; a writer whose contribution is theoretical will group by theoretical framework, making the theoretical gap visible. This is not necessarily dishonest — it is the writer's analytical perspective showing through — but it is _partial_. Honest practice involves: (a) acknowledging alternative groupings ("an alternative way to organize this literature would be by…"); (b) not omitting work that doesn't fit the chosen scheme; (c) characterizing strands fairly even when they're not the writer's own. The deepest answers notice that the choice of grouping is itself a kind of intellectual contribution — and that disclosing the choice makes it defensible. (Connection to Chapter 2's Move 4: citations are rhetorical moves, and grouping schemes are too. Both should be deployed deliberately and disclosed honestly.)

**Q2.** Some fields (particularly in the humanities) reject the four-move structure for lit reviews, on the grounds that it imposes a quasi-scientific framework on traditions that work differently. How might a literary studies dissertation, a historical-archival project, or a philosophy paper handle the lit review move differently? Sketch your view in 250 words.

**Discussion:** Literary, historical, and philosophical work often integrates literature review _throughout_ the paper rather than confining it to a single section, in part because the boundary between "what others have said" and "what I argue" is more porous in these fields. A philosophy paper may engage prior work conversationally, paragraph by paragraph, throughout. A historical paper may weave secondary literature into the narrative of evidence. A literary studies paper may treat critical conversation as ongoing throughout the analysis. The four moves we named are still present, but they may be distributed across the paper rather than concentrated. The skilled humanities writer still situates, groups, evaluates, and locates a gap — but the architecture of how they do so differs. (Connection to Chapter 2's Move 1: the genre and venue determine the structure; what is conventional for a science research article may not be conventional for a humanities monograph.)

**Q3.** AI tools can summarize hundreds of papers in seconds. Some current advice (and many graduate students' practice) is: have the AI summarize the literature, then write the lit review based on those summaries. What are the risks of this approach, and where might it nonetheless be acceptable? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** The risks are substantial. AI-generated summaries (a) may misrepresent the source's nuance or context; (b) may hallucinate findings; (c) may smooth over disagreements by averaging across positions; and (d) crucially, deprive the writer of the _reading_ that builds the field-knowledge a competent lit review draws on. A writer who has not read the sources cannot fairly characterize them, identify real debates, or locate genuine gaps; they can only repackage what the AI repackaged. There may be acceptable uses: (a) using AI to _spot_ sources you should then read; (b) using AI to check whether you have missed an important strand; (c) using AI to draft an _alternative grouping scheme_ you then evaluate. But the writing of the lit review itself — and especially the synthesis moves — must come from the writer's actual reading and judgment. (Connection to Chapter 2's Move 6: use AI as a thinking partner, not as a substitute for reading. Connection forward to Chapter 14: this is one of the bright lines that integrity policies in 2025 most clearly enforce.)


### Chapter Summary

The literature review is the genre most graduate students attempt first and where most graduate students first lose serious time. Its central demand is **synthesis, not summary** — the production of an analytical map of the field that combines, evaluates, and locates a gap, rather than a paragraph-by-paragraph walk through individual sources.

A literature review performs four moves: situate the conversation, group the literature, evaluate the strands, and locate the gap. We saw the contrast between Mira's first-draft list and a synthesis revision (§3.1), the six questions a senior reader asks while reading (§3.2), the four moves (§3.3), and the application of the six moves from Chapter 2 to Mira's specific case (§3.4). We laid out five templates that scaffold the move from list to synthesis (§3.5), six common pitfalls (§3.6), and the contribution of John Swales — the linguist who made academic genre conventions explicit and whose CARS model anchors the next chapter (§3.7).

The manuscript audit prompt (§3.8) launched Thread B: throughout the rest of the book, you will revise sections of your own current manuscript. The first revision is a synthesis-vs-summary audit of your literature section.

In Chapter 4 we turn to the **introduction** , the genre-bookend most directly governed by Swales's CARS model. The lit review feeds the introduction: the gap you located in your lit review becomes the niche your introduction occupies. Mira will write an introduction next, and we will see whether they have absorbed the synthesis lessons of this chapter.

> _A literature review tells the reader the shape of a field. If after reading yours, the reader cannot draw that shape, the genre's central job has not been done._

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: The Introduction — Create A Research Space
blocks.src:
It is the fall of Mira's second year, and they are drafting the introduction to their first solo paper — a comparative study of three mid-sized coastal cities. Their qualifying-exam lit review (Chapter 3) has been passed and praised. Their advisor has said: _"This is going to be a real paper. Write me a draft introduction by Monday."_

Mira sits down on Friday afternoon and writes:

> _"Climate change is one of the greatest challenges of our time. Sea-level rise threatens coastal cities around the world. Many cities face difficult choices about how to adapt under tight budgets. This paper examines how three mid-sized coastal cities in different countries have made these choices."_

It is grammatical. It is on topic. It is, their advisor will tell them on Monday, a perfect example of an introduction that will be rejected by every reviewer in the field.

The reason has a name: **the missing Move 2 problem.** Mira has established the territory (climate change matters; coastal cities are at risk). They have stated their contribution (we look at three cities). What they have _not_ done is establish the niche — the specific gap in the literature that their paper will occupy. And without Move 2, no reviewer can answer the most basic question they will ask: _what is new about this paper?_

This chapter is about how to write an introduction that survives that question.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: The Introduction — Create A Research Space
blocks.src:
### 4.1 Vignette: The Two-Page Difference

Let me put two introductions side by side. Both are about the same imaginary paper. Both are 200 words. Both are grammatically clean.

**Version A (Mira's first draft, lightly edited):**

> _Climate change is one of the most pressing challenges of our time. Among its most visible effects is sea-level rise, which threatens hundreds of millions of coastal residents worldwide. As global temperatures continue to rise, coastal cities face increasingly difficult choices about how to protect their populations and infrastructure. Many cities have begun to consider adaptation measures, but the costs are high and budgets are often constrained. This is especially true for cities that are not large enough to attract international attention or funding. In this paper, we examine how three mid-sized coastal cities in different countries — Da Nang in Vietnam, Cartagena in Colombia, and Casablanca in Morocco — have made adaptation decisions under fiscal constraint. We use a comparative case study methodology and draw on policy documents, interviews, and budget data. The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature; Section 3 describes our methods; Section 4 presents findings; Section 5 discusses implications._

**Version B (after a CARS rewrite):**

> _Coastal cities concentrate roughly 40% of the world's population and a disproportionate share of its climate-vulnerable infrastructure. Adaptation policy in such cities has been studied along two largely disconnected tracks: top-down quantitative work projecting losses across global samples of large cities (e.g., Hallegatte, 2013), and bottom-up case studies of individual large cities (e.g., New York, Rotterdam, Singapore). Mid-sized coastal cities — those with populations between 100,000 and 1 million — have received much less attention, despite housing approximately 30% of the global coastal population and facing a distinctive constraint: they lack the fiscal capacity of megacities while also lacking the high-resolution data on which both prior strands of work rely. We address this gap through a comparative analysis of adaptation decisions in three mid-sized cities — Da Nang, Cartagena, and Casablanca — selected for diversity in regional context, fiscal regime, and adaptation history. Our findings show that fiscal constraint shapes adaptation through a previously undocumented mechanism: it forces a sequencing logic in which short-term, visible interventions crowd out longer-horizon investments. Section 2 develops this argument by reviewing prior work; Sections 3–4 present our methods and findings; Section 5 discusses theoretical and policy implications._

Both are 200 words. The difference is not length. The difference is that Version B performs a recognizable structure that allows the reader to answer four questions: _What field am I in? What's missing? What is the contribution? What's the road map?_ Version A answers only the first and a partial fourth.

This structure has a name. It is the **CARS model** , developed by John Swales (whom we met in Chapter 3). It is the most studied, most universal, and most useful structural template in academic writing.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: The Introduction — Create A Research Space
blocks.src:
### 4.2 What Reviewers Look For in an Introduction

Reviewers and editors read introductions with a small number of fixed questions. If your introduction answers all of them well, the paper has a fighting chance regardless of what comes after. If it fails to answer them, the paper is in trouble before a single result has been read.

**Is this paper in the journal's territory?** Editors triage at this level. An introduction that doesn't immediately signal its field membership is at risk of being desk-rejected before it reaches reviewers.

**Is the contribution stated, and is it specific?** "We examine X" is too vague. "We show that fiscal constraint reshapes adaptation through a sequencing logic" is specific. Reviewers look for the specific claim.

**Is the gap real?** Reviewers often know the field better than the writer; if the writer claims a gap that doesn't exist (because the field has already filled it), this is fatal. Reviewers will write _"This work is not novel; see Smith 2018"_ and recommend rejection.

**Is the contribution proportionate?** Too much claim relative to the evidence the paper will offer comes off as overclaiming; too little claim makes the reader wonder why the paper exists.

**Is the road map clear?** Reviewers want to know what they're about to read. A short final paragraph specifying the structure of the paper aids navigation and is conventional in many fields.

Each of these questions corresponds to a CARS move. The model is not arbitrary — it is the inverse of the questions reviewers actually ask.


### 4.3 The CARS Model in Detail

CARS stands for **Create A Research Space.** Swales analyzed hundreds of published academic introductions across disciplines and observed that they mostly performed four sequential rhetorical moves. He named them as follows.


#### Move 1 — Establish the territory

Claim that the field of work is important, central, or active. This is where you signal what conversation you are entering. Common sub-moves include claiming centrality ("Coastal cities concentrate roughly 40% of the world's population…"), generalizing about prior work ("A substantial literature has examined…"), or simply naming the topic and its salience.

A common error is to make Move 1 _too generic_. "Climate change is one of the greatest challenges of our time" is technically a Move 1 but it could be the opening of a thousand papers. Specific Move 1 statements signal expertise: _"Coastal cities concentrate roughly 40% of the world's population and a disproportionate share of its climate-vulnerable infrastructure"_ tells the reader you know something specific about the field.

Move 1 typically takes 1–3 sentences in a research article introduction. It is short. It is not an essay on importance. It is a tap on the shoulder: _here is the field we are in._

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: The Introduction — Create A Research Space
blocks.src:
#### Move 2 — Establish the niche

Identify a gap, a problem, an unaddressed question, or an unresolved tension in the literature. This is the move most often skipped, and skipping it is the single most common cause of rejected drafts.

Move 2 sub-moves include:

* _Counter-claiming:_ "However, this assumption has not been tested empirically."
* _Indicating a gap:_ "Mid-sized coastal cities have received much less attention…"
* _Question-raising:_ "It remains unclear whether the same mechanism operates at smaller scales."
* _Continuing a tradition:_ "Building on this line of work, we extend the analysis to…"

The niche must be _specific_ — generic claims like _"more research is needed"_ do not establish a niche, they signal that you don't know exactly what is missing. The niche must also be _real_ — manufactured gaps (gaps that already exist in the literature) will be flagged by reviewers.

A useful diagnostic: after writing your Move 2, ask _"What is the one sentence that names what is specifically missing?"_ If you can't point at it, you haven't done Move 2 yet.

Move 2 typically takes 2–6 sentences, often a full paragraph. It is the longest CARS move in many introductions.


#### Move 3 — Occupy the niche

State your contribution. Announce that the paper will fill the gap, address the problem, or answer the question that Move 2 set up. The structure is _"We address this gap by…"_ , _"We propose…"_ , _"We argue that…"_

Move 3 should be specific. _"We examine X"_ is weak. _"We show that fiscal constraint reshapes adaptation through a sequencing logic"_ is strong. The latter both names the topic _and_ the specific finding or argument.

Move 3 is the bridge. It tells the reader: _this is what is new; this is what you will learn._

Move 3 typically takes 2–4 sentences. It can be a single paragraph or part of one.


#### Move 4 — Outline the structure

Tell the reader what comes next. _"Section 2 reviews the literature; Section 3 describes the methods…"_ This move is conventional in many fields, optional in others (some humanities papers do not include it, especially short ones), and almost always brief.

A skilled Move 4 does double duty: it both lists sections _and_ signals what argumentative work each section does. Compare:

**Weak Move 4:** _"Section 2 reviews the literature."_

**Strong Move 4:** _"Section 2 develops the argument by reviewing prior work, with particular attention to the gap between quantitative and case-study traditions."_

The strong version uses the structural list as another opportunity to do positioning work.

Move 4 typically takes 2–5 sentences.


#### Definition: The CARS Model

The **CARS model** (Create A Research Space) describes the recurring four-move structure that Swales identified in published academic introductions: (1) establish the territory, (2) establish the niche, (3) occupy the niche, and (4) outline the structure of the paper.

In plain language: the CARS model is the implicit playbook for academic introductions. Most published introductions across most disciplines perform these four moves, in roughly this order, often without the writer or reader being consciously aware of the structure. Once you can see it, you can engineer your introductions deliberately.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: The Introduction — Create A Research Space
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

A common misconception is that CARS is a formula — that you should write four paragraphs corresponding exactly to four moves and check them off. In practice, the moves can be distributed and interleaved. Move 1 can take a single sentence; Move 2 can take three paragraphs and contain its own embedded mini-territory and mini-niche; Move 3 may overlap with Move 2 in some humanities papers. Skilled writers use CARS as a _checklist of work that must be done_ , not a paragraph-counting recipe.

If you can point at the four moves in your introduction, the model has been used. If you can't, the model has been violated and your draft is at risk.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: The Introduction — Create A Research Space
blocks.src:
### 4.4 The Complete Worked Example

Per the book's design, this chapter must include at least one complete CARS-model rewrite, showing the four moves explicitly. Here it is, with a different topic from Mira's, to demonstrate that the structure travels across topics and methodological traditions.

**Topic:** A study of how university faculty adopt (or resist) AI tools in undergraduate teaching, based on a survey of 800 faculty across 40 institutions.

**Bad (typical rejected) version:**

> _"Artificial intelligence is changing higher education. Many faculty are using AI tools in their teaching, while others are not. In this paper, we look at faculty AI adoption."_

This version has a generic Move 1, a vague (almost non-existent) Move 2, a vague Move 3, and no Move 4. A reviewer reading this would write: _"The motivation is unclear and the contribution is not stated. Reject."_

**CARS version:**

> **Move 1 (Territory):** _"Generative AI tools have spread through higher education at unprecedented speed: by mid-2024, more than 60% of U.S. undergraduates reported regular use of large language models for coursework. Faculty response has been less uniform — and is the subject of growing institutional concern, since the way faculty integrate or resist AI shapes both pedagogy and policy._
> 
> **Move 2 (Niche):** _Existing scholarship on faculty AI adoption has focused on two narrow contexts: STEM faculty at research-intensive universities (e.g., a series of recent surveys at Carnegie R1 institutions) and faculty who have voluntarily participated in AI training programs. The much larger population of faculty across the spectrum of institutional types and disciplinary backgrounds — including humanities and social-science faculty who may be skeptical of AI, and faculty at teaching-focused institutions where adoption may be driven by different pressures than at research-intensive ones — remains largely unstudied. As a result, current claims about 'faculty AI adoption' often generalize from samples that are not representative of the population about which the claims are made._
> 
> **Move 3 (Occupy):** _We address this gap with a survey of 800 faculty drawn from 40 institutions, stratified by institutional type and disciplinary cluster. We characterize four distinct adoption profiles and show that institutional type, more than disciplinary background, predicts which profile a faculty member occupies — a finding that contradicts the dominant assumption in the existing literature._
> 
> **Move 4 (Outline):** _Section 2 reviews prior work on faculty technology adoption and identifies the methodological limits we address. Section 3 describes our sampling design and survey instrument. Section 4 presents the four profiles and their predictors. Section 5 discusses implications for institutional policy and identifies open questions for the next round of work."_

The CARS version is roughly 280 words. It performs all four moves clearly. A reviewer reading this can answer the four questions immediately: _What field? What's missing? What's the contribution? What's the structure?_

The contrast between the two versions is what teaches. Side-by-side, the CARS version is not "more polished" — it is _doing different work_. The writer has stopped reporting that the topic exists and started telling the reader why this paper, specifically, is worth their time.

You should perform this rewrite for at least one of your own introductions before the chapter ends.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: The Introduction — Create A Research Space
blocks.src:
#### A Humanities Variant

CARS is not strictly universal. In philosophy, some literary criticism, and certain traditions in history, introductions follow different surface conventions — opening with a vivid example, an interpretive provocation, or a close reading of a primary text rather than a territory-statement. The "gap," in such introductions, is often _interpretive_ (a previous reading missed something) rather than _empirical_ (a population or method is understudied). And the contribution may emerge cumulatively across the introduction rather than being announced in a Move 3 declaration.

Consider this opening, drafted for an imagined article in a literary studies journal:

> _In the final pages of Toni Morrison's_ Beloved _(1987), Sethe asks Paul D, "Was that you?" — a question that reaches across the present action toward the murdered child whose presence has shadowed the novel's surface for two hundred pages. Critics have read this question as a moment of recognition, mourning, or recovery. None of these readings, I will argue, fully accounts for the question's grammatical strangeness: its tense, its addressee, and the slippage between them. That slippage names a problem the novel's first readers — and most of its critics since — have not addressed: how the literary representation of historical trauma negotiates the impossibility of locating its addressee. This essay reads the closing sequence of_ Beloved _to develop a theoretical account of what I will call_ trauma's grammatical address*, with implications for how we read other twentieth-century narratives of inherited violence.*

Both the empirical CARS rewrite above and this humanities opening perform recognizable rhetorical work — but the work is differently distributed.

* **Territory** is established not by a statistic but by a _literary moment_ : a specific sentence on a specific page of a specific novel. The territory-as-particular is a humanities convention; readers of literary criticism expect the field's territory to be made visible through close reading, not through population claims.
* **Niche** is named — but as an _interpretive miss_ rather than a literature gap: prior readings have not addressed the grammatical strangeness of Sethe's question. The move is recognizably Move 2, but its evidentiary character is different.
* **Contribution** is announced (_"This essay reads… to develop…"_) and is recognizably Move 3, though distributed across two sentences and gesturing at a broader implication rather than concentrating.
* **Outline** is absent. Many humanities articles, especially shorter ones, do not include a road-map paragraph. The argument's structure is meant to emerge through the unfolding analysis.

This is not a CARS introduction in the strict sense. But it performs CARS's _underlying work_ — territory, gap, contribution — in conventions adapted to a humanities tradition that reads texts closely and develops argument through extended interpretation rather than through declarative announcement.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: The Introduction — Create A Research Space
blocks.src:
The lesson: CARS is a checklist of rhetorical work that introductions must do, not a sentence-template. In empirical disciplines, the four moves often appear cleanly and in order. In humanities disciplines, the four moves often appear distributed, interleaved, or in different forms. A humanities writer who can name where their introduction performs Move 1, Move 2, and Move 3 has used the model — even when no reader would describe the introduction as "CARS-shaped." A humanities writer who cannot point at any of the moves has, like an empirical writer who cannot, written an introduction at risk.


### 4.5 The Six Moves Applied to Mira's Introduction

Mira and their advisor sit down on Tuesday morning to plan a new draft.

**Move 1 (genre/venue from Chapter 2).** They confirmed this last week: research article, public-administration journal. The three-paper read showed introductions in this venue running 600–900 words, with a CARS structure that places special emphasis on Move 2 (the gap) and includes a substantial Move 4 (the outline doubles as a navigational aid).

**Move 2 (structure).** They will write a CARS introduction. Move 1: 1–2 sentences. Move 2: 1–2 paragraphs (Mira's gap is at the _intersection_ of two strands and needs space to characterize both before locating the gap between them). Move 3: 2–4 sentences naming the contribution, including the specific finding. Move 4: 3–4 sentences mapping the paper's structure.

**Move 3 (calibration).** Public-administration journals tolerate moderate hedging in introductions. The contribution claim ("we show that…") can be made firmly. The gap claim must be defended, but Mira can be specific without being combative. Voice: first-person plural, since this is a single-author paper using the conventional academic "we."

**Move 4 (positioning through citation).** Mira maps citations into roles in the introduction: _Hallegatte and Tessler_ are the quantitative-modeling allies; _Kim and Brown_ are the case-study allies; the gap is between them, and no single antagonist needs to be named — the gap is structural, not adversarial.

**Move 5 (anticipated reviewer).** Predictable objections to the introduction: _"Is the gap real?"_ (Mira will defend it by characterizing what each of the two strands has and hasn't done.) _"Is your contribution specific enough?"_ (Mira will state the finding — _fiscal constraint shapes adaptation through a sequencing logic_ — directly in Move 3.) _"Is your case selection defensible?"_ (Mira will signal the case-selection logic in Move 3, with details to follow in §3.)

**Move 6 (AI).** Mira asks AI to read their first draft and identify which CARS moves are present, weakly performed, or missing. The AI returns: _Move 1 present but generic; Move 2 missing; Move 3 weak; Move 4 present but underspecified._ Mira accepts the diagnosis (consistent with what their advisor said) and rewrites.

Mira's second draft introduction is the Version B example from §4.1. Their advisor returns it on Wednesday with the comment: _"Now that's a paper. Send it out."_

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: The Introduction — Create A Research Space
blocks.src:
### 4.6 Templates and Examples

A few CARS-aligned sentence stems that can scaffold each move:

**Move 1 (Territory):**

* _"[Topic] has become central to [field], with [specific claim/statistic about importance]."_
* _"A substantial literature has examined [topic], using [methods] in [contexts]."_
* _"[Topic] has been the subject of growing attention since [event/decade], particularly in light of [development]."_

**Move 2 (Niche):**

* _"However, prior work has focused predominantly on [population/method/scale], with much less attention to [the gap]."_
* _"While [Strand A] has examined [aspect], and [Strand B] has examined [other aspect], the relationship between the two has remained unexplored."_
* _"It remains unclear whether [established finding] holds under [condition not yet tested]."_
* _"This assumption — that [common assumption] — has not been directly tested."_

**Move 3 (Occupy):**

* _"We address this gap by [specific contribution]."_
* _"We argue that [specific claim], drawing on [evidence/methods]."_
* _"This paper develops [framework/model] and applies it to [case], showing [finding]."_

**Move 4 (Outline):**

* _"Section 2 [does what argumentatively], focusing on [aspect]."_
* _"Sections 3 and 4 present [methods and findings]."_
* _"Section 5 discusses [implications], with particular attention to [extension]."_

These are scaffolds, not formulas. Once you have written a few CARS introductions deliberately, you stop needing the templates — but they are useful in the early stages.


### 4.7 Common Pitfalls

**The missing Move 2.** Already named several times. The single most common failure mode for graduate-student introductions. Diagnostic: can you point at one or two sentences that name _what specifically is missing in the literature_? If not, your Move 2 is missing. Fix: add it before submitting.

**The generic Move 1.** "Climate change is one of the greatest challenges of our time." "AI is transforming education." Generic openings signal lack of specific expertise. Fix: lead with a specific fact, statistic, or framing that tells the reader you know the field.

**The bait-and-switch contribution.** The introduction promises one contribution; the rest of the paper delivers another. Reviewers feel this even when they can't articulate it. Fix: write the introduction _last_ , or at least revise it after the methods and findings are written.

**The over-promised contribution.** The introduction claims a finding more sweeping than the data supports. The reviewer reads the introduction, then the results, and feels deceived. Fix: align the introduction's contribution claim with what the methods can actually deliver.

**The ten-page introduction.** Some writers (especially in the humanities) treat the introduction as a place to do all the work — extensive lit review, theory development, methodological reflection. In most empirical papers this is wrong: the introduction should be 600–1200 words and dense; the lit review and theory belong in their own sections. Fix: ruthlessly cut.

**The road-map-only introduction.** All Move 4, no Moves 1–3. The introduction tells you what's coming but not why. Fix: ensure the four moves are balanced, with Moves 2 and 3 carrying the most weight.

**The hidden contribution.** The contribution is named, but only halfway through the introduction or buried in a subordinate clause. Fix: state Move 3 prominently — usually as its own paragraph or as the lead sentence of one.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: The Introduction — Create A Research Space
blocks.src:
### 4.8 Scholar Profile: Greg Colomb and the Architecture of Academic Argument

Greg Colomb (1951–2011) was a writing scholar who, with Wayne Booth and Joseph Williams, co-authored _The Craft of Research_ — a book that has shaped how generations of graduate students think about academic argument. Colomb's contribution was to insist that academic introductions follow recognizable structures across disciplines. His framework, slightly different from but compatible with Swales's, identifies similar moves: _territory → gap → method → contribution._

A surprising fact: across genre-analysis studies of empirical academic introductions — including Swales's foundational corpus work and the Booth–Colomb–Williams analyses that built on it — the great majority of published introductions in empirical disciplines perform approximately these four moves, in roughly this order. The exact proportion depends on the corpus and the coding scheme; published estimates cluster around 80–95% in empirical fields, lower in pure humanities. The pattern is not specific to STEM; it appears across the social sciences, in much of history and economics, and in law. Disciplines that violate the pattern — pure philosophy, certain traditions in literary theory, theoretical mathematics — usually do so deliberately, and their introductions are still recognizably argumentative; the moves are distributed or replaced rather than absent.

The pedagogical implication is direct: if you teach the CARS / Booth-Colomb-Williams structure to graduate students explicitly, their introductions improve dramatically and quickly. This is one of the largest measurable effects in graduate writing pedagogy, and it has been replicated across writing-center programs at many institutions.

A second surprising fact: students whose first language is not English often _over-perform_ on the CARS structure once it has been taught explicitly, because they treat it as a pattern to learn (which it is) rather than a natural style they should already possess (which it isn't, even for native speakers). Native speakers sometimes resist the model on aesthetic grounds — _"this feels formulaic"_ — and consequently produce introductions that quietly violate it. The aesthetic is misplaced: every great academic essayist you admire is doing CARS, just smoothly.

Colomb's larger gift was the argument that academic writing is _teachable craft_ rather than mysterious talent. Every chapter of this book is in his lineage.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: The Introduction — Create A Research Space
blocks.src:
### 4.9 Reader's Manuscript Audit Prompt

Take an introduction from your current work-in-progress (an article draft, dissertation chapter intro, proposal abstract). Perform a CARS audit:

**Locate each move.** Mark in the margin where Move 1, Move 2, Move 3, and Move 4 appear. If you cannot locate one of them, write **MISSING** in the margin at the appropriate place.

**Diagnose.** Which move is the weakest? In most graduate drafts, Move 2 is the weakest. Sometimes Move 3 is too vague. Sometimes Move 1 is too generic.

**Rewrite the weakest move.** Don't try to rewrite the whole introduction. Pick the weakest move and rewrite that section, applying the templates from §4.6 and the diagnostics from §4.7.

**Compare.** Place the original and the rewritten move side by side, as we did with Versions A and B in §4.1. The contrast should be visible at a glance. If it isn't, the rewrite hasn't done enough work.

Save this rewrite. Together with the synthesis-vs-summary audit from Chapter 3, you now have two revised sections of your manuscript.


### 4.10 Exercises


#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What does CARS stand for, and what are its four moves?

Hint

The acronym is named in §4.3, and the moves are unpacked in §4.3 and the Definition box.

**Answer:** CARS stands for **Create A Research Space.** The four moves are: (1) Establish the territory — claim that the field of work is important, central, or active; (2) Establish the niche — identify a gap, problem, or unresolved tension in the literature; (3) Occupy the niche — state your contribution specifically; (4) Outline the structure of the paper.

**Q2.** What is "the missing Move 2 problem," and why is it the most common cause of rejected drafts?

**Answer:** The missing Move 2 problem is when a writer establishes the territory and states a contribution but skips the move that identifies the specific gap in the literature. It is the most common cause of rejected drafts because reviewers cannot answer the basic question _what is new about this paper?_ without Move 2 — the gap is what makes the contribution legible and necessary. Drafts without Move 2 read as competent but unmotivated, and reviewers reject them with comments like "novelty unclear."

**Q3.** Why does the chapter argue that the CARS model is a _checklist of work that must be done_ , not a paragraph-counting recipe?

**Answer:** Because in practice the four moves can be distributed and interleaved across paragraphs, and skilled writers vary the proportion and ordering of moves to suit the genre and venue. A CARS introduction can have one-sentence Move 1, three-paragraph Move 2, and a paragraph that combines Moves 3 and 4. What matters is that all four moves are _present and identifiable_ , not that they correspond to a fixed paragraph count.

**Q4.** Name three sub-moves a writer can use to perform Move 2 (Establish the Niche).

**Answer:** From §4.3: counter-claiming ("However, this assumption has not been tested empirically"); indicating a gap ("Mid-sized coastal cities have received much less attention"); question-raising ("It remains unclear whether the same mechanism operates at smaller scales"); continuing a tradition ("Building on this line of work, we extend…"). Any three of these are correct.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: The Introduction — Create A Research Space
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Take Mira's first-draft introduction from §4.1 (Version A). Identify which CARS moves are present, weakly performed, or missing. For each missing or weak move, write a one-paragraph diagnosis and a one-paragraph fix.

Hint

Move 1 is present but generic. Move 2 is essentially missing. Move 3 is present but vague. Move 4 is present but mechanical.

**Answer:** _Move 1 is present but generic_ ("Climate change is one of the most pressing challenges of our time"). Diagnosis: any introduction in any paper on any climate topic could open this way; the writer signals no specific expertise. Fix: replace with a specific framing that signals expertise, e.g., a statistic about coastal city populations or a characterization of recent policy debates. _Move 2 is missing._ Diagnosis: there is no statement of what is missing in the literature; the writer goes straight from territory to contribution. Fix: insert a paragraph characterizing the existing literature in two strands (quantitative and case-study) and locating the gap (mid-sized cities at the intersection). _Move 3 is present but vague_ ("we examine how three mid-sized coastal cities…"). Diagnosis: this names the topic but not the finding or argument. Fix: state the specific finding ("we show that fiscal constraint shapes adaptation through a sequencing logic"). _Move 4 is present but mechanical_ ("Section 2 reviews the literature; Section 3…"). Fix: have each section name not just its content but its argumentative work ("Section 2 develops this argument by reviewing prior work").

**Q2.** Take an introduction from one of your own papers — published, drafted, or submitted. Perform the CARS audit from §4.9: mark each move, identify the weakest, and rewrite the weakest move. Submit the original, the rewritten move, and a 100-word reflection on what changed.

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful response will (a) accurately identify which CARS moves are present and which are weak in the original, (b) produce a rewrite that is specifically targeted at the weakness, and (c) reflect on the change. The most useful reflections often note that the diagnostic is sharper than the writer expected — that they had assumed Move 2 was present, but on careful reading it was not. (Connection to Chapter 3's manuscript audit prompt: this is your second portfolio revision.)

**Q3.** Read the introduction of two papers in your field — one you found compelling, one you found dull. For each, mark the CARS moves and characterize how each move is performed. Write a 250-word comparison: where does the compelling paper's introduction do work the dull paper's introduction doesn't? (This connects to Chapter 1's diagnostic exercise on territory–gap–contribution.)

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A typical successful response will note that the compelling paper performs Move 2 specifically and at length, while the dull paper either skips Move 2 or does it generically. A second common finding: the compelling paper makes Move 3 (the contribution) bold and specific, while the dull paper hedges Move 3 into vagueness. A third: the compelling paper uses Move 4 to do positioning work (each section's argumentative function is named), while the dull paper uses Move 4 mechanically.

blocks.src:
**Sample Response (Mira's CARS diagnostic on two introductions):** _Compelling paper. Move 1: a specific statistic about the population exposed to coastal flooding (one sentence). Move 2: a one-paragraph characterization of two existing strands (megacity-quantitative and single-case-qualitative) and the precise gap between them (mid-sized cities are housed in neither). Move 3: an explicit claim ("we show that fiscal constraint reshapes adaptation through a sequencing logic") with the specific finding named. Move 4: three sentences naming each section's argumentative function. Dull paper. Move 1: "Climate change is one of the greatest challenges of our time" — a sentence that could open a thousand papers in the field. Move 2: missing; a single sentence ("more research on adaptation is needed") that gestures at a gap without specifying one. Move 3: "we examine how cities respond to climate change" — naming a topic but not a contribution. Move 4: "Section 2 reviews the literature; Section 3 describes the methods" — mechanical listing without argumentative function. The compelling paper's strength concentrates in Move 2's specificity and Move 3's claim. The dull paper's weakness concentrates in the same two places. CARS makes the diagnostic explicit; the diagnostic was always there._

**Q4.** Compose a CARS introduction for a paper you are _not_ currently writing — a hypothetical paper in your field. Pick a topic, sketch the gap, name the contribution, and write 250–400 words performing all four moves. The exercise teaches the moves at low stakes, before you apply them to a real draft.

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ The exercise's value is in the production. A successful response will perform all four moves, with Move 2 specific and Move 3 bold. The most common failure modes are: Move 2 too generic ("more research is needed"); Move 3 too vague ("we examine X"); Move 4 missing or mechanical. The exercise is worth doing twice if the first attempt has any of these failures.
