**Sample Response (a prose-as-table paragraph from Mira's earlier draft, redesigned):** _Original paragraph (95 words): "Across the three cities, infrastructure budgets grew differently. In Da Nang the infrastructure budget rose from 12.4% of municipal expenditure in 2018 to 18.7% in 2023, while in Cartagena it grew from 9.8% to 14.2% over the same period, and in Casablanca it rose from 11.1% to 16.3%. Operating expenditure as a share of total budget fell from 64% to 58% in Da Nang, from 71% to 67% in Cartagena, and from 68% to 62% in Casablanca. The pattern is consistent across the three cases."_ _Redesign (52 words of prose plus a 4-row table):_

> _Across all three cities, infrastructure spending grew faster than operating expenditure between 2018 and 2023 (Table 1). The pattern is consistent across regional contexts._
> 
> _Table 1. Budget composition, 2018 → 2023._
> 
> City | Infrastructure (% of budget) | Operating (% of budget)  
> ---|---|---  
> Da Nang | 12.4 → 18.7 | 64 → 58  
> Cartagena | 9.8 → 14.2 | 71 → 67  
> Casablanca | 11.1 → 16.3 | 68 → 62  
  
_Reflection: total word count drops from 95 to 52, but the more important change is _legibility_ — the reader can scan the table in three seconds and see the pattern, where the prose required reading three sentences and holding twelve numbers in working memory. The redesign also exposed an analytical weakness: the original paragraph implied uniformity ("the pattern is consistent") but the table makes visible that Cartagena's shift is smaller than the other two — a fact the prose smoothed away._

**Q3.** Read the results section of two papers in your field — one heavily quantitative, one heavily qualitative. For each, characterize the channel-assignment: what does the writer use tables for, figures for, and prose for? Where does the assignment work? Where could it be improved? Write 250 words.

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ Typical findings: heavily quantitative papers often use tables for descriptive statistics and regression coefficients, figures for marginal effects or interaction patterns, and prose for interpretation. Heavily qualitative papers often use prose for theme presentation, with tables (when present) used for participant characteristics or theme prevalence, and figures (rare) used for conceptual diagrams. Common improvement opportunities: quantitative papers often have figures that should be tables (when precise values matter) or tables that should be figures (when the headline finding is a pattern); qualitative papers often have over-long quotation paragraphs that could be compressed by tabulating themes.

**Q4.** Find a published null result in your field — ideally one that contradicts a previously published positive finding. How is the null result framed in the results section? Does the writer treat it as informative? Compare to a paper in your field that contains a positive result and consider: do the two results sections receive equal care? Write 250 words. (Connection to Chapter 5: pre-registration norms have begun to require null results to be reported as carefully as positive ones.)

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A typical successful response notes that null results in well-pre-registered work are increasingly reported with care equal to positive results (this is one of the post-replication-crisis reforms working). In non-pre-registered fields the asymmetry remains: null results often appear briefly, in supplementary tables, or are folded into discussion as caveats. The exercise teaches that the file-drawer problem is partly a writing problem — the technology of equal-care reporting exists; whether writers use it is a discipline question.

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The chapter argues that signposting interpretation belongs in results, theoretical interpretation in discussion. Some venues — notably _Nature_ , _Science_ , and high-impact disciplinary journals with combined Results-and-Discussion sections — collapse the distinction. Where is the discipline between sections valuable, and where is it bureaucratic? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** The discipline is valuable when it forces the writer to _show before telling_ — to present the evidence clearly before claiming what it means. It is bureaucratic when it forces artificial separation between findings that genuinely belong together (e.g., a result whose interpretation is part of how the result was generated). Combined Results-and-Discussion sections work best for short papers with single tightly integrated findings; they work less well for long mixed-methods papers where the reader needs to absorb the data before being asked to interpret it. The most useful diagnostic: even in combined sections, the _order_ matters — show first, interpret second, even within a paragraph. The discipline is partly about word order and partly about section labels; the word order matters more.

**Q2.** Tufte's principles were developed for static print. AI-era tools now generate interactive visualizations, animated explanations, and figure variants on demand. How might Tufte's principles need to evolve? Sketch your view in 250 words.

**Discussion:** Tufte's core principles (data-ink ratio, no chartjunk, comparison, honesty) translate well to interactive media. The principle of _small multiples_ — showing many panels of the same chart type for comparison — is enhanced by interactive media (the reader can flip through panels). The principle of _avoid chartjunk_ arguably tightens (interactive elements that don't communicate data are new chartjunk). New principles may emerge: _the static state must be informative_ (so that screenshots and prints carry the message); _interactivity must be discoverable_ (the reader shouldn't have to hunt for affordances); _animation must serve comparison_ (animated chart transitions can both clarify and confuse). The principles of clarity and honesty don't change; the surface area to apply them grows. (Connection forward to Chapter 14: AI-generated visualizations need the same Tufte audit as human-generated ones, often more.)

**Q3.** The chapter says that "the line between _signposting_ and _theoretical interpretation_ is subtle but learnable." Some critics argue this line is _artificial_ — that the choice of what to signpost is already an interpretive choice. How do you weigh the convention's value against the critic's point? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** Both views are right. The choice of what to signpost is interpretive (deciding to highlight the budget growth pattern over, say, the year-to-year variance is a choice that frames what the reader sees). But this kind of _low-level_ interpretation is unavoidable; even pure tables embed interpretive choices about what to include and how to organize. The convention is preserving a higher-level distinction: between _what the data shows_ (low-level interpretation that is also accountable to the data directly) and _what the data means_ (theoretical interpretation that requires the additional step of connecting findings to theory and prior work). The distinction is real, even if the line is fuzzy. Most reviewers can distinguish a results paragraph that drifts into discussion from one that doesn't, even if they can't articulate the exact rule. Skilled writers internalize the rule by reading a lot of well-written results sections in their venue and noticing where their drafts diverge. (Connection to Chapter 1's foreign-language thesis: the convention is one of the unwritten rules best learned by extensive reading.)


### Chapter Summary

The results section uses three channels — tables, figures, and prose — to communicate findings. Each channel is good at different work, and the skilled writer assigns each piece of evidence to the channel where it works best: tables for side-by-side comparison and precise values, figures for patterns and trends and skim-readers, prose for interpretation and signposting. The most common failure is _prose-as-table_ — paragraphs that report multiple numbers in sequence when a table would communicate them better.

This chapter laid out the channel assignments (§6.3), applied the six moves to Mira's results (§6.4), offered templates for opening, table introduction, figure introduction, quantitative reporting, qualitative reporting, and null-result reporting (§6.5), eight common pitfalls (§6.6), and the contribution of Edward Tufte to the design of tables and figures (§6.7). The manuscript audit prompt (§6.8) added a fourth revision to your portfolio: a prose-to-table redesign.

Results sit at the center of the empirical paper. The introduction (Chapter 4) promised a contribution; the methods (Chapter 5) made it replicable; the results show what was found; the discussion (Chapter 7) interprets what it means. The discipline of _signpost before interpret_ — showing what is in the data before claiming what it means — is the structural backbone of this chain.

In Chapter 7 we turn to the **discussion section** , where the interpretive work that results held back finally happens. Mira will write a discussion next, and we will see whether they can stay calibrated — neither overclaiming the meaning of their findings nor under-claiming what they have honestly shown.

> _Show what is in the data. Tell the reader what to look at. Save the meaning for later. Results discipline is the difference between a paper that earns its discussion and a paper that has skipped its results._

---

It is the fall of Mira's third year. The introduction (Chapter 4), methods (Chapter 5), and results (Chapter 6) are drafted and clean. Now Mira faces the section every experienced writer will tell them is the hardest in the paper.

The discussion.

A draft results section can be checked against the data: did you report what you found, accurately? A draft methods section can be checked against the procedure: did you describe what you did, replicably? A draft introduction can be checked against the literature: did you locate a gap, fairly? But a discussion section is checked against something fuzzier — _did you say the right things about what your work means?_ — and that is a question with no objective answer.

What makes the discussion hardest is that it is the section where reviewers exercise the most judgment. They expect interpretation, but they will mark you down for over-interpretation. They expect implications, but they will mark you down for over-reach. They expect engagement with prior work, but they will mark you down for failing to engage _the right_ prior work. The room for sophisticated work is large, and the room for self-inflicted wounds is also large. Mira's first draft will manage to step on several of these wounds before the chapter is over.

This chapter is about how to walk the discussion's narrow path. We will introduce the **hedging vocabulary matrix** that ESL writers especially benefit from, and we will meet Bruno Latour, the scholar who first wrote frankly about academic discussion sections as _negotiations_ rather than _summaries_.


### 7.1 Vignette: The First Draft and Its Quiet Overclaim

Mira's first-draft discussion opens as follows:

> _Our findings demonstrate that fiscal constraint is a fundamental driver of climate adaptation in mid-sized coastal cities. The results conclusively show that adaptation in such cities is structured by a sequencing logic in which short-term, visible interventions crowd out longer-horizon investments. This finding has profound implications for climate adaptation policy: international funding programs must shift from supporting megacities to supporting mid-sized cities, where the highest leverage exists._

Three sentences. Each one a problem.

_"Demonstrate that fiscal constraint is a fundamental driver"_ — Mira's data, recall, comes from three cities. Three. They have shown a pattern across three cases. Calling fiscal constraint _a fundamental driver_ generalizes far beyond what three cases can support.

_"Conclusively show"_ — three case studies do not conclusively show anything. Even three hundred cases would not justify "conclusively." The phrase signals overclaim.

_"Profound implications… international funding programs must shift"_ — the policy claim outruns the evidence. The data may _suggest_ that mid-sized cities are understudied; they do not establish that international funding should change.

When Mira's advisor reads this, the comment is gentler than it should be: _"Calibrate."_ Mira spends a week trying to figure out what that means.

This chapter answers it.

### 7.2 What Reviewers Look For in a Discussion

**Are the claims proportionate to the evidence?** This is the question reviewers ask most often, and the question discussions most often fail. Hedging is the answer.

**Are limitations engaged honestly?** A discussion that pretends to have no limitations gets marked down. A discussion that engages limitations and shows their implications for interpretation gets marked up.

**Are alternative explanations considered?** Is the writer interpretively monogamous (only their preferred interpretation is mentioned) or polygamous (alternatives are named and addressed)? Polygamy reads as scientific maturity.

**Is prior work engaged?** Where does this work sit in the conversation? What does it confirm, complicate, or extend? A discussion without prior-work engagement reads as solipsistic.

**Are implications calibrated?** Theoretical implications proportionate to the contribution; practical implications proportionate to the evidence. Not "this changes everything" but "these findings suggest that the assumption common in prior work — that X — needs to be re-examined under conditions Y."

**Is there an honest "what we don't know"?** Discussions that close with a future-work paragraph that names what _remains_ uncertain (rather than a triumphalist summary) read as more credible.

A discussion that satisfies these six criteria is a discussion that survives review. A discussion that fails any of them — and especially the first, the proportionality of claim to evidence — is at risk.


### 7.3 The Layers of a Discussion

A well-built discussion has a layered structure. The layers do not need to map to subsections; they describe the _logical work_ the discussion does. The layers are:


#### Layer 1 — Restate the contribution

Open with a brief restatement of the contribution claim. Not a summary of the results, but a statement of what the paper has shown. _"This paper has shown that fiscal constraint shapes adaptation in mid-sized coastal cities through a sequencing logic in which short-term, visible interventions crowd out longer-horizon investments."_

This opener does several jobs at once. It tells the reader what the discussion will be about. It anchors the rest of the discussion to the specific claim of the paper. And it sets the calibration: a sentence here that overclaims will infect every claim that follows.


#### Layer 2 — Engage prior work

Where do the findings sit relative to the prior literature? Confirming? Complicating? Extending? Contradicting? Each kind of engagement requires different language and different supporting moves.

_Confirming:_ "Our results are consistent with [prior work], which found [X]. We extend that finding to [new context/scale]."

_Complicating:_ "Whereas prior work has emphasized [factor A], our findings suggest that [factor B] is also operative — and that the two factors interact in ways prior single-factor analyses could not detect."

_Contradicting:_ "Our findings are inconsistent with [prior work], which reported [X]. The discrepancy may reflect [methodological difference / scope difference / boundary condition]."

The convention is to engage prior work specifically (named authors, named claims) rather than vaguely (_"some scholars have argued"_). The conversation metaphor matters here: in academic discussion sections, you are speaking _to_ people, not just about them.

#### Layer 3 — Address limitations

Every empirical paper has limitations. Discussion sections that pretend otherwise look amateur and trigger reviewer suspicion. The skilled limitations paragraph names the most consequential limits, says briefly how they affect interpretation, and indicates what kind of evidence would resolve them.

_"Our analysis is limited in three ways. First, the three cases were selected for diversity but cannot be claimed to be representative of mid-sized coastal cities globally; the sequencing logic we identify may operate differently in cities outside the regional contexts we examined. Second, our budget data span four years; longer time horizons would clarify whether sequencing patterns persist or attenuate. Third, our interview sample, while purposive, did not include private-sector actors who participate in adaptation financing in some of our cases. Each of these limits indicates a direction for future work."_

Note what this paragraph does not do: it does not call the limitations _minor_ ; it does not promise that future work _will resolve_ them; it does not minimize. Honest limitations land harder than apologetic ones, because honest writers are easier to trust on the rest of the discussion.


#### Layer 4 — Discuss alternative explanations

What other explanations could account for the findings? Are they ruled out, or are they live? Naming alternatives — and engaging them seriously — is one of the highest-leverage moves in a discussion. It demonstrates that the writer has thought about counter-interpretations and chosen the preferred one for reasons.

_"An alternative interpretation of our findings is that the sequencing logic we observe reflects not fiscal constraint but local political dynamics — short-term interventions are visible to voters and serve electoral incentives. We considered this interpretation seriously and find it partly compatible with our data: in two of three cases, electoral pressure was indeed a contributing factor. However, the third case (Casablanca) shows the sequencing logic in the absence of electoral pressure, suggesting that fiscal constraint operates as an independent driver. The two factors likely interact, and disentangling them is a question for future work."_

This paragraph is doing serious analytical work. It names the alternative; engages it; shows where it has purchase and where it doesn't; concludes with calibrated language.

#### Layer 5 — Implications

Theoretical, practical, policy. Calibrated to the evidence. Specific where possible.

_Theoretical implications:_ what the findings mean for theory or for the analytical framework. _"These findings extend the fiscal-constraint literature on developmental policy to the climate-adaptation domain and suggest that the sequencing dynamics that frame fiscal-constraint debates in other policy areas have analogues in adaptation."_

_Practical implications:_ what the findings mean for practitioners, with care to scale claims to evidence. _"For municipal officials in similarly constrained contexts, our findings suggest that the political pressure toward visible short-term interventions is real but that this pressure can be offset by..."_

_Policy implications:_ what the findings mean for the broader policy conversation. _"For international funding agencies, our findings raise questions about the fit between megacity-targeted programs and mid-sized city needs — questions the present analysis cannot answer but can productively pose."_

Note the calibration. _"Suggest"_ and _"raise questions"_ — not _"prove"_ and _"require."_ Each implication paragraph is an opportunity to overclaim; each one should be drafted carefully, then read back skeptically.


#### Layer 6 — Close with future work and what remains uncertain

The strongest discussions end not with a triumphalist summary but with a statement of what remains uncertain and what the next study would need to do. This convention has two functions: it lowers the reader's resistance (you have shown yourself to be calibrated) and it actively contributes to the field by pointing toward productive next steps.


#### Definition: Hedging

In academic writing, **hedging** is the use of language that calibrates a claim to the strength of the evidence supporting it — typically by softening or qualifying assertions about causation, generality, or certainty.

In plain language: hedging is how you say "I'm fairly sure" instead of "I'm sure," "in this sample" instead of "in general," "may suggest" instead of "proves." Hedging is not equivocation. It is precision about epistemic status. Skilled academic writers hedge constantly — and the strength of their hedging is finely calibrated to the strength of their evidence.

To readers outside the academy, hedged prose can sound timid. To readers inside the academy, _unhedged_ prose sounds amateurish and overconfident. The discussion section is the most hedging-intensive part of a paper because it is where claims about meaning are made — and meaning claims are the most epistemically vulnerable.


#### Common Misconception

A common misconception is that hedging is a stylistic flourish — that you can write a discussion in confident prose and then insert _"may"_ and _"suggest"_ before submission. In practice, hedging is structural. The right hedging is built into the _argumentative shape_ of the paragraph, not pasted on after. A paragraph that builds toward an overclaim and then softens the overclaim with _"may"_ still reads as overclaim. A paragraph whose structure inherently makes a calibrated claim reads as calibrated.

This is why the most-cited discussions in any field are written by senior scholars who have internalized the calibration so deeply that they don't notice they're doing it. The patterns are learnable, but they are learned by writing many discussions and being marked up many times.

### 7.4 The Hedging Vocabulary Matrix

Here is a concrete matrix that ESL writers especially have found useful. The matrix maps confidence levels to the verbs and adverbs that fit them.

Confidence Level | Hedging Verbs | Hedging Adverbs / Phrases | Use When  
---|---|---|---  
**Established (consensus)** | _demonstrate, show, establish, document_ | (none needed) | Findings have been replicated across many studies in the field  
**Strong support (your study)** | _indicate, suggest, point to_ | _clearly, consistently_ | Your data robustly support the claim within scope  
**Reasonable support** | _suggest, appear to, are consistent with, may suggest_ | _likely, in this context, in our sample_ | Your data lean this way but with caveats  
**Speculative** | _could, might, may, is conceivable that_ | _tentatively, provisionally, in principle_ | Hypotheses, theoretical implications, future-work suggestions  
**Reporting others' speculation** | _have proposed, argue for, hypothesize, contend_ | _(attribution to specific authors)_ | Other authors' contested or speculative claims  
  
Pair this with the **what NOT to use** list:

* _**prove, proves, proven**_ — almost never appropriate in empirical writing. Even in mathematics, the social-science register avoids it.
* _**definitely, absolutely, clearly**_ (when used as standalone confidence markers) — read as overclaim.
* _**most experts agree, it is well-known that**_ — vague gestures toward consensus that often signal weak evidence; cite specifically or omit.
* _**revolutionary, paradigm-shifting, fundamental**_ — almost always reads as overclaim, regardless of how good the work is.

ESL writers often arrive at the discussion having been taught (correctly, for non-academic English) that confident, active, declarative writing is good. The matrix is a translation key: in academic English, confidence is not a stylistic virtue; _calibrated_ confidence is. Skilled academic writers use the entire matrix in the same paragraph, sometimes the same sentence: _"Our results indicate that fiscal constraint may shape adaptation in mid-sized cities, although the magnitude of the effect could vary substantially across regional contexts."_ The verbs _indicate_ , _may shape_ , and _could vary_ span three confidence levels in one sentence.

A drill: take a discussion paragraph from your work and underline every verb of claim. Map each verb to a row of the matrix. Are the verbs proportionate to the evidence behind them? Where one verb claims more than the evidence supports, swap for a verb one row down. Do the reverse where the discussion is too weak for the evidence behind it.

#### Hedging in Interpretive Disciplines

The matrix above is calibrated to empirical writing — fields where claims are evaluated against evidence and the hedging language tracks the strength of the evidence-claim fit. In interpretive disciplines (philosophy, literary criticism, theoretical history, much of cultural anthropology, parts of theology, and large parts of legal scholarship), the matrix applies with adjustments.

The first adjustment: in interpretive writing, "evidence" often means _textual or conceptual support_ rather than empirical data. The verb _suggest_ hedges in roughly the same way as in empirical writing, but its referent is different — _"the close reading suggests"_ rather than _"the regression suggests."_ Skilled interpretive writers calibrate their verbs to the strength of their textual or conceptual case, not to the strength of a statistical fit.

The second adjustment: interpretive writing makes _argumentative_ rather than _evidential_ claims, and the hedging vocabulary shifts accordingly. Verbs like _argue, contend, propose, maintain, hold_ are ordinary in philosophy and literary criticism, where they would read as overconfident in empirical writing. The reason is that interpretive writers are not making claims that data could falsify; they are making claims that other readings of the text or concept did not adequately develop. The standard for "calibrated confidence" is the strength of the argument's purchase on the textual or conceptual material, not the strength of its empirical support.

The third adjustment: hedges that read as appropriate in empirical writing can read as evasive in interpretive writing. Phrases like _"may suggest that some readers might find that…"_ — modeled on empirical hedging — read as ducking the interpretive commitment. Interpretive writers are expected to _make_ readings, not merely propose them. Skilled interpretive writers commit to readings while acknowledging the alternative readings they are arguing past.

The fourth adjustment: the _"what NOT to use"_ list shifts. _"Prove"_ is still inappropriate, but _"demonstrate"_ — in the sense of _demonstrate by argument_ — is acceptable in philosophy and parts of literary criticism. _"Revolutionary"_ and _"paradigm-shifting"_ still overclaim. _"It is well known"_ is still vague. But _"clearly"_ and _"obviously"_ — which empirical writing avoids as overclaim markers — sometimes appear in interpretive writing when the writer is signaling that the next claim follows transparently from the analysis.

A practical heuristic for interpretive writers: read the matrix as _advice for empirical-style claims you may be making_ , even within an interpretive paper. When you cite an empirical fact inside a literary or philosophical article, the matrix's verbs apply. When you make an interpretive argument about how a text or concept functions, the matrix's verbs apply less directly — and reviewers from the interpretive tradition will calibrate to a different standard.

The deepest point: hedging is _calibration of claim to support_ , and what counts as support varies by discipline. The matrix is a tool, not a fixed grammar. ESL writers in interpretive disciplines benefit from the matrix's habit of paying attention to verb choice, even where the specific entries need adjustment for the tradition they write within.

A brief illustration. Consider three sentences that could open a discussion section in three different traditions, all making the same general kind of claim — that a prior reading or model is incomplete:

> _(Empirical, social science):_ "Our results suggest that the megacity-focused literature has overestimated the generality of its findings; the magnitude of the divergence at mid-sized scales remains to be characterized."
> 
> _(Literary criticism):_ "I argue that prior readings of Sethe's question have not adequately attended to its grammatical strangeness; the slippage between tense and addressee, I contend, is doing analytical work the existing readings miss."
> 
> _(Philosophy):_ "I propose that the standard internalist account of justification cannot handle the testimony cases described in §3, and I maintain that an externalist supplementation is required to preserve the account's plausibility."

All three perform Move 5 of the six (anticipating the reviewer / interlocutor) by acknowledging that they are arguing past prior work. But the verbs differ in calibrated ways. The empirical sentence uses _suggest_ (one row down from _demonstrate_) and _remains to be characterized_ (deferring to future evidence). The literary sentence uses _argue_ and _contend_ (committal verbs that empirical writing would consider over-claim) because the standard for support in literary criticism is the strength of the close reading, and a hedged literary claim ("Sethe's question may possibly suggest…") would read as evasive. The philosophy sentence uses _propose_ (introducing a position) and _maintain_ (defending it) — both standard in philosophical writing, both stronger than empirical hedges, both calibrated to the genre's expectation that the writer commit to a position while acknowledging its argumentative status. Reviewers in each tradition calibrate to a different default; readers crossing traditions need to read for the calibration before mapping the matrix.

### 7.5 The Six Moves Applied to Mira's Discussion

**Move 1 (genre/venue).** Same. Discussion sections in this venue typically run 1,500–2,500 words, with substantial engagement of prior work, an explicit limitations subsection, and a closing future-work paragraph.

**Move 2 (structure).** Mira drafts the discussion in five subsections matching the layers in §7.3: _7.1 Summary of contribution. 7.2 Relation to prior work. 7.3 Limitations. 7.4 Alternative explanations. 7.5 Implications and future work._ In their venue, this layered structure is conventional.

**Move 3 (calibration).** This is where the discussion lives or dies. Mira applies the hedging matrix. The verb in their opening sentence shifts from _demonstrate_ to _suggest_. The phrase _conclusively show_ is deleted entirely. The policy claim _"international funding programs must shift"_ becomes _"these findings raise questions about the fit between megacity-targeted programs and mid-sized city needs."_

**Move 4 (positioning).** Mira engages prior work specifically. The Hallegatte (2013) and Tessler et al. (2015) work that anchored the introduction's territory is now revisited as work this paper _complicates_ — by showing that megacity findings may not transfer. The case-study work that anchored the introduction's other strand is revisited as work this paper _extends_ — to a comparative scale. Citations are rhetorical moves, not bibliography ornaments.

**Move 5 (anticipated reviewer).** Predictable discussion objections: _"You're generalizing from three cases; the limitations paragraph needs to engage this seriously."_ Mira's revised limitations paragraph names case-selection limits explicitly. _"You haven't ruled out alternative explanations."_ Mira adds the political-dynamics alternative interpretation paragraph (§7.3 Layer 4). _"Your policy implications outrun your data."_ Mira softens implications and adds the _"raises questions"_ hedging.

**Move 6 (AI).** Mira uses AI to: identify every verb of claim and map it to the hedging matrix; flag implications that overrun the data; suggest alternative interpretations the writer hadn't considered. They do _not_ use AI to _make_ claims, only to audit them.

The rewritten discussion is 2,200 words. It opens with a calibrated contribution statement, engages prior work specifically across two subsections, contains a substantial limitations paragraph, takes seriously two alternative explanations, and closes with a future-work paragraph naming three uncertainties the present study cannot resolve.

### 7.6 Templates and Examples

**Opening a discussion (Layer 1):**

> _"This paper has [argued / shown / examined] [contribution claim]. We now [discuss / develop] the implications of these findings for [theoretical question] and [practical question], engage their relation to prior work, and consider their limitations and the directions they suggest for future research."_

**Engaging prior work (Layer 2 — confirming):**

> _"These findings are consistent with [prior work] (Citation), which reported [X] in [context]. The present study extends that finding to [new context/scale/method], lending additional support to the claim that [generalization]."_

**Engaging prior work (Layer 2 — complicating):**

> _"Whereas prior work has emphasized [Factor A] (Citations), our findings suggest that [Factor B] also plays a substantial role. The two factors are not independent — [Citations] have suggested possible interactions — but the present study is among the first to characterize the interaction at [scale / context]."_

**Limitations paragraph (Layer 3):**

> _"Several limitations of the present analysis should be noted. First, [limit, with implication for interpretation]. Second, [limit]. Third, [limit]. None of these limits, in our view, undermines the central finding that [contribution], but each indicates a direction for productive future work."_

**Alternative-explanation paragraph (Layer 4):**

> _"An alternative interpretation of these findings is [alternative]. We considered this interpretation seriously. [Evidence consistent with alternative; evidence inconsistent.] On balance, our reading is that [preferred interpretation] is more strongly supported, although [alternative] likely contributes [in scope]."_

**Implications paragraph (Layer 5):**

> _"Theoretically, these findings [extend / refine / challenge] the [framework]. [Specific implication.] Practically, our results suggest [calibrated practical claim]. For [policy actor], the findings raise the question of [calibrated policy claim] — a question the present study cannot answer but can productively pose."_

**Future work / what remains uncertain (Layer 6):**

> _"Several questions remain unresolved. [Question 1.] [Question 2.] [Question 3.] We hope the present analysis serves not as a closing of these questions but as a productive opening of them."_

These templates scaffold a layered discussion. Use them to structure a first draft; revise into your own voice in the second draft.

### 7.7 Common Pitfalls

**The summary discussion.** The discussion just restates the results section. No engagement with prior work, no limitations, no implications. Fix: each layer is a different kind of work; do them all.

**The over-confident discussion.** Verbs of claim outrun evidence. _"Demonstrate," "establish," "prove."_ Fix: apply the hedging matrix; downgrade verbs to fit evidence.

**The interpretively monogamous discussion.** Only the preferred interpretation is named. Reviewers will ask _"what about alternative X?"_ and you should already have answered. Fix: name two alternatives; engage at least one seriously.

**The decorative limitations.** _"Our sample is small. Future research is needed."_ Generic, unactionable, self-protective. Fix: name limits specifically and tie each to its implication for interpretation.

**The drift into Results 2.0.** The discussion reports findings that should have been in results. The reverse — interpreting in results — is also a common error (Chapter 6). Fix: discipline the section to interpret only; cite results sections by number rather than restating values.

**The triumphalist close.** The discussion ends with _"This study has fundamentally advanced understanding of X."_ Reviewers wince. Fix: close with future work and what remains uncertain.

**The unmotivated implications.** Practical or policy implications that don't follow from the findings. Fix: each implication should be traceable to a specific finding or pattern.

**The buried prior work.** Prior work is engaged briefly and superficially, with citations doing decoration rather than rhetorical work. Fix: spend at least one paragraph in serious engagement with the most relevant prior work.

### 7.8 Scholar Profile: Bruno Latour and Discussions as Negotiations

Bruno Latour (1947–2022) was a French sociologist and philosopher of science whose work on the rhetoric of scientific writing has shaped how generations of scholars understand academic discussions. His 1987 book _Science in Action_ opens with a question: how does a fact become a fact?

Latour's answer, developed across hundreds of pages, is: through a long process of social and rhetorical work, much of which is visible in academic writing if you know how to read it. The discussion section is one of the most concentrated sites of this work. In a discussion, the writer is not merely reporting — they are _negotiating_. They are negotiating with prior literature (which findings to confirm, complicate, or contradict). They are negotiating with reviewers (which alternative explanations to take seriously, which to dismiss). They are negotiating with future readers (which interpretations to make available for citation, which to leave aside).

A surprising fact, central to Latour's argument: discussions are _bargains over what counts as the contribution_. The writer offers a version of what their findings mean; reviewers and future citers will accept some version of that, modify others, and contest still others. The version that survives is not necessarily the version the writer intended. Skilled writers know this — they shape their discussions to make the survivable version of their contribution clear and defensible.

A second surprising fact: the language of hedging is, on Latour's reading, _not_ an admission of uncertainty so much as a _strategic positioning move_. By hedging, the writer leaves room for the finding to be _modified_ by future work without being _refuted_. Strong unhedged claims invite refutation; calibrated claims invite extension. Skilled academic writers, Latour observed, are master hedgers — and the hedging is part of how they get cited.

A third fact, perhaps the most important for graduate students: Latour's analysis can be unsettling because it shows academic writing as more political than the official rhetoric admits. But the analytical move is not cynical. It is realistic. Academic writing operates within a social system, and skilled participants understand the system without being captured by it. The book you are reading is partly Latour's intellectual descendant: the conventions exist for reasons, are partly performative, and are still worth learning to use well.

For graduate writers entering 2026, Latour's lesson is direct: your discussion is a negotiation, not a report. Treat it as such. Calibrate your claims, anticipate the alternatives, engage prior work specifically, and remember that what you write will be cited and modified by readers you do not yet know — and the version of your contribution that survives is the one your prose makes durable.

### 7.9 Reader's Manuscript Audit Prompt

Take the discussion section of your current manuscript. Perform the following audit:

**Identify three places your discussion overclaims.** Read the discussion looking specifically for verbs of claim that outrun evidence and for implications that go beyond what your data support. The hedging matrix in §7.4 is your guide.

For each overclaim, write the corrected version. Not just a softer phrasing — a phrasing that is _calibrated_ to the actual evidence. Often the rewrite is one or two words (a verb swap, an added scope phrase). Sometimes the rewrite is structural (the paragraph's argumentative shape was leading toward overclaim, and only structural revision helps).

**Identify one place your discussion underclaims.** Sometimes the opposite problem appears: the writer has hedged so far that the contribution sounds tentative beyond what the evidence justifies. If you find such a place, rewrite to be more direct.

**Identify one alternative explanation you have not engaged.** What is an interpretation of your findings that someone in your field might offer that you have not addressed? Draft a paragraph that names this alternative, engages it, and concludes with calibrated language about why your preferred interpretation is supported.

This is your fifth manuscript revision. The portfolio is now: synthesis-vs-summary audit (Ch.3), CARS introduction rewrite (Ch.4), methods replication test (Ch.5), prose-to-table redesign (Ch.6), and now the discussion calibration audit.


### 7.10 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Name the six layers of a well-built discussion section.

Hint

The layers are unpacked across §7.3.

**Answer:** (1) Restate the contribution; (2) Engage prior work (confirming, complicating, contradicting); (3) Address limitations; (4) Discuss alternative explanations; (5) Implications (theoretical, practical, policy); (6) Close with future work and what remains uncertain.

**Q2.** What is _hedging_ , as the chapter has defined it, and why does the chapter call it _structural_ rather than stylistic?

**Answer:** Hedging is the use of language that calibrates a claim to the strength of the evidence supporting it — typically by softening or qualifying assertions about causation, generality, or certainty. The chapter calls it structural rather than stylistic because the right hedging is built into the _argumentative shape_ of a paragraph, not pasted on at the end. A paragraph that builds toward an overclaim and softens it with "may" still reads as overclaim; calibrated paragraphs make calibrated claims throughout their structure.

**Q3.** Why does the chapter argue that engaging _alternative explanations_ is one of the highest-leverage moves in a discussion?

**Answer:** Because naming alternatives — and engaging them seriously — demonstrates that the writer has thought about counter-interpretations and chosen the preferred one for reasons. Reviewers and future readers can spot interpretively monogamous discussions (where only the preferred interpretation is named) and discount them. Discussions that engage alternatives read as scientifically mature and increase the credibility of the preferred interpretation.

**Q4.** What does Bruno Latour mean when he says discussions are "negotiations rather than summaries"?

**Answer:** That a discussion is not a neutral report of what findings mean; it is an active negotiation with prior literature, reviewers, and future readers over what the findings will count as. The writer offers a version of the contribution; readers will accept some version, modify others, and contest still others. Skilled writers shape their discussions to make the _survivable version_ of their contribution clear and defensible — and hedging is part of how they leave room for findings to be extended without being refuted.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Take Mira's first-draft discussion opening from §7.1 (the three-sentence overclaim). Rewrite each sentence so that the claims are calibrated to the evidence (three case studies). Use the hedging vocabulary matrix from §7.4.

Hint

For each sentence, ask: which row of the matrix does the evidence support? Then rewrite using verbs and phrases from that row.

**Answer:** A successful rewrite might read: _"Our findings suggest that fiscal constraint shapes climate adaptation in mid-sized coastal cities. Across our three cases, adaptation was structured by a sequencing logic in which short-term, visible interventions appeared to crowd out longer-horizon investments. These findings raise questions about the fit between megacity-targeted international funding programs and the needs of mid-sized cities, though the present analysis cannot directly evaluate funding policy."_ Changes: _demonstrate_ → _suggest_ ; _conclusively show_ → _appeared to_ with scope phrase _across our three cases_ ; _profound implications, must shift_ → _raise questions_ with explicit scope-limiting clause.

**Q2.** Take a discussion section from a paper of your own. Apply the hedging-matrix audit: underline every verb of claim, map each to a row of the matrix, and identify three places where the verb is one row higher than the evidence supports. Rewrite those three places. Submit the original, the rewrites, and a 100-word reflection.

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful response will (a) accurately identify three overclaiming verbs, (b) produce rewrites that swap to more proportionate language, and (c) reflect on the change. The most useful reflections often note that the rewrites _strengthen_ the discussion in a paradoxical way — calibrated claims are more credible than overclaims and more useful for future readers and citers (Latour's point in §7.8).

**Sample Response (three overclaiming verbs from Mira's earlier discussion draft, with rewrites):** _(1) Original: "Our findings prove that fiscal constraint determines adaptation choices." Diagnosis: "prove" claims certainty no empirical study can deliver; "determines" implies single-cause sufficiency that three cases cannot establish. Rewrite: "Our findings suggest that fiscal constraint shapes adaptation choices through a sequencing logic, with the magnitude of the effect varying across cases." (2) Original: "These results conclusively establish that megacity-focused programs fail in mid-sized contexts." Diagnosis: "conclusively establish" overclaims; "fail" is binary where the evidence supports a more graduated claim. Rewrite: "These results indicate that megacity-focused programs transfer poorly to mid-sized contexts, though the boundary conditions of this finding warrant further investigation." (3) Original: "International funding agencies must redirect resources toward mid-sized cities." Diagnosis: "must" carries policy authority the analysis cannot underwrite; the leap from finding to policy directive is unhedged. Rewrite: "Our findings raise questions about the fit between megacity-targeted funding and mid-sized city needs — questions that the present analysis cannot resolve but can productively pose." Reflection: the rewrites are not weaker. The original ("prove… determines… must") would be cited skeptically; the rewrites would be cited as careful work. The discussion's authority comes from calibration, not from confidence._

**Q3.** Read the discussion section of a paper in your field and identify the _alternative explanations_ the writer engages. How are they engaged — seriously, briefly, or dismissively? What additional alternative could the writer have engaged? Write a 250-word commentary.

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A typical successful response notes that strong discussions engage alternatives substantively — naming, evaluating, and concluding with calibration; weaker discussions name alternatives only to dismiss them in a sentence ("we cannot, of course, rule out X"). The exercise teaches the diagnostic eye: skilled engagement of alternatives is rare and signals careful authorship. (Connection to Chapter 4: the alternative engagement should be foreshadowed in the introduction's anticipated-reviewer move and developed in the discussion.)

**Q4.** Pick a finding from your own research. Draft a discussion paragraph that performs _all six layers_ — restate, engage prior work, address limitations, engage one alternative, state implications, name what remains uncertain — in a single paragraph of 200–300 words. The exercise teaches compression of the layered structure.

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful response will perform every layer in compressed form. Example structure: sentence 1 — restate contribution; sentence 2 — relation to prior work; sentence 3 — limitations; sentence 4 — alternative explanation engaged; sentence 5 — implication; sentence 6 — what remains uncertain. The exercise teaches that the layers are work that must be done; they don't necessarily require dedicated subsections. Many strong discussions are just six well-built paragraphs, each performing one layer.

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The chapter argues that hedging is structural — built into the argumentative shape of a paragraph, not pasted on. Some critics argue that excessive hedging leads to academic writing that is dull, over-cautious, and resistant to bold claims. Where is the line between calibrated hedging and excessive hedging? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** Both positions have merit. Calibrated hedging is genuinely valuable: it allows future readers to extend findings rather than refute them; it protects readers from overclaim; it reflects honest uncertainty. Excessive hedging is also real: a discussion in which every claim is qualified into vagueness fails to make the contribution legible. The line: hedge the _claim about meaning_ , not the _claim about findings_. "Our findings show X" can be direct; "X means Y for the field" should be hedged. The other diagnostic: hedge what is genuinely uncertain; do not hedge what is clearly established. A good discussion paragraph often makes one direct claim (about findings) and several hedged claims (about meaning). The hedging matrix is the tool: use the entire matrix, including its _Established / Strong support_ rows, when the evidence justifies it. (Connection to Chapter 1's foreign-language thesis: this calibration is one of the conventions native speakers absorb by reading, and explicit teaching of the matrix accelerates it for everyone.)

**Q2.** Latour's reading of academic writing as _negotiation_ — and discussions as _bargains over what counts as the contribution_ — can sound cynical. Some readers worry it implies academic writing is just rhetoric, not science. How should we hold Latour's analytical insight together with the genuine epistemic ambitions of academic writing? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** Latour's insight is descriptive, not prescriptive. He is observing that academic writing involves rhetorical work; he is not arguing that the rhetoric is divorced from epistemics. The most useful synthesis: academic writing is _both_ a record of empirical work and a negotiation over how that work will count. The rhetoric matters because the social system through which findings become consensus is rhetorical; the epistemics matter because the rhetoric is constrained by what the data can support and what reviewers will accept. Skilled academic writers do not see these as in tension — they see them as joint requirements. The cynical reading ("it's all rhetoric") and the naive reading ("it's all epistemics") are both incomplete. (Connection to Chapter 17: this synthesis becomes especially urgent in the AI era, where the rhetorical work can be automated but the epistemic work cannot.)

**Q3.** AI tools can generate discussion sections at speed. They can match conventions of hedging, prior-work engagement, and limitations. But they cannot, by definition, _understand_ what a finding means or what alternatives are most live. Where does this leave AI-assisted discussion writing? What is safe, and what is dangerous? Sketch your view in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** AI is genuinely useful for discussion-section _audit_ — applying the hedging matrix, identifying overclaim, flagging missing layers, suggesting alternative interpretations the writer can then evaluate. AI is dangerous for discussion-section _generation_ — producing whole discussions whose claims, prior-work engagements, and alternative explanations are plausible-looking but not specifically verified. The gap is exactly the difference between _plausible_ and _specifically true_ in a paper's contribution. A discussion is the writer's strongest interpretive bet about what their findings mean; outsourcing that bet to a tool that does not understand the findings produces text that reads well and is hollow. Safe uses: hedge auditing, alternative-explanation brainstorming (as a check against the writer's own interpretive monogamy), structure checking. Dangerous uses: full generation; prior-work engagement (where AI hallucinates citations); implications writing (where AI produces generic-sounding claims that may not connect to the specific evidence). The bright line: the writer must own every claim about meaning. (Connection forward to Chapter 14 and Chapter 17: this is one of the highest-stakes places where AI use must be carefully bounded.)

The discussion section is the hardest section in an empirical paper, because it is judged on calibration rather than correctness. The single most consequential failure mode is **overclaim** — verbs and phrases that outrun the evidence — and the single most useful tool for fixing it is the **hedging vocabulary matrix** from §7.4.

This chapter laid out the layers (§7.3), the hedging matrix (§7.4), the application of the six moves to Mira's discussion (§7.5), templates for each layer (§7.6), eight common pitfalls (§7.7), and the contribution of Bruno Latour's analysis of academic writing as negotiation (§7.8). It is the spring of Mira's third year. The full paper from Chapters 4 through 7 — introduction, methods, results, discussion — is drafted, calibrated, polished. Mira has spent four months on roughly 8,500 words of careful prose. Their advisor reads the paper, suggests minor revisions, and finally says: _"Now do the abstract. Two hundred words. Submit by Friday."_

Mira sits down on Wednesday afternoon and tries to compress their paper into 200 words.

It is the hardest writing task they have ever attempted.

The first draft runs to 380 words. Cutting it to 320 takes an hour. Cutting from 320 to 250 takes another hour. Cutting from 250 to 200 takes the rest of the afternoon, the evening, and most of Thursday morning. By Thursday afternoon Mira has 198 words, and they are not sure the abstract is good. They are sure it is short.

Their advisor reads it Thursday evening: _"Better. But the contribution is buried in sentence five. It needs to be in sentence two. And the methods sentence is too long. Try again."_

Mira does. By Friday morning they have an abstract that is 196 words and well-structured. They submit. The conference accepts the paper.

A surprising fact, attributed to Helen Sword: a typical academic abstract is read approximately 100 times more often than the full paper it summarizes. The effort-per-reader ratio inverts dramatically — most readers will only ever see the abstract, and the abstract will determine whether they cite, share, or pursue the work. The abstract is not a summary; it is a _miniature paper_ that has to do all the work the full paper does, in 200–300 words.

This chapter is about how to write that miniature paper.

### 8.1 Vignette: The Buried Contribution

Here is Mira's first real try at the abstract — the one their advisor sent back as "needs work":

> _"This paper examines climate adaptation policy in mid-sized coastal cities. Climate change poses an increasing threat to coastal regions, and adaptation has become a central concern for policymakers worldwide. Most prior research has focused on either large global samples of megacities or on single-city case studies, leaving a substantial gap in our understanding of how mid-sized cities navigate adaptation. We address this gap through a comparative case study of three mid-sized coastal cities: Da Nang in Vietnam, Cartagena in Colombia, and Casablanca in Morocco. Drawing on policy document analysis, semi-structured interviews with 24 city officials, and four years of municipal budget data, we identify a pattern we term 'fiscal sequencing,' in which short-term, visible adaptation interventions consistently crowd out longer-horizon investments. The pattern was observed across all three cases despite substantial regional, political, and institutional differences. We discuss implications for adaptation theory and for international funding agencies that currently focus their attention disproportionately on megacities."_

This is 196 words. It performs all the necessary moves. It is also, as Mira's advisor observed, badly structured. Read it again, looking specifically for _the contribution_. The sentence that names the finding — "fiscal sequencing" — is sentence five of seven. By the time the reader reaches it, they have already absorbed a sentence on context, a sentence on prior work, a sentence on cases, a sentence on data, and only then the finding. Most readers won't make it to sentence five.

Here is the rewritten abstract:

> _"Climate adaptation in mid-sized coastal cities is shaped by a sequencing logic in which short-term, visible interventions crowd out longer-horizon investments — a pattern we observe across three cases (Da Nang, Cartagena, Casablanca) despite substantial regional, political, and institutional variation. This finding extends prior work on megacity adaptation to a previously understudied population that houses 30% of the global coastal population. We draw on policy document analysis, semi-structured interviews with 24 city officials, and four years of municipal budget data. The sequencing logic operates through fiscal mechanisms identifiable in budget allocation patterns and corroborated by official testimony. We discuss implications for adaptation theory — including the limits of generalizing megacity findings — and for international funding agencies currently underweighting mid-sized cities. The findings raise questions about the scale at which adaptation policy is being designed; the present analysis cannot resolve those questions but can productively pose them."_

This is 174 words. The finding is in the first clause of the first sentence. The reader knows what they're being shown before they know anything else. The remaining sentences support, contextualize, and close.

The structural difference matters. The first version reads like a paper progressing chronologically: motivation, prior work, methods, finding, implications. The second version reads like a _paper viewed from above_ : contribution first, support second. Most senior abstract writers structure this way, and most graduate students learn to only after several rounds of being told.

### 8.2 What Reviewers and Editors Look For in an Abstract

**Is the contribution legible in the first 30 seconds?** Editors triage submissions partly by abstract. Reviewers decide whether to commit to a full read partly by abstract. Citers decide whether to read further partly by abstract. The contribution must be obvious immediately.

**Is the abstract self-contained?** A reader who never reads the full paper should still understand the work. This means key terms must be defined (briefly), key findings must be stated (concretely), and the contribution must be specific.

**Is it the right length?** Word limits vary by venue (typically 150–300 for journal articles, 100–200 for conferences). Going substantially over is a signal of inability to compress; going substantially under is a signal of insufficient content.

**Is it appropriately calibrated?** The hedging matrix from Chapter 7 applies. Abstracts that overclaim invite reviewer suspicion before the paper is even read.

**Does it match the paper?** A surprisingly common failure: the abstract claims findings the paper does not deliver, or omits findings the paper centers. Reviewers cross-check, and the mismatch is held against the paper.

**Does it match the venue?** Some venues expect structured abstracts (Background / Methods / Results / Conclusions as labeled subsections). Others expect prose abstracts. Some venues require a "significance statement" alongside the abstract. The three-paper read tells you which conventions apply.


### 8.3 The Conventions of Abstract Writing


#### Length and structure

Most empirical journals require abstracts of 150–250 words. Conferences run shorter (often 100–200). Some venues — particularly biomedical and clinical journals — require _structured abstracts_ with labeled sections. Some — particularly humanities journals — permit longer, more discursive abstracts.

The conventional structure of a prose abstract, regardless of length, is:

* **Background / motivation** (1–2 sentences). What is the field, what is the question, why does it matter?
* **Approach** (1–2 sentences). What did you do?
* **Findings** (2–4 sentences). What did you find?
* **Implications** (1–2 sentences). What does it mean?

A common variation, recommended by many editors and used in the Mira example above, is to **lead with the finding**. The first sentence states the contribution; the remaining sentences support it. This is sometimes called _inverted-pyramid_ structure (borrowed from journalism), and it serves the editor-and-skim-reader audience well.

A second variation, common in high-impact general-interest journals (_Nature_ , _Science_ , and their cousins), is the **two-paragraph structure** : a one-paragraph "general audience" abstract followed by a one-paragraph technical abstract. The general-audience version is the harder write — compressing a specialized contribution for a non-specialist reader without losing precision.

#### Voice and tense

Voice in abstracts mirrors the paper. If the paper uses first-person plural ("we examine"), the abstract does too. If the paper uses third-person passive ("samples were prepared"), the abstract does too. Consistency matters because the abstract is read as a window onto the paper's voice.

Tense in abstracts is often mixed. Background and motivation are frequently in _present tense_ ("climate adaptation in mid-sized cities is shaped by…"). Methods and findings are typically in _past tense_ ("we conducted… we found…"). Implications can be either. The mixing is conventional and rarely causes confusion.


#### Citation density

Abstracts almost never cite specific works. The convention is to refer to prior work generically ("prior research has focused on…") rather than with explicit citations. The convention exists for word-economy reasons (citations consume words abstracts cannot afford) and because abstracts often appear in indexing systems where citations would not render correctly.

The exception is in fields where the methods or framework being applied has a single canonical reference (e.g., "we use a CARS-based analysis"); a brief citation may be permitted then. But the default is _no citations in the abstract_.


#### Definition: The Inverted Pyramid Abstract

An **inverted pyramid abstract** is one structured so that the most important information — typically the contribution or main finding — appears in the first sentence, with supporting context, methods, and implications following in decreasing order of importance.

In plain language: the inverted pyramid puts the conclusion first. The structure mirrors how readers actually engage with abstracts: most readers decide within the first sentence or two whether to continue. If the contribution is in sentence one, those readers see it. If it's in sentence five, they don't.

The inverted pyramid is one of two dominant abstract structures (the other being the chronological background-methods-results-implications structure). Both are acceptable; the inverted pyramid is more reader-friendly for skim audiences and is increasingly favored by editors of high-volume journals.


#### Common Misconception

A common misconception is that the abstract should be the _first_ part of the paper you write — that you should outline an abstract and then expand it into a full paper. In practice, this almost never works. Abstracts written before the paper is drafted reflect the writer's hopes for what the paper will show; they rarely match the paper that actually emerges. The result is the _abstract-paper mismatch_ problem reviewers detect.

The convention among experienced writers is to write the abstract _last_ — sometimes the very last task, after the paper is otherwise complete. By then the writer knows what the paper actually says, and the abstract can be a faithful compression. Some writers draft a "working abstract" early to focus the project, but they rewrite it from scratch at the end.

If you have written abstract first and paper second, you are not alone — many graduate students do. But the rewrite at the end is essential. The abstract you submit must reflect the paper you wrote.

### 8.4 The Six Moves Applied to Mira's Abstract

**Move 1 (genre/venue).** Mira is submitting to a public-administration journal whose word limit for abstracts is 200 words. The three-paper read shows that abstracts in this venue typically use prose structure (not labeled sections), favor the inverted pyramid (contribution first), and never include citations.

**Move 2 (structure).** Mira drafts the abstract structure in advance: _Sentence 1 — finding (inverted pyramid). Sentence 2 — relation to prior work. Sentence 3 — methods. Sentence 4 — additional finding detail. Sentences 5–6 — implications. Sentence 7 — what remains uncertain (echoing the discussion's close)._

**Move 3 (calibration).** The hedging matrix applies, in compressed form. The first sentence — _"is shaped by"_ — uses the _Strong support_ row; _"crowd out"_ is direct because the data robustly support it. Implications language uses the _Reasonable support_ row: _"raise questions about the scale at which adaptation policy is being designed."_ Notice the phrase _"the present analysis cannot resolve those questions but can productively pose them"_ — borrowed from the discussion's closing convention.

**Move 4 (positioning).** Light positioning. Generic reference to _prior work on megacity adaptation_ without naming specific authors. The positioning the paper does at length in the lit review and discussion is compressed to a clause.

**Move 5 (anticipated reviewer).** The abstract's reviewer is two-tier: the editor (who will decide whether to send out for review based partly on the abstract) and the assigned reviewers (who will read the abstract before the paper). Mira's revised abstract anticipates both: it states the contribution clearly enough for the editor to triage favorably, and it states scope and methods specifically enough that reviewers can match the abstract to the paper.

**Move 6 (AI).** Mira uses AI to: produce three alternative orderings of the abstract sentences (the writer evaluates which works best); count words and flag overlong sentences; suggest tighter phrasings of specific sentences. They do _not_ use AI to _draft_ the contribution sentence — that sentence is the paper's most important, and they want to write it themselves.

The submitted abstract is 174 words. It survives editorial triage. The paper is sent out for review.

### 8.5 Templates and Examples

**Inverted pyramid prose abstract:**

> _"[Finding, stated directly in 1–2 sentences]. This finding [extends / refines / challenges] prior work on [topic] by [specific contribution]. We [methods, in 1 sentence]. [Additional finding detail or scope clarification, 1–2 sentences]. The findings have implications for [theoretical area] and [practical/policy area]. [What remains uncertain, 1 sentence]."_

This template hits 6–8 sentences and 150–250 words depending on the verbosity of each component. It works for most empirical journal venues.

**Structured abstract (biomedical / clinical convention):**

> _"**Background:** [1–2 sentences on the question and its importance]. **Methods:** [1–2 sentences on study design, sample, key procedures]. **Results:** [2–3 sentences on key findings with effect sizes / key statistics]. **Conclusions:** [1–2 sentences on interpretation and implications]."_

Word limits vary. Major medical journals (e.g., _NEJM_ , _Lancet_) often allow 250–350 words for structured abstracts because the labeled structure consumes words.

**Two-paragraph high-impact-journal abstract:**

> _"Paragraph 1 (general audience): [Hook sentence that frames the question for non-specialists]. [Background, accessible]. [Finding, in non-technical language]. [Why it matters for a broad audience]. Paragraph 2 (technical audience): [Specific finding with technical language]. [Methods]. [Additional findings]. [Implications for the field]."_

Used at _Nature_ , _Science_ , _Cell_ , _PNAS_ , and similar venues. Hard to write well. The general-audience paragraph is typically the harder of the two.

**Conference abstract (often 100–150 words):**

> _"[Question or finding, 1 sentence]. [Method, 1 sentence]. [Key result, 1–2 sentences]. [Implication, 1 sentence]."_

Conference abstracts compress further. The discipline is brutal: every word must earn its place.

**Humanities abstract (often more discursive):**

> _"This [paper / chapter / essay] [argues / examines / develops] that [thesis]. Drawing on [archive / corpus / theoretical tradition], it [explores / shows / develops]. The central contribution is [specific contribution]. The argument has implications for [theoretical area]."_

Humanities abstracts often retain the more discursive academic voice and may run longer (250–400 words). The convention is more variable across humanities subfields than it is in the empirical sciences.

### 8.6 Common Pitfalls

**The buried contribution.** The contribution appears in sentence five or later. Fix: lead with the contribution; restructure around it.

**The mismatch with the paper.** The abstract claims findings the paper does not deliver, or vice versa. Fix: write the abstract last; cross-check against the paper before submission.

**The over-padded background.** Three sentences on context before the contribution is named. Fix: compress background to one sentence; some abstracts do without it entirely.

**The generic implications.** _"This work has implications for theory and policy."_ Vague enough to fit any paper. Fix: name _which_ theoretical question and _which_ practical or policy decision.

**The cited abstract.** Citations appear in the abstract where they should not. Fix: refer to prior work generically; save citations for the body.

**The sentence-fragment abstract.** The writer compresses by deleting subjects, articles, and verbs. _"Examines climate adaptation. Three mid-sized cities. Identifies sequencing logic. Implications for funding."_ Fix: compression by _cutting unnecessary sentences_ , not by mutilating the ones that remain. Abstracts read poorly when they sound like telegrams.

**The hedge-paralyzed abstract.** Every claim is hedged so heavily that no contribution is legible. Fix: hedge _meaning_ claims; be more direct on _finding_ claims (per the matrix in Chapter 7).

**The wrong-venue abstract.** A structured biomedical abstract submitted to a humanities journal; a discursive humanities abstract submitted to a clinical journal. Fix: the three-paper read.

### 8.7 Scholar Profile: Helen Sword and the Stakes of the Abstract

Helen Sword is a New Zealand-based writing scholar whose 2012 book _Stylish Academic Writing_ and 2017 book _Air & Light & Time & Space_ have shaped how thousands of academics think about their own writing process. Sword's contribution is partly diagnostic — she has analyzed thousands of academic articles for stylistic patterns — and partly therapeutic, helping writers see their own habits and improve them.

A surprising fact, central to Sword's analysis: _the typical abstract is read approximately 100 times more often than the full paper it summarizes._ The effort-per-reader ratio inverts dramatically. A writer might spend hundreds of hours on a paper and twelve hours on an abstract, but the abstract will determine the paper's reception in the world. Most readers will only ever encounter the abstract — through search results, citation indexes, social media shares, conference programs, AI summarization layers. The full paper is for the few; the abstract is for the many.

The implication is direct: the abstract deserves disproportionate attention. The hours spent compressing a paper into 200 careful words may be, in expected-impact terms, the most valuable hours in the project.

A second surprising fact: in Sword's surveys of academic writers, fewer than 20% reported writing the abstract last (the convention recommended by editors and the convention this chapter recommends). The plurality wrote the abstract first, before the paper was complete, and never substantially revised it. This is one of the largest places where best practice and actual practice diverge in academic writing — and it is one of the easiest to fix once a writer is told.

A third fact: Sword's broader argument in _Stylish Academic Writing_ is that academic writing can be _both_ conventionally rigorous and stylistically distinctive — that the convention does not force prose to be dull. The discussion in Chapter 7 of academic writing as a foreign language pretending to be normal English is partly Sword's lineage: the conventions are real, they must be respected, and they leave room for voice.

For graduate writers in 2026, Sword's lesson is direct: spend more time on the abstract than your intuition tells you to. It is your paper's ambassador to the world; it does more reader-facing work than the rest of the paper combined; and it is the most-leveraged 200 words of writing in your career.

### 8.8 Reader's Manuscript Audit Prompt

Take the abstract of your current manuscript. (If you don't have a current manuscript with an abstract, use a paper of your own that has one.) Perform the following audit:

**Compress by 30%.** Whatever your current word count, write a version 30% shorter. If your abstract is 250 words, write a 175-word version. If it's 200 words, write a 140-word version.

The compression forces every sentence to justify its presence. Sentences that don't earn their words get cut. Sentences that do get tightened. The result is almost always sharper than the original — and almost always still complete.

After compressing, ask:

* Is the contribution still legible?
* Are the methods still specified at the level the venue expects?
* Are the implications still present?
* Is the calibration still appropriate?

If the answer to all four is yes, the original was over-padded and the compressed version is your new draft. If the answer to any is no, restore selectively — but try to add back fewer words than you cut.

This is your sixth manuscript revision. The portfolio: synthesis-vs-summary audit (Ch.3), CARS introduction rewrite (Ch.4), methods replication test (Ch.5), prose-to-table redesign (Ch.6), discussion calibration audit (Ch.7), and now the abstract compression.

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is an _inverted pyramid abstract_ , and why does the chapter argue it serves skim readers better than a chronological abstract?

Hint

The Definition box in §8.3 names this structure.

**Answer:** An inverted pyramid abstract is one structured so that the most important information — the contribution or main finding — appears in the first sentence, with supporting context, methods, and implications following. It serves skim readers better than a chronological (background-methods-results-implications) structure because most readers decide within the first sentence or two whether to continue; placing the contribution in sentence one ensures even the most cursory reader sees it, while a chronological structure may bury the contribution at sentence four or five.

**Q2.** Why does the chapter recommend writing the abstract _last_ , after the paper is otherwise complete?

**Answer:** Because abstracts written before the paper is drafted reflect the writer's hopes for what the paper will show; they rarely match the paper that actually emerges. The result is the _abstract-paper mismatch_ problem reviewers detect. Writing the abstract last ensures it faithfully compresses the paper that was actually written. (Helen Sword's surveys, in §8.7, show that this is one of the largest gaps between best practice and actual practice in academic writing.)

**Q3.** What is the surprising fact, attributed to Helen Sword, about the effort-per-reader ratio of abstracts?

**Answer:** That a typical abstract is read approximately 100 times more often than the full paper it summarizes. The effort-per-reader ratio inverts dramatically — a writer may spend hundreds of hours on a paper and twelve on the abstract, but the abstract will determine the paper's reception. Most readers will only ever encounter the abstract.

**Q4.** Name three of the conventional components of a prose abstract, in their typical order.

**Answer:** Background/motivation; approach (methods); findings; implications. (The chapter notes that the inverted pyramid variation leads with the findings/contribution and follows with motivation, methods, and implications.)
