**Q1.** The widely cited claim — discussed by Sword and others in the academic-writing literature — that abstracts are read many times more often than full papers (estimates of the ratio range across studies, but the order of magnitude is consistent: abstracts reach far more readers than papers do) raises a question: should academic writers spend more time on abstracts and less on full papers? What would the costs and benefits be? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** The naive answer (yes, allocate more time to abstracts) misses the structural point: an abstract that doesn't have a strong paper behind it is detected eventually. The papers that get cited heavily are usually papers whose abstracts and full text both deliver. The deeper answer: writers should allocate _more time to abstracts than they currently do_ , but not at the expense of the full paper — instead, by drafting the abstract last and giving it disproportionate attention in the final revision phase. The hours of abstract refinement are some of the highest-leverage hours in the project, and they are typically the hours most often skimped (a common pattern: the writer spends three months on a paper, then writes the abstract in two hours the night before submission). Sword's diagnosis is correct; the response is more careful abstract-writing, not paper-writing reallocation.

**Q2.** Some venues (notably _PLOS One_ , _eLife_ , and others) now publish _plain-language summaries_ alongside technical abstracts — short, accessible versions for non-specialist readers. How is the writing problem different for plain-language summaries? Where does the skill transfer from regular abstract-writing, and where does it not? Sketch your view in 250 words.

**Discussion:** Plain-language summaries push the abstract problem further: the contribution must be legible not only to specialist skim readers but to non-specialists who lack the field's vocabulary. The skills that transfer: inverted-pyramid structure (lead with the finding); compression discipline (every word earns its place); calibration (don't overclaim). The skills that don't transfer: comfort with technical vocabulary (must be replaced by analogies, examples, simpler synonyms); reliance on field-specific framing (must be re-grounded for a general audience). The writing problem is harder, and the failure mode is often _infantilizing_ the prose — explaining at the level of a child rather than a non-specialist adult. The best plain-language summaries respect the reader's intelligence while not assuming the reader's specialist training. (Connection to Chapter 13: cross-disciplinary writing requires similar moves.)

**Q3.** AI tools can now generate abstracts at speed. Many writers paste their full paper into an AI and ask for a 200-word abstract. What are the risks? Where might this be acceptable? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** AI-generated abstracts are often plausible but flat. The risks: (a) the AI may emphasize the wrong contribution (whatever appeared most prominently in the paper, which is not always the most important); (b) the AI's calibration is generic, often overclaiming or under-claiming relative to what the writer would choose; (c) the AI may include details that aren't in the paper or omit details that are; (d) the abstract is the writer's most important 200 words, and outsourcing the writing of those 200 words deprives the writer of the opportunity to compress their own thinking. Acceptable uses: (a) using AI to suggest _alternative orderings_ of writer-drafted sentences; (b) using AI to flag overlong sentences or word-count overruns; (c) using AI to produce a _first_ compressed version that the writer then heavily revises. Bright line: the contribution sentence — the most important sentence — must be the writer's own. (Connection forward to Chapter 14: this is one of the many places where AI-assisted academic writing is widely used, partly accepted, and requires the writer to retain interpretive ownership.)


### Chapter Summary

The abstract is the most-read 200 words a writer will ever produce. It is not a summary; it is a _miniature paper_ that must do all the work the full paper does, in a tight word limit. Helen Sword's finding that abstracts are read approximately 100 times more often than their parent papers makes abstract-writing one of the highest-leverage activities in academic writing, and one of the most consistently under-resourced.

This chapter laid out the conventions of abstract structure (inverted pyramid, chronological, structured, two-paragraph), voice, tense, citation density, and length (§8.3). It applied the six moves to Mira's abstract (§8.4), offered templates for five common structures (§8.5), eight common pitfalls (§8.6), and the contribution of Helen Sword to making the stakes of the abstract visible (§8.7). The manuscript audit prompt (§8.8) added a sixth revision to your portfolio: a 30% compression of your own abstract.

The abstract closes the empirical-paper sequence that Chapters 3 through 8 have walked through. The lit review located the gap; the introduction promised the contribution; the methods made it replicable; the results showed it; the discussion interpreted it; the abstract compresses all of them. A reader who absorbs the conventions of these six genres has internalized roughly half of what skilled academic writing requires.

In Chapter 9 we turn to the **research proposal** — a fundamentally different genre, because it sells _future_ findings rather than reporting _past_ ones. Mira will write a proposal next, for a dissertation grant, and we will see how the conventions invert when the writer must promise findings they have not yet generated.

It is the fall of Mira's fourth year. The first solo paper from Chapters 4–8 has been published. Mira is now mid-way through their dissertation, and they need money to finish it — specifically, to expand the comparative study from three cities to twelve. Their advisor has identified an NSF dissertation improvement grant program with an October deadline.

Mira sits down to draft the proposal. Within an hour they realize that everything they have learned about academic writing for the last three years is about to be inverted.

A research article reports findings that exist. The reviewer asks: _did you find what you say you found?_

A research proposal sells findings that do not yet exist. The reviewer asks: _will you find anything worth funding the search for?_

The genres look superficially similar — both have introductions, methods, and budgets-or-results — but they do fundamentally different rhetorical work. A proposal must be confident about a future the writer cannot yet verify. It must be specific about findings the writer cannot yet name. It must be persuasive about importance the writer cannot yet demonstrate. The hedging matrix from Chapter 7, which served the discussion section so well, becomes only partly applicable: a proposal that hedges too much fails to motivate funding; a proposal that hedges too little promises what cannot be guaranteed.

This chapter is about navigating that inversion.

### 9.1 Vignette: Selling a Future You Cannot Promise

Mira's first attempt at a proposal opens like a research-article introduction:

> _"Climate adaptation in coastal cities is a topic of increasing scholarly attention. Most existing work has focused on either large global samples or single-city case studies, leaving a gap in our understanding of mid-sized cities. Building on prior work (Chapter 4 of this dissertation), this proposal extends a comparative case-study approach from three to twelve mid-sized coastal cities. We will use document analysis, semi-structured interviews, and budget data analysis to examine adaptation patterns across the expanded sample."_

It is competent. It is calibrated. It will not get funded.

The reason: it sounds like a paper, not a pitch. It tells the reviewer what the writer will _do_ , but not what the reviewer will _get_. It positions the work in the literature, but not in the funder's priorities. It promises methods, but not findings. It hedges where a proposal must commit.

Here is the rewritten opening:

> _"Coastal adaptation funding currently flows disproportionately to megacities, in part because the policy literature has overwhelmingly studied them. Mid-sized coastal cities — home to 30% of the global coastal population — face distinctive constraints that megacity findings do not capture. This proposal will produce the first systematic comparative analysis of adaptation in mid-sized coastal cities, identifying patterns that will inform both adaptation theory and the international funding programs whose effectiveness depends on understanding the contexts they aim to support. We expect to identify three to five generalizable adaptation typologies and to test the fiscal-sequencing hypothesis (developed in our prior work on three cities) across a sample of twelve. The findings will fill a gap that current funding allocations cannot address without empirical guidance."_

The rewritten opening is more direct. It names the _importance_ (funding flows are misallocated). It names the _contribution_ (the first systematic comparative analysis). It names the _expected findings_ (three to five typologies; fiscal-sequencing hypothesis test). It names the _audience_ (adaptation theory and international funding programs). And it commits — _will produce, will inform, expect to identify_ — where the first version hedged.

The shift in voice is not aggression. It is the genre's demand. A proposal that does not commit cannot motivate the reader to commit.

### 9.2 What Reviewers Look For in a Proposal

**Is the problem important?** Reviewers ask first whether the question is worth asking. A proposal that doesn't establish importance is in trouble before the methods are read.

**Is the proposed work feasible?** Even if the question is important, can the writer actually do the work in the proposed time and budget? Reviewers triage on feasibility.

**Is the writer credible?** Has the writer demonstrated the relevant skills — through prior publications, training, preliminary data? Proposals from new researchers must work harder to establish credibility.

**Is the contribution proportionate?** Some proposals overpromise (small project, claims to revolutionize the field); some underpromise (modest project, doesn't articulate why it matters). Reviewers want proportionality.

**Are the methods specific?** Vague methods ("we will conduct interviews") are weaker than specific methods ("we will conduct 96 semi-structured interviews — 8 per city across 12 cities — using the protocol developed in our pilot study (attached)"). Specificity signals readiness.

**Are the budget and timeline realistic?** Reviewers check whether the proposed work can be done with the requested resources in the proposed time. Unrealistic budgets and timelines are red flags.

**Does the proposal fit the funder?** Each funder has its own priorities, conventions, and review criteria. A proposal that doesn't match the funder's stated priorities will be triaged out, regardless of intellectual merit.

A proposal that satisfies these seven criteria has a fighting chance. Funding is competitive — even strong proposals often fail — but proposals that fail any of these criteria rarely succeed.


### 9.3 The Conventional Structure of a Proposal

Proposals vary by funder and by genre (NSF, NIH, ERC, Wellcome, foundation grants, dissertation improvement grants, internal university fellowships — each with different conventions). But a common structural template can be adapted to most:


#### Section 1 — Significance and Background

Why does this work matter? What is the gap in the literature it addresses? This section is the proposal's CARS introduction (Chapter 4) — but pitched harder than a paper introduction, because the reviewer has not yet committed to reading the rest. The hook in sentence one matters disproportionately.

The significance argument operates at two levels: the scholarly significance (what the work contributes to theory or method) and the practical significance (what the work contributes to a problem outside the academy). Some funders emphasize one over the other; the three-funder read (the proposal-writing equivalent of the three-paper read) tells you which.

#### Section 2 — Specific Aims (or Research Questions)

What, specifically, will the project do? Most successful proposals organize around 2–4 specific aims, each one a focused, achievable subgoal. Aims should be:

* _Specific_ (not "examine adaptation" but "characterize the pathways by which fiscal constraint shapes adaptation sequencing across 12 mid-sized coastal cities")
* _Measurable_ (you should be able to tell whether the aim has been achieved)
* _Related but independent_ (no aim should be wholly contingent on another; if Aim 1 fails, Aim 2 should still be possible)
* _Proportionate_ (the aims together should be doable in the proposed time and budget)

Aims structure the rest of the proposal. The methods section answers each aim; the timeline allocates time to each aim; the deliverables map to each aim.


#### Section 3 — Approach (Methods)

How will you do the work? This section parallels a research-article methods section (Chapter 5) but with two differences: it is _prospective_ (you describe what you _will_ do, not what you _did_), and it must include _contingencies_ (what will you do if the data don't cooperate?).

Methods sections in proposals must be specific enough to be evaluable as feasible, but not so detailed that they read as inflexible (reviewers know research evolves). The right level: enough specificity to demonstrate readiness, with brief acknowledgment of how you will adapt if circumstances change.


#### Section 4 — Expected Outcomes and Significance

What will the project produce? This section names the deliverables (papers, data, frameworks) and the contributions (theoretical, practical, policy). It also addresses _what if_ — what alternative outcomes are possible, and how would they still constitute valuable contributions?

This section is where the genre's central tension shows: you must commit to expected outcomes specifically, while acknowledging that the outcomes are not yet known.


#### Section 5 — Timeline and Budget

When and at what cost? Most funders provide templates; fill them precisely. The timeline should be realistic with reasonable buffer; the budget should be justified line-by-line.


#### Section 6 — Investigator Qualifications

Why are you the right person to do this work? Prior publications, training, preliminary data, institutional context. Doctoral students proposing dissertation work lean heavily on advisor relationships and pilot work; postdocs and faculty lean on track record.


#### Definition: The Specific Aim

A **specific aim** in a research proposal is a focused, achievable subgoal of the proposed project, stated specifically enough to be evaluable for both feasibility and contribution.

In plain language: a specific aim is a piece of the project that you will plausibly do and that will produce a particular contribution. Most funded proposals organize around 2–4 specific aims; below 2 aims looks thin, above 5 aims looks scattered. The skill is to define aims that are _specific_ (the reviewer can tell what's being proposed), _related but independent_ (no single failure kills the project), and _proportionate_ (achievable in the proposed time and budget).

The specific aim is a unit of analysis distinctive to the proposal genre. Research articles do not have specific aims; their unit of analysis is the finding. Proposals are organized around aims because the genre is prospective: you cannot organize around findings that don't yet exist.

#### Common Misconception

A common misconception is that proposals should hedge the same way discussions hedge. _"We may find," "it is conceivable that," "the data could suggest."_ The hedging matrix from Chapter 7 partially applies here, but proposals demand more commitment than discussions. _"We expect to find," "this work will produce," "the project will demonstrate"_ — these are the proposal voice.

The reason: a discussion is about claims made on evidence already collected. A proposal is about claims a funder is being asked to underwrite. Excessive hedging in a proposal communicates that the writer is uncertain whether the project is worth funding — which is a self-defeating signal. The convention is to commit specifically while acknowledging risk in dedicated sections (the contingencies subsection, the limitations section if present).

The trick: hedge on _outcomes that depend on what nature does_ (the data may turn out differently than expected); commit on _outcomes you control_ (we will conduct the analysis; we will produce the deliverables).


### 9.4 The Hook Test

Proposals live or die in the first paragraph — and often in the first sentence. The hook is the proposal's most important sentence; it determines whether the reviewer reads carefully or skims.

A useful diagnostic is **the hook test** : read your proposal's first sentence aloud. Then ask:

  1. _Does it state what is at stake?_
  2. _Could it be the first sentence of any other proposal?_
  3. _Would a busy reviewer want to read sentence two?_

If the answer to (1) is no, your hook fails. If the answer to (2) is yes — it could open any proposal — your hook is too generic. If the answer to (3) is no, your hook isn't earning its place.

Mira's first hook (_"Climate adaptation in coastal cities is a topic of increasing scholarly attention"_) fails all three. Their rewritten hook (_"Coastal adaptation funding currently flows disproportionately to megacities, in part because the policy literature has overwhelmingly studied them"_) passes all three: it names what is at stake (misallocated funding); it could not open any other proposal (it is specifically about a known asymmetry); and it makes the reviewer want to read sentence two (which presumably names the writer's contribution).

The hook test is brutal but useful. Apply it before submission.

### 9.5 The Six Moves Applied to Mira's Proposal

**Move 1 (genre/venue).** NSF dissertation improvement grant — a specific funder with a specific page limit (10 pages of project description), specific review criteria (intellectual merit and broader impacts), and a specific reviewer pool (scholars in the writer's broad subfield, but not necessarily specialists). The three-funder read shows that successful proposals in this program tend to have a strong significance section, 2–3 specific aims, methods that demonstrate feasibility, a section addressing broader impacts (an NSF priority), and a clear timeline.

**Move 2 (structure).** Mira drafts the proposal structure: _§1 Significance (1.5 pages) — including the rewritten hook from §9.1. §2 Specific Aims (0.5 page) — three aims. §3 Approach (3.5 pages) — methods organized by aim. §4 Expected Outcomes and Broader Impacts (1.5 pages). §5 Timeline (0.5 page). §6 Qualifications and Pilot Work (1 page). §7 Bibliography (separate, doesn't count toward page limit)._

**Move 3 (calibration).** This is where proposal voice diverges from paper voice. Mira commits in the significance section ("this proposal will produce"); commits in the aims ("Aim 1 will characterize…"); commits in the methods ("we will conduct"); hedges on findings ("we expect to identify three to five typologies; the specific number will depend on…"); commits on deliverables ("the project will produce two journal articles, a public dataset, and a policy brief").

**Move 4 (positioning).** The proposal positions the work both within the academic conversation (the gap from prior chapters) and within the funder's priorities (NSF's interest in adaptation policy and broader impacts). Citations appear in the significance and methods sections; the bibliography is separate.

**Move 5 (anticipated reviewer).** Predictable proposal objections: _"Is the sample of 12 cities feasible?"_ — addressed in the methods section's case-selection rationale and timeline. _"What if the fiscal-sequencing hypothesis doesn't replicate at 12 cities?"_ — addressed in the contingencies subsection and reframed as itself a publishable finding. _"What are the broader impacts beyond academia?"_ — addressed in §4, with specific attention to the policy brief deliverable and a planned workshop with practitioners. _"Why is this writer the right person?"_ — addressed in §6, leveraging the prior published paper from Chapter 4 and the pilot interview protocols.

**Move 6 (AI).** Mira uses AI to: audit the hook against the three hook-test questions; identify hedges that should be commitments and commitments that should be hedges; generate alternative orderings of the specific aims (the writer evaluates which sequence builds best); flag implausible budget items. They do _not_ use AI to draft the significance argument or the aims — these are the proposal's most important content.

The submitted proposal is 9.8 pages. It is not funded on the first round. Mira receives reviewer comments, revises, and resubmits the following spring. The resubmission is funded.

Failure-then-resubmission is the modal experience for academic proposals. Successful researchers absorb this and treat first-round rejection as part of the process, not as evidence the work isn't worth doing.

### 9.6 Templates and Examples

**Hook (significance section opener):**

> _"[Specific problem with stakes named in concrete terms]. [Why current scholarship cannot address it.] This proposal will [specific contribution]."_

**Specific aim:**

> _"**Aim N: [Specific, measurable goal].** This aim will [verb] [object] using [methods]. Expected outcomes: [specific deliverables]. Significance: [brief sentence on contribution]."_

Three to four such aims, each on its own paragraph, structures the aims section.

**Approach (methods) per-aim opener:**

> _"To accomplish Aim N, we will [methods, briefly]. Specifically, [step 1]; [step 2]; [step 3]. Analysis will follow [protocol], yielding [type of deliverable]. We will manage risk to this aim by [contingency plan]."_

**Expected outcomes:**

> _"The project will produce [deliverable 1, e.g., 'two peer-reviewed journal articles'], [deliverable 2, e.g., 'a publicly available dataset'], and [deliverable 3, e.g., 'a policy brief']. The expected contributions are: theoretically, [specific theoretical contribution]; methodologically, [specific methodological contribution]; practically, [specific practical contribution]. We discuss alternative scenarios in §[contingencies]: in particular, if [risk materializes], the project will instead deliver [alternative outcome] which would itself be a meaningful contribution."_

**Broader impacts (NSF-specific but adaptable):**

> _"Beyond academic contributions, the project will engage [stakeholder community] through [specific mechanism, e.g., a workshop, an open dataset, a policy brief]. We have already established relationships with [partner organization or community] (see attached letter of support). The project will also [training/mentorship/diversity contribution]."_

**Timeline:**

> _"**Year 1, Months 1–6:** [activities]. Deliverable: [interim output]. **Year 1, Months 7–12:** [activities]. Deliverable: [interim output]. … **Year 2, Months 19–24:** [activities]. Deliverable: [final output]."_

A specific monthly or quarterly timeline signals readiness; a vague "Year 1 / Year 2" timeline signals planning gaps.

**Investigator qualifications:**

> _"The PI brings [specific relevant skills], demonstrated through [prior publications]. Pilot work for this proposal (see attached preprint) established [specific pilot contribution] and developed [specific tools/protocols] that will be deployed in the funded project."_

### 9.7 Common Pitfalls

**The paper-not-pitch proposal.** The writing reads like a research article introduction; it tells the reviewer what the writer will do but doesn't sell why it matters. Fix: rewrite the significance section with the hook test in mind.

**The vague aims.** _"Aim 1: Examine adaptation in mid-sized cities."_ Not specific enough to be evaluable. Fix: each aim should specify the action, the object, the method, and the expected contribution.

**The over-aggregated aims.** _"Aim 1: Develop a comprehensive theory of climate adaptation."_ Aims that are too large to be doable. Fix: scale aims to the time and budget; aggregation can come in the cumulative contribution.

**The dependent aims.** Aim 2 cannot proceed if Aim 1 fails. Reviewers see this as project risk. Fix: aims should be related but independent; if one fails, the others should still be doable.

**The unrealistic timeline.** A 24-month project that requires 36 months of work to deliver. Fix: honest scoping; better to propose less and deliver well than to overpromise.

**The under-justified budget.** Line items without explanation; equipment costs that seem high. Fix: budget justification should be specific and defensible per line.

**The misaligned funder.** A proposal pitched to a funder whose priorities don't match the work. Fix: read the funder's call for proposals carefully; align the significance section to the funder's stated priorities (without compromising intellectual honesty).

**The buried broader impacts.** NSF and many other funders weight broader impacts substantially; a proposal that treats them as a brief afterthought loses points. Fix: dedicate appropriate space; specify mechanisms and partners.

**The overconfident contingencies.** _"Risks are minimal."_ Reviewers know risks are not minimal. Fix: name the actual risks, briefly, with how you will manage them.

#### A Practical Note: Predatory Funders and Solicitation Schemes

Most graduate students who fall into proposal trouble do so by submitting to legitimate funders and writing under-prepared proposals. A small minority fall into a different trouble: they submit to _predatory funders or solicitation schemes_ — organizations that solicit proposals or accept submissions for fees but provide little or no actual review, no genuine funding pipeline, or terms that expose the writer's intellectual property without protection. Predatory funders parallel predatory journals (Chapter 9 of the publishing-side concerns) and have grown alongside them.

A few practical signals: legitimate funders rarely solicit unsolicited proposals from graduate students through cold email; legitimate funders publish their review process, panel composition, and prior awardees; legitimate funders do not charge a meaningful "submission fee" to applicants (administrative fees, where they exist, are nominal). Specific resources to consult before submitting: your institution's _Office of Sponsored Research_ (or the equivalent — every research university has one, and they keep watchlists internal to the institution), the _Committee on Publication Ethics_ (COPE) general guidance on integrity in research funding, professional-society discipline-specific guidance (e.g., the AAUP, the AAAS, and field-specific societies often publish or link such guidance), and — for cross-checking a specific funder — the _Pivot_ and _GrantForward_ databases, which legitimate university funding offices already license. When in doubt, ask before applying. Submitting to a predatory funder costs more than time: it can foreclose later submission of the same work to legitimate funders if the predatory entity claims publication rights or first-refusal terms. Treat the funder selection as a first move worthy of careful research, not as an afterthought to a strong proposal.

### 9.8 Scholar Profile: Przeworski, Salomon, and the Four Questions of a Proposal

In 1988 the Social Science Research Council asked **Adam Przeworski** (a political scientist at New York University) and **Frank Salomon** (an anthropologist and historian at the University of Wisconsin–Madison) to write a brief practical guide for SSRC fellowship applicants. The result — _On the Art of Writing Proposals_ — is a pamphlet of barely 7,000 words that has become one of the most circulated documents in social-science graduate training. It exists because SSRC program officers had noticed that the proposals they received clustered around a small number of recurring failure modes, and that a short, frank guide might do more pedagogical work than longer treatises.

A surprising fact, central to Przeworski and Salomon's framework: **every proposal must answer four implicit questions, and reviewers triage on whether the answers can be located.** The four questions, in their formulation, are — _What is the intellectual problem? Why does it matter? How will the project address it? What outcomes will the project produce, and how will we recognize them?_ A proposal where any of these is missing or unanswerable is a proposal that fails, regardless of the underlying project's merit. The pamphlet's contribution is to make these implicit questions _explicit_ — and therefore answerable.

The deeper claim is that proposal writing is a _specific genre with its own rhetorical demands_ , distinct from the research article. A proposal must commit to outcomes that have not yet been generated. Research articles report past work; proposals sell future work. The asymmetry is uncomfortable but real: the writer must say what the methods will produce while honestly acknowledging that the precise findings depend on data not yet collected. Skilled proposal writers learn to commit on _what they will do_ (methods, deliverables, timeline) while hedging on _what nature will reveal_ (specific findings, effect sizes, theoretical conclusions). Calibrated commitment is the proposal's voice.

A second surprising fact, recurrent in interviews with grant program officers across funders: **the most common cause of rejection is not weak ideas but poor proposal craft** — generic openings, vague aims, inadequately specified methods, unrealistic timelines, missed funder priorities. Intellectual merit and proposal craft are partly independent; strong projects with weak proposals routinely fail, and adequate projects with strong proposals routinely succeed. This is one of the most important — and one of the most uncomfortable — facts about academic funding.

A third fact: success rates for many major grant programs in the 2020s are 10–25%. Multi-round revision is the norm, not the exception. Successful researchers absorb this and develop a _resubmission practice_ — treating the first submission as the start of a feedback loop rather than a one-shot bet. Przeworski and Salomon explicitly recommend the resubmission posture: the worst that can happen, on their telling, is that the writer will receive useful criticism for the next round.

For graduate writers entering 2026, the Przeworski–Salomon lesson is direct: proposal writing is a craft distinct from paper writing, with its own four-question architecture and its own rhetorical demands. Treat it as such. Commit where the genre demands commitment; hedge where it permits hedging; revise on rejection rather than abandon. The hardest part of grant writing is not finding the words; it is finding the words again, after rejection.


### 9.9 Reader's Manuscript Audit Prompt

If you have a current proposal in progress (or a recent past proposal you can revise), apply the **proposal hook test** from §9.4:

**Read the first sentence aloud.**

Then answer:

  1. Does it state what is at stake?
  2. Could it be the first sentence of any other proposal?
  3. Would a busy reviewer want to read sentence two?

If the answer to any is unsatisfactory, rewrite the first sentence. The rewrite often takes thirty minutes — and often improves the proposal more than thirty hours of methods refinement would.

**Then audit your aims.** Read each specific aim. For each, ask:

* Is it specific enough to be evaluated?
* Is it independent enough that its failure wouldn't kill the project?
* Is it proportionate to the time and budget?

Rewrite any aim that fails one of these tests.

This is your seventh manuscript revision. The portfolio: synthesis-vs-summary audit (Ch.3), CARS introduction rewrite (Ch.4), methods replication test (Ch.5), prose-to-table redesign (Ch.6), discussion calibration audit (Ch.7), abstract compression (Ch.8), and now the proposal hook + aims audit.

(If you don't have a current proposal, take the first paragraph and aims from a published proposal you can find — many funded proposals are publicly archived — and apply the audit. The exercise teaches the diagnostic eye even without your own draft.)


### 9.10 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is the core rhetorical inversion that distinguishes a proposal from a research article?

Hint

The opening of the chapter and the Przeworski–Salomon profile (§9.8) name this inversion directly.

**Answer:** A research article reports findings that exist; the reviewer asks "did you find what you say you found?" A proposal sells findings that do not yet exist; the reviewer asks "will you find anything worth funding the search for?" The proposal must be specific about importance, methods, and expected outcomes for work that has not yet been done — committing where the genre demands commitment while acknowledging the unknowns where appropriate.

**Q2.** Name and define the _specific aim_ as the chapter has used the term.

**Answer:** A specific aim is a focused, achievable subgoal of the proposed project, stated specifically enough to be evaluable for both feasibility and contribution. Most funded proposals organize around 2–4 specific aims; aims should be specific (the reviewer can tell what's being proposed), related but independent (no single failure kills the project), and proportionate (achievable in the proposed time and budget).

**Q3.** What is the _hook test_ , and what three questions does it ask?

**Answer:** The hook test is a diagnostic for the proposal's first sentence. It asks: (1) Does it state what is at stake? (2) Could it be the first sentence of any other proposal? (3) Would a busy reviewer want to read sentence two? A failing hook usually requires rewriting; the rewrite is often the highest-leverage half-hour of work in the entire proposal.

**Q4.** Why does the chapter argue that excessive hedging in a proposal is a mistake, even though it is virtuous in a discussion?

**Answer:** Because a proposal asks a funder to underwrite future work; excessive hedging communicates that the writer is uncertain whether the project is worth funding, which is self-defeating. The convention is to commit specifically while acknowledging risk in dedicated sections (contingencies, alternative outcomes). Calibrated commitment — commit on what you will do (methods, deliverables, timeline); hedge on what nature will reveal (specific findings) — is the proposal voice.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Take Mira's first-draft proposal opening from §9.1 (the paper-style opening) and rewrite it as a proposal hook that passes the hook test. Apply the three hook-test questions to your rewrite.

Hint

The §9.1 example shows one possible rewrite. Try producing your own version with a different stakes-naming approach (e.g., naming the policy stakes differently, or naming the theoretical stakes more prominently).

**Answer:** A successful response will (a) produce a hook that names specific stakes (not just "topic of growing attention"), (b) be distinctive (could not open any other proposal), (c) make the reviewer want to read sentence two, and (d) explicitly evaluate the rewrite against the three hook-test questions. The most common improvement in successful rewrites is the move from _abstract topic identification_ ("X is important") to _specific stake naming_ ("X is misallocated / unstudied / contested").

**Q2.** Take a current or recent proposal of your own and apply the audit from §9.9: hook test plus aims audit. Submit the original hook, the rewritten hook, the original aims, the rewritten aims (where any are revised), and a 200-word reflection on what changed. (If you don't have your own proposal, use a publicly archived funded proposal — many grant agencies post examples — and apply the audit.)

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful response will (a) accurately identify weaknesses in the original hook, (b) produce a rewrite that passes the hook test, (c) audit the aims for specificity, independence, and proportionality, and (d) reflect on what changed. The most useful reflections often note that the proposal's apparent weakness was not the methods or the contribution but the _framing_ — the hook and aims weren't doing the persuasive work the genre demands. (Connection to Chapter 4: hooks for proposals are like CARS introductions but more aggressive; the moves are similar but the calibration is more committal.)

**Sample Response (Mira's NSF proposal hook + aims audit, abridged):** _Original hook: "Climate change adaptation in coastal cities is increasingly important." Hook-test diagnosis: (1) Stakes? Generic, not specific. (2) Could open any other proposal? Yes. (3) Would a busy reviewer want sentence two? No. Failed all three. Rewrite: "Approximately 30% of the global coastal population — over 250 million people — lives in mid-sized cities that fall below the data thresholds of the dominant climate-adaptation literatures, leaving their adaptation pathways largely undocumented." Hook-test diagnosis: (1) Stakes? Specific. (2) Distinctive? Yes. (3) Pulls reader forward? Yes. Pass. Aims audit (original): "Aim 1: Study adaptation in mid-sized cities. Aim 2: Develop a framework. Aim 3: Engage policy." Diagnosis: all three are too vague (no specific actions/objects/methods); Aim 2 depends on Aim 1; Aim 3 is not an aim but an implication. Rewritten aims: "Aim 1: Characterize adaptation sequencing in 12 mid-sized coastal cities through 96 semi-structured interviews and document analysis (Year 1). Aim 2: Test the sequencing hypothesis against the 12-city budget data and identify cross-case typologies (Year 2). Aim 3: Develop a fiscal-adaptation typology usable by international funders, with policy-brief deliverable and practitioner workshop (Year 3, building on Aims 1 and 2 but standing alone if either yields negative results)." Reflection: the original aims would have triaged out of NSF review. The rewrites pass the specificity, independence, and proportionality tests. The change is not in what Mira plans to do but in how the proposal makes the plan legible._

**Q3.** For a hypothetical project in your field, draft three specific aims that would structure a proposal. Each aim should be 2–4 sentences and should specify the action, object, method, and expected contribution. Then check: are the aims independent? Are they proportionate? (Connection to Chapter 2: the aims are the proposal's analog to the paper's contribution claim — Move 3 of CARS made operational at proposal scale.)

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful response will produce three aims that are (a) specific (action, object, method, contribution all named), (b) independent (no aim wholly contingent on another), and (c) proportionate (together doable in the implied time and budget). Common failure modes for first attempts: aims too vague ("Aim 1: Study X"); aims dependent on each other (Aim 2 requires Aim 1's success); aims too aggregated ("Aim 1: Develop a comprehensive theory"). Worth doing twice if any of these failures appear.

**Q4.** Find a publicly available funded grant proposal in your field. Read the significance section and the specific aims. Apply the audit: does the hook pass the hook test? Are the aims specific, independent, and proportionate? What is the proposal doing rhetorically that you could learn from? Write a 250-word commentary.

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A typical successful response will note specific moves the funded proposal makes that distinguish it from a typical paper introduction — e.g., explicit stakes-naming, commitment language ("we will" rather than "we may"), explicit deliverables, broader-impacts engagement. The exercise teaches that funded proposals are written deliberately to a different genre than research articles, and that the genre's conventions can be learned by reading widely in funded proposals rather than only in published papers.

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The chapter argues that "intellectual merit and proposal craft are partly independent" — that strong projects with weak proposals routinely fail and adequate projects with strong proposals routinely succeed. Is this a defect of the funding system or a feature? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** Both, depending on the angle. As a defect: it skews funding toward writers (and institutions, and demographic groups) with strong proposal-writing training, regardless of underlying intellectual merit. As a feature: proposal craft signals readiness, communication ability, and the discipline to think a project through end-to-end before requesting resources — qualities that correlate (imperfectly) with project success. The reform challenge: how to make proposal craft _trainable_ rather than _inheritable_ through informal mentorship networks. This book is partly an attempt at that — explicit teaching of proposal conventions to writers who didn't get them by osmosis. It is also why some funders have moved toward shorter, idea-focused first-stage proposals (followed by full proposals only for shortlisted ideas), to partially decouple intellectual merit from proposal craft. (Connection to Chapter 1's foreign-language thesis: like all academic-writing conventions, proposal craft is learnable; the conventions aren't the problem, but the lack of explicit teaching is.)

**Q2.** The proposal-genre framing — that proposals require "selling future findings you cannot yet verify" — has an uncomfortable implication: the writer must commit specifically to outcomes that may not materialize. Is this honest? When does committed proposal language cross from confidence into overpromise? Sketch your view in 250 words.

**Discussion:** Honest committed proposal language commits to _what you will do_ (methods, deliverables, timeline) and to _what would constitute success_ (findings of any of several specified types) without committing to the specific direction of those findings. _"We will conduct interviews and code them; we expect to identify three to five typologies; the typologies' specific characteristics will depend on the data"_ is honest committed language. _"We will demonstrate that mid-sized cities follow a sequencing logic"_ — committing to a specific finding direction — crosses into overpromise unless the prior evidence is strong enough to justify near-certainty. The line is similar to the hedging matrix line for findings, but shifted toward more commitment by the genre's demands. The honest writer commits to what they control and hedges on what they don't.

**Q3.** AI tools can now generate proposal drafts at speed. Some writers paste a research idea and generate a full proposal; some have AI write the significance section based on bullet points; some use AI to write the aims based on a project sketch. What are the integrity concerns? What is acceptable use? Sketch your view in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** Proposals are funder-facing documents in which the writer is making a contractual-style commitment. Integrity concerns include: (a) AI-generated significance sections may overclaim importance in ways the writer cannot specifically defend; (b) AI-generated aims may be vague or misaligned with what the writer actually intends to do; (c) AI may invent or misattribute prior work in the literature engagement; (d) AI-generated proposals may pass funder triage on craft alone, decoupling funding decisions further from intellectual merit. Acceptable uses: (a) using AI to audit a writer-drafted hook against the hook test; (b) using AI to suggest alternative orderings or phrasings of writer-drafted aims; (c) using AI to flag specific weaknesses (vague language, dependent aims, unrealistic timelines); (d) using AI to format budget tables and timeline charts. Bright line: every commitment in the proposal must be a commitment the writer would defend to the funder in person. The writer must be able to say _"I wrote this, I mean it, I will do it."_ AI can help draft; AI cannot make commitments on the writer's behalf. (Connection forward to Chapter 14: this is one of the AI-use spaces where disclosure norms in 2025 are most still-evolving — funder policies are mixed.)


### Chapter Summary

The research proposal inverts the rhetorical task of the research article: it sells future findings the writer cannot yet verify, commits to outcomes the writer cannot yet name, and persuades funders to underwrite work the writer has not yet done. The genre's voice is therefore more committed than the discussion section's voice — commit on what you will do; hedge on what nature will reveal — and the genre's structure is organized around _specific aims_ : focused, evaluable, independent subgoals.

This chapter laid out the conventional structure of a proposal (significance, aims, approach, expected outcomes, timeline, qualifications) (§9.3); the hook test (§9.4); the application of the six moves to Mira's NSF proposal (§9.5); templates for hooks, aims, methods, expected outcomes, broader impacts, timeline, and qualifications (§9.6); nine common pitfalls (§9.7); and Przeworski and Salomon's four-question framework for the proposal as a genre (§9.8). The manuscript audit prompt (§9.9) added a seventh revision to your portfolio: a hook test plus aims audit on a current or recent proposal.

Proposals are also the genre most often _resubmitted_ — first-round rejection is the modal outcome, not a verdict. Successful researchers develop a resubmission practice that treats reviewer feedback as input, revises substantially, and resubmits without spiraling. Mira's proposal, in our running example, was funded on resubmission.

In Chapter 10 we turn to the **conference paper and poster** — a genre that compresses full-paper material into talk- and visual-friendly formats, with conventions that have shifted dramatically as the _better poster_ movement and remote conference formats have spread.

> _Commit on what you will do. Hedge on what nature will reveal. Lead with stakes the funder cares about. Resubmit when rejected. The proposal is a craft, and the craft is the difference between funded and unfunded work._

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
It is the spring of Mira's fourth year. The dissertation expansion is funded (Chapter 9). The original three-city paper has been cited a few times. And Mira has been accepted to present at a major international conference on climate adaptation policy.

Two formats are involved. Mira's full paper has been accepted for a 15-minute _talk_ in a panel session. Their preliminary findings on three additional cities — early data from the funded expansion — have been accepted as a _poster_ in the conference's evening poster session.

Mira opens their laptop on a Saturday morning and stares at two empty slide decks (one for the talk, one for the poster) and asks the question every conference newcomer asks: _what's the difference between a paper and a talk? What's the difference between a paper and a poster?_

The answers are not obvious. Many conference talks are simply read-aloud papers, and they are uniformly bad. Many conference posters are simply shrunk-down papers, and they are similarly bad. Both genres are _visual + verbal_ media that demand different rhetorical work than print prose, and both have distinct conventions that most graduate students absorb only through years of attending conferences and noticing what works.

This chapter compresses those years of absorbed convention into explicit rules. We will meet Mike Morrison, whose _better poster_ movement has dramatically shifted poster design conventions in the last several years.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
### 10.1 Vignette: When a Conference Paper Should Not Be Read Aloud

Mira's first instinct for the talk is to write a 15-minute version of the paper. They open their published paper, count the words (about 8,500), divide by 150 words per minute (the typical conference speaking rate, since fast-talking loses listeners), and conclude that 15 minutes will accommodate about 2,250 words. They set out to compress the paper to 2,250 words and read it aloud.

This will be a bad talk. Listening to spoken academic prose is fundamentally different from reading written academic prose. Listeners cannot rewind. They cannot check the references. They cannot skim past dense passages. They cannot pause to think. Everything they receive must be processed in real time, in the order delivered, without external aids.

The implications for the writing — because a talk is a kind of writing — are large:

* **Linear, not branching.** Written academic prose can branch (parenthetical asides, footnotes, qualifications). Spoken academic prose must move forward; every sentence depends on the listener having retained the previous one.
* **Repetition is helpful, not redundant.** Written prose can state a key point once and trust the reader to remember; spoken prose must restate, reframe, and conclude with the same point that opened, because listeners' attention drifts.
* **Visual support is structural, not decorative.** Slides do not just illustrate the talk; they carry the weight of detail that the listener cannot retain from speech alone. Tables, figures, key terms — these belong on slides.
* **Conversational register, not paper register.** Spoken prose can use first person, contractions, occasional informality, rhetorical questions. Slavishly formal academic register sounds dead when spoken.

Mira's revised plan: write a _talk script_ of about 1,800 words (slightly under the time budget, leaving room for pauses and questions); design 12–15 slides that carry the weight of detail; rehearse three times before the conference. The talk will be related to the paper but is not the paper. It is a different genre.


### 10.2 What Conference Audiences Look For

**Can I follow along?** The single most important question. Audiences who lose the thread by minute three rarely catch up.

**Why should I care?** The hook from the paper applies, but for a talk it must arrive even faster — usually in the first 60 seconds.

**What's the headline finding?** Audiences want to know what you found before they hear how you did it. A talk that builds chronologically from background through methods to findings risks losing the audience before the findings arrive.

**Can I see what you mean?** Visual support carries the comprehension load that written prose's careful structure carries. Bad slides — text-heavy, low-contrast, busy — actively undermine the talk.

**Is this calibrated?** The hedging matrix from Chapter 7 still applies. Spoken overclaim is just as detectable as written overclaim, and Q&A audiences will probe.

**Will I want to talk to you after?** Conference talks have a secondary purpose beyond the talk itself: to attract follow-up conversations, collaborations, citations. A talk that engages the audience invites these; a talk that bores them does not.


### 10.3 The Conventions of the Conference Talk

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
#### Length and pacing

Most conference talks in the social sciences and humanities run 15–20 minutes (with 5–10 minutes for Q&A). STEM conferences sometimes have shorter slots (10–12 minutes) and sometimes longer. The first rule: _do not run over._ Running over signals disrespect for the audience and the chair, and chairs in well-run sessions will cut you off.

A useful pacing guide: 100–150 words per slide of speech, and one slide per minute on average. A 15-minute talk corresponds to 12–15 slides and roughly 1,800 words of speech. This leaves room for pauses, transitions, and the occasional joke.


#### Structure

The conventional structure of a conference talk inverts a paper's chronology in favor of a _contribution-first_ structure resembling the inverted-pyramid abstract:

  1. **Hook (1 minute):** Why should the audience care? A specific stake, a vivid example, a counterintuitive finding.
  2. **Headline finding (1 minute):** What did you find? State it in one sentence; gesture at the slide that summarizes it.
  3. **Setup (2–3 minutes):** Brief background, brief gap, brief contribution claim.
  4. **Approach (2–3 minutes):** What you did, in enough detail to make the findings credible. Not a methods section; just the headlines.
  5. **Findings (4–6 minutes):** The substance. One slide per major finding. Tables and figures carry the data.
  6. **Implications (1–2 minutes):** What does it mean? Brief. Theoretical and practical.
  7. **Closing (30 seconds):** A memorable closing sentence that the audience will retain.

Variations: research-in-progress talks emphasize methods and questions over findings; literature-review talks reorganize around the synthesis. The contribution-first opening, however, is widely beneficial.


#### Slide design

Slides are the visual companion to the talk. Bad slides — too much text, low contrast, bullet-point-heavy — actively damage the talk. Good slides:

* **One key idea per slide.** If you have two ideas, make two slides.
* **Minimal text.** Headlines and key terms only; the speech carries the prose.
* **High contrast.** Dark text on light backgrounds (or vice versa); avoid low-contrast color combinations.
* **Large fonts.** A back-row attendee should be able to read every word. Generally 24-point or larger.
* **One figure or table at a time, large.** A small figure crammed into a slide alongside text is unreadable.
* **No distracting transitions or animations.** Reveal-on-click is acceptable for staged builds; flying text is not.

The Tufte principles from Chapter 6 apply here even more strictly than in print: every visual element must communicate; chartjunk is even more damaging on a screen than on a page.


#### Voice and register

Conference talks are spoken. Drop the third-person passive academic prose. Use first person ("I argue," "we found"). Use contractions where natural. Ask occasional rhetorical questions ("Why does this matter?"). Pause for emphasis. The register is conversational-but-precise — the register of an excellent lecture, not a journal article.

A common mistake: reading the talk verbatim from a script. Audiences detect this immediately and disengage. Better practice: rehearse from speaker notes that contain the structure and the key sentences (the hook, the headline finding, the closing) verbatim, but allow the connecting prose to be ad-libbed in conversational register.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
#### Definition: The Spoken Register

The **spoken register** of an academic talk is the linguistic style appropriate to live presentation: conversational but precise, using first person, contractions, occasional rhetorical questions, and structural repetition that supports listener memory.

In plain language: the spoken register is how a skilled lecturer speaks, not how a journal article is written. A talk delivered in journal-article register sounds stilted and is hard to follow. A talk delivered in conversational register but lacking precision sounds unserious. The spoken register sits between — it sounds like an intelligent friend explaining the work to you, with the discipline of a careful argument.

ESL speakers often face an additional challenge: the spoken register varies more across languages than the written register does, and a speaker who has mastered written academic English may still default to an over-formal spoken register. The fix is exposure (listening to many talks in the target conference style) and rehearsal (recording oneself, listening back, adjusting toward conversational warmth).


#### Common Misconception

A common misconception is that a good conference talk should _cover_ as much of the paper as possible. In practice, talks should cover _less_ than the paper — typically the most important contribution, one or two key supporting analyses, and the implications. Trying to compress the whole paper into 15 minutes produces a rushed, unreadable talk.

The fix: identify the _one thing_ you most want the audience to take away. Build the talk around that one thing. Sacrifice subsidiary findings to the slides without speaking to them; mention them as available in the paper. The talk is a _teaser_ for the paper, not a _replacement_ for it.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
### 10.4 The Better Poster Movement

Posters have a longer and stranger history than talks. The conventional academic poster — descended from print-shop conventions of the 1980s — typically packs 1,000+ words of small text across multiple columns, mimicking a research article on a 4'×6' surface. These posters are nearly impossible to engage with at a poster session, where attendees walk past hundreds of posters in a 90-minute window and stop at perhaps a dozen.

A surprising fact: studies of poster session engagement have repeatedly found that _the average attendee spends less than one minute engaging with a typical poster._ Most attendees walk past without stopping; those who stop usually move on within seconds. The traditional poster format — text-heavy, structurally identical to a paper — is mismatched to how people actually interact with posters.

Mike Morrison, a graduate student at Michigan State University, made this observation in a 2019 video that went viral and launched the **better poster movement.** The Morrison redesign:

* **Headline finding in giant type, center.** The poster's central element is the finding itself, in font size readable from across the room. Not the title of the project; the _finding._
* **Brief supporting detail on the sides.** Methods, additional findings, citations — all secondary, in smaller type, on the sides.
* **A QR code or URL for the full paper.** Attendees who want details can access the paper directly; the poster does not need to deliver them.

The redesign trades comprehensiveness for _engagement_. A traditional poster delivers a paper to a reader who will not read it. A Morrison-style poster delivers a finding to a viewer who will read it in three seconds, then either move on (informed) or stop to ask questions (engaged). Engaged stops are how posters actually generate value: through conversations, follow-up emails, collaborations.

The movement has spread quickly. By the mid-2020s, Morrison-style posters are common at major conferences in psychology, biology, education research, and increasingly other fields. Some traditional fields remain attached to dense-text posters; the trend is toward better posters across the board.

For graduate writers in 2026, the implication is direct: design your poster around the finding, not around the paper. Lead with the headline visible from across the room. Use the rest of the poster to support the headline for the engaged stopper, not to deliver the paper to the disengaged passer-by.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
### 10.5 The Six Moves Applied to Mira's Talk and Poster

**Move 1 (genre/venue).** The talk is a 15-minute panel presentation at a public-administration conference; the audience is mostly mid-career and senior scholars in adaptation policy. The poster is in a poster session at the same conference; the audience is mixed (graduate students, scholars from adjacent fields, occasional practitioners). Different audiences, different rhetorical demands.

**Move 2 (structure).** Talk: contribution-first structure (§10.3). Hook (the funding-mismatch stake from the proposal). Headline finding (the fiscal-sequencing logic). Setup. Approach. Findings (four slides, one per major finding). Implications. Close. Poster: Morrison structure. Headline finding center. Methods, additional findings, scope, and contact info on sides. QR code linking to the published paper.

**Move 3 (calibration).** Talk: spoken register, first person, conversational but precise. Hedging matrix applies. Poster: minimal prose, high-stakes hedging on the headline finding (a single sentence; calibrate carefully).

**Move 4 (positioning).** Talk: brief gestures at prior work; the talk leads with finding, not literature engagement. Poster: even briefer; one sentence on the gap, max.

**Move 5 (anticipated reviewer/questioner).** Q&A predictions: _"How representative are your three cases?"_ (Mira will answer with the case-selection rationale.) _"Doesn't the sequencing logic generalize beyond mid-sized cities?"_ (Answer: probably yes in some forms; that's the next study.) _"What about [author X]'s work?"_ (Mira will be ready with the four most likely cited authors and a sentence on each.) Poster: similar questions in conversational format; rehearse short answers.

**Move 6 (AI).** Mira uses AI to: rehearse Q&A by playing the role of a hostile audience member; flag slides with too much text; suggest tighter phrasings of the headline finding for the poster. They do _not_ use AI to draft the talk script — the talk needs to sound like Mira, in their voice.

The talk is well received. Two senior scholars approach Mira after for follow-up conversations. The poster gets ten engaged stops over a 90-minute session — well above average for the conference — and three exchange business cards.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
### 10.6 Templates and Examples

**Talk hook (first 60 seconds):**

> _"Imagine [vivid scene relevant to the topic]. This is the situation in [location/context]. And the question I want to ask today is [specific question]. Because [stakes — why this matters]. [Pause.] In the next 14 minutes I'll show you [one-sentence preview of the contribution]."_

The hook is harder than it looks. It must be specific, vivid, and short. Rehearse it until you can deliver it without notes.

**Talk headline-finding sentence:**

> _"The headline finding is this: [one-sentence statement of the contribution, slow and clear, ideally with a slide that displays it in large type]."_

This sentence is the talk's anchor. The audience will retain it; everything else supports it.

**Talk transition sentence (between sections):**

> _"So that's [previous section]. Let me show you [next section]."_

Explicit transitions help listeners track the structure. Do not under-signal.

**Talk closing:**

> _"To wrap up: [restate the headline finding in one sentence]. The implications I see are [one or two implications, briefly]. And the question I'll leave you with is [a question that invites Q &A engagement]. Thank you."_

The closing is the second-most-retained part of a talk (the hook is first). Rehearse it.

**Better poster headline:**

> _"[Specific finding in giant type, ideally one declarative sentence, ideally with a number or specific detail]."_

The headline is the poster. The rest is decoration. If a viewer sees only the headline, they should know the contribution.

**Better poster supporting elements:**

> _"What we did: [one-sentence methods]. What we found beyond the headline: [2–3 brief findings]. Why it matters: [one sentence implications]. More: [QR code to paper]. Contact: [name, email]."_

Each element should be readable from 6 feet. If text is too small to read from that distance, it's too small.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
### 10.7 Common Pitfalls

**The read-aloud paper talk.** A talk that consists of reading the paper verbatim. Audiences detect this and disengage. Fix: write a talk script in spoken register, rehearse it, and don't read.

**The text-saturated slide.** A slide with 200 words of bullet points that the speaker reads aloud. Fix: cut text by 80%; let the speech carry the prose; let the slide carry the headline and the visual.

**The chronological talk that buries the finding.** A talk that builds chronologically from background through methods, with the finding revealed at minute 11. Audiences are often gone by then. Fix: contribution-first structure.

**The over-running talk.** A talk that exceeds its time slot. Fix: rehearse with a timer; cut content until the rehearsal lands at minus 1 minute (you will go over in real performance).

**The inaudible voice.** A talk delivered too quietly or too quickly. Fix: rehearse out loud, ideally with someone listening; use the microphone; slow down.

**The traditional dense poster.** A poster that crams the paper onto a 4'×6' surface. Fix: Morrison-style redesign; finding centered, large.

**The headline-less poster.** A Morrison-style poster whose "headline" is the project title rather than a finding. Fix: the headline must be the _finding_ , not the topic.

**The QR-codeless poster.** A poster without a way for engaged stoppers to access the full paper. Fix: include the QR code or URL prominently.

**The unrehearsed Q &A.** The speaker hasn't anticipated likely questions and stumbles in Q&A. Fix: pre-rehearse the three most likely questions with explicit short answers.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
### 10.8 Scholar Profile: Mike Morrison and the Better Poster Movement

Mike Morrison was a graduate student in industrial-organizational psychology at Michigan State University when, in 2019, he posted a 9-minute YouTube video titled _"How to Create a Better Research Poster in Less Time"_ that fundamentally changed the conventions of academic poster design. The video, as of the mid-2020s, has been viewed several million times and has spawned a movement of researchers redesigning their poster practices.

The pre-Morrison status quo was the _traditional academic poster_ : typically a 4'×6' or A0 surface filled with text in three to four columns mimicking a research article (introduction / methods / results / discussion), often with hundreds of words at small font sizes that no reader could engage with in the few seconds of attention a poster session allows. These posters were the convention because they had always been the convention; the format had drifted from a mid-century origin without anyone interrogating whether it served its purpose.

Morrison's diagnosis was empirical and obvious-once-stated: poster sessions are crowded environments with limited attention. The average attendee gives any single poster less than a minute. Traditional posters cannot communicate their contribution in less than a minute. Therefore, traditional posters fail the genre's basic communication test.

His redesign — _the headline finding in giant type, with supporting detail relegated to side panels and a QR code for the paper itself_ — was specifically engineered for the actual viewing conditions. A Morrison-style poster communicates its central finding in three seconds (a headline visible from across the room). Engaged viewers can then read the supporting detail; less engaged viewers leave informed of the finding rather than confused by a wall of text.

A surprising fact, sometimes underweighted: the Morrison redesign also serves the _poster presenter_ better. Standing next to a Morrison-style poster, the presenter has a natural conversational opener — the headline — and can adapt their explanation to the engaged viewer's interests. Standing next to a traditional poster, the presenter must compete with the poster's text for the viewer's attention, and the conversation is harder to start.

The movement's spread has not been universal. Some traditional fields (parts of clinical medicine, some engineering subdisciplines) remain attached to dense-text posters, partly because their poster sessions are linked to abstract booklets that include the dense detail in print. But across most of the social and biological sciences, Morrison-style posters are now common and increasingly expected.

For graduate writers in 2026, Morrison's lesson generalizes beyond posters: every academic communication should be designed for _the actual conditions of its reception_ , not for an idealized reader who reads everything carefully. Conference talks should be designed for listening in real time. Posters should be designed for 3-second triage and 90-second engagement. Abstracts should be designed for skim-readers. Discussions should be designed for reviewers. The medium and the moment matter as much as the message.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
A second surprising fact: although Morrison's video focused on visual design, the deeper move was _re-asking what the genre is for._ The poster's purpose is not to deliver a paper; it is to start a conversation. The redesign followed from that re-asking. This kind of genre re-examination — _what is this format actually for?_ — is a powerful move in many academic-writing contexts, and we will return to it in Chapter 15 when we look at patterns across the twelve forms.


### 10.9 Reader's Manuscript Audit Prompt

Take a paper of your own — published, drafted, or in progress — and design a Morrison-style poster for it.

The exercise has three parts:

**Identify the headline finding.** Read your paper and identify the single most important finding or claim. Compress it to one declarative sentence. Calibrate per the hedging matrix (Chapter 7).

**Sketch the poster.** Draw or build (in slide software, presentation software, or paper) a Morrison-style poster:

* Headline finding centered, in giant type — readable from 12 feet.
* "What we did" in 1–2 sentences on one side.
* "What we found beyond the headline" in 2–3 brief items on the other side.
* "Why it matters" in 1 sentence at the bottom.
* QR code or URL placeholder.
* Your name and contact information.

**Run the 3-second test.** Show your poster sketch to a colleague (or imagine one) for 3 seconds. Ask: _what was the headline finding?_ If they can name it, the poster works. If they can't, the headline is too long, too small, or too vague.

This is your eighth manuscript revision. The portfolio: synthesis-vs-summary audit (Ch.3), CARS introduction rewrite (Ch.4), methods replication test (Ch.5), prose-to-table redesign (Ch.6), discussion calibration audit (Ch.7), abstract compression (Ch.8), proposal hook + aims audit (Ch.9), and now the Morrison-style poster sketch.

(Bonus: take the same paper and outline a 15-minute talk, applying the contribution-first structure from §10.3. Compare the talk to the paper. What did the compression force you to clarify?)


### 10.10 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Why does the chapter argue that a conference talk should not be a read-aloud version of the paper?

Hint

The four implications of spoken vs. written prose are unpacked in §10.1.

**Answer:** Because listening to spoken academic prose differs fundamentally from reading written academic prose: listeners cannot rewind, skim, check references, or pause to think. A talk must be linear (not branching), repetitive (not redundant), visually supported (slides carry detail), and conversational in register. Reading a written paper aloud violates all four constraints, producing a talk that is dense, hard to follow, and visually under-supported.

**Q2.** What is the _better poster movement_ , and what is its core design principle?

**Answer:** The better poster movement, launched by Mike Morrison's 2019 YouTube video, redesigned the conventional academic poster around the empirical fact that poster session attendees give each poster less than a minute. The core design principle: the headline finding in giant type, centered and readable from across the room; supporting detail (methods, additional findings, citations) relegated to side panels in smaller type; and a QR code or URL for the full paper. The redesign trades comprehensiveness for engagement.

**Q3.** What is the conventional structure of a contribution-first conference talk, in seven parts?

**Answer:** From §10.3: (1) Hook (~1 minute) — why care; (2) Headline finding (~1 minute) — what was found; (3) Setup (~2–3 minutes) — brief background and gap; (4) Approach (~2–3 minutes) — methods headlines; (5) Findings (~4–6 minutes) — substance; (6) Implications (~1–2 minutes) — what it means; (7) Closing (~30 seconds) — memorable sentence to retain.

**Q4.** What is the _spoken register_ , and why does the chapter argue it is necessary for a conference talk?

**Answer:** The spoken register is the linguistic style appropriate to live presentation: conversational but precise, using first person, contractions, occasional rhetorical questions, and structural repetition that supports listener memory. The chapter argues it is necessary because written academic prose, when delivered orally, sounds stilted and is hard to follow; live presentation requires the warmth and discipline of an excellent lecture, not the formality of a journal article. ESL speakers especially benefit from explicit attention to spoken register, which varies across languages more than written register does.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Take a paper of your own and design a Morrison-style poster for it (the audit prompt from §10.9). Submit a description of your poster sketch (you may describe it in prose if you cannot build it visually) and a 200-word reflection on what the redesign exposed about the paper.

Hint

The hardest part is usually identifying the _headline finding_ — compressing the paper's contribution to a single declarative sentence. The other elements follow from the headline.

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful response will (a) identify a clear headline finding compressed to one sentence, (b) describe the supporting elements (methods, additional findings, implications), and (c) reflect on what the redesign exposed. The most common observation in successful reflections: that the headline-finding sentence was harder to write than expected — the paper's central claim was diffuse across multiple sections, and forcing it into one sentence required a clarifying choice that the paper itself had ducked. This is a common phenomenon: poster-design exposes argumentative weaknesses in the paper.

**Sample Response (Mira's three-cities paper as a Morrison-style poster):** _Headline (centered, ~120 pt): "Fiscal constraint pushes mid-sized coastal cities toward short-term, visible adaptation." Left panel (~24 pt): "What we did: 12 mid-sized cities, mixed methods (interviews + policy documents + budget data), 2018–2023." Right panel (~24 pt): "What we found beyond the headline: (i) the pattern holds across three regional contexts; (ii) electoral pressure amplifies but does not solely cause the sequencing; (iii) megacity-targeted funding programs do not transfer well to the mid-sized scale." Bottom: "Why it matters: ~30% of the global coastal population lives in mid-sized cities the field's tools have not seen well." QR code → full paper; below it, name and email. Reflection: building the poster forced Mira to rank the paper's findings — a discipline the paper's discussion section had hedged. The headline does the work the abstract used to do; the side panels do the work the introduction's gap-statement used to do; the bottom does the work of the implications paragraph. Compression revealed which of the paper's claims could survive 12-foot type and which could not._

**Q2.** Outline a 15-minute conference talk for the same paper, using the contribution-first structure from §10.3. Submit a section-by-section outline (with rough timing) and a 200-word reflection comparing the talk's structure to the paper's structure. What did the compression and reordering force you to clarify?

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful outline will (a) follow the seven-part structure with appropriate timing, (b) lead with the contribution and only later supply the background and methods, and (c) reflect on the structural reordering. Common observations: the talk forces explicit choice about which findings to feature and which to omit (the paper accommodates more); the contribution-first structure feels backward at first but reads as more engaging once tried; the closing sentence is harder to write than the opening.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
**Q3.** Attend a conference talk (live or recorded — many conferences post recordings) in your field. Identify: (a) the talk's structure (contribution-first, chronological, or other); (b) where the headline finding appears (in minutes from the start); (c) the talk's pacing (overrun? rushed? well-paced?); (d) the slide design quality. Write a 250-word commentary on what worked and what didn't. (Connection to Chapter 6: this is the same diagnostic eye that sharpens when you read other people's results sections, applied to a different medium.)

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A typical successful response will note that talks lacking a contribution-first structure tend to lose audience attention by the methods section; talks with text-heavy slides tend to feel slow and dense; talks that overrun their time tend to feel rushed at the end. The exercise teaches the diagnostic eye for talks the way reading published papers teaches the eye for prose.

**Q4.** Pick the most important finding from a paper you have written or are writing. Compose three different versions of the _headline-finding sentence_ for a Morrison-style poster — one calibrated as _Strong support_ (per the hedging matrix), one as _Reasonable support_ , and one as _Speculative_. Which is honest given your evidence? Submit all three and a 100-word reflection. (Connection to Chapter 7: the hedging matrix applied to ultra-compressed prose.)

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful response will produce three sentences with calibrated language differences (e.g., "shapes" vs. "may shape" vs. "could conceivably shape") and reflect on which is honest given the evidence. The exercise teaches that headline finding sentences are calibration-sensitive: the same finding can be claimed at different strengths, and the strength must match the evidence. Most graduate students discover that _Reasonable support_ is honest for most of their findings; _Strong support_ is rare; _Speculative_ is appropriate only for genuinely tentative claims.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The Morrison poster redesign was driven by an empirical observation about how attendees actually engage with posters. What other academic-writing genres might benefit from similar empirical re-examination — _what is this format actually for, given how it is actually consumed?_ Sketch your view in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** Many genres are ripe for similar re-examination. Conference programs (which are typically read briefly to triage talks): could be redesigned around abstracts of abstracts. Academic websites: rarely designed for the actual audiences (prospective collaborators, grant program officers, journalists). Department research statements: typically formatted around faculty preferences rather than reader needs. Annual reports: similar issue. The Morrison move generalizes: ask what the format is actually for, observe how it is actually consumed, redesign around the gap.
