Some recent reform movements (registered reports for journal articles, plain-language summaries for journal abstracts, video abstracts for some venues) follow the same logic. The deepest implication: academic conventions persist not because they serve their purpose well but because they exist; periodic empirical re-examination would benefit many of them. (Connection forward to Chapter 15: this is one of the patterns we'll see across the 12 forms.)

**Q2.** Conference formats have changed substantially in the 2020s — hybrid sessions, virtual posters, recorded talks, asynchronous Q&A. How should the conventions in this chapter adapt to these new formats? What stays the same, what changes? Sketch your view in 250 words.

**Discussion:** Much stays the same. Contribution-first structure, calibrated hedging, conversational spoken register, slide design principles — all transfer to recorded and virtual talks. What changes: virtual poster sessions often allow longer engagement than live sessions (attendees can return to a virtual poster across days), so denser supporting detail may be more valuable; recorded talks can include richer visual transitions because the speaker is not constrained by live presentation; asynchronous Q&A allows more deliberate, longer-form responses than live Q&A. The core principles persist; the implementation adapts. The new formats also expose previously hidden inequities (recorded talks favor speakers with high-quality home recording setups; asynchronous Q&A favors fluent text writers over fluent speakers). Designing for the actual conditions of reception remains the master principle. (Connection forward to Chapter 14: AI-mediated conferences — AI summaries of talks, AI-generated talk videos — are emerging and complicate the picture.)

**Q3.** AI tools can now generate slide decks, talk scripts, and poster designs from a paper. Where is this useful, and where is it dangerous? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: The Conference Paper and Poster
blocks.src:
**Discussion:** AI-generated talk scripts and slide decks are often plausible but flat — generic structure, generic phrasing, missed calibration. Useful applications: (a) generating a _first_ slide outline from a paper, which the writer then heavily revises; (b) producing alternative orderings of slides for the writer to evaluate; (c) flagging text-heavy slides that should be cut; (d) auditing slide design for high-contrast and font-size issues. Dangerous applications: (a) generating a talk script the writer then reads verbatim — the conversational warmth that makes a talk work cannot be AI-generated; (b) generating poster headlines without the writer's calibration judgment; (c) generating talks the writer has not internalized — the talk works only when the speaker can ad-lib and answer Q&A from understanding. Bright line: the writer must be able to deliver the talk in their own voice, ad-lib transitions, and answer questions in calibration. AI can scaffold; AI cannot present. (Connection forward to Chapter 14: the disclosure norms for AI-assisted presentation development are less mature than for AI-assisted paper writing.)


### Chapter Summary

Conference talks and posters are visual + verbal media that demand different rhetorical work than print prose. A conference talk is not a read-aloud paper; it is a contribution-first, slide-supported, spoken-register performance for an audience that cannot rewind. A poster is not a shrunk-down paper; it is a 3-second triage display whose central element is the headline finding, designed for the actual conditions of poster sessions in which most attendees give each poster less than a minute.

This chapter laid out the conventions of conference talks (length, pacing, structure, slide design, spoken register) (§10.3); the Morrison-style poster redesign (§10.4); the application of the six moves to Mira's talk and poster (§10.5); templates for talk hooks, headline findings, transitions, closings, and poster headlines (§10.6); nine common pitfalls (§10.7); and the contribution of Mike Morrison to making poster design empirically grounded (§10.8). The manuscript audit prompt (§10.9) added an eighth revision to your portfolio: a Morrison-style poster sketch.

The chapter's master principle — design for the actual conditions of reception, not for an idealized reader who reads everything carefully — generalizes beyond posters and talks. Every academic communication should be reverse-engineered from how it will be read, listened to, or skimmed. We return to this principle in Chapter 15.

In Chapter 11 we turn to the **peer review response** — the genre nobody teaches and almost everyone needs. Mira will receive their first major-revision request from a journal and learn that the response letter is one of the highest-leverage documents they will ever write.

> _Lead with the finding. Carry detail with visuals. Speak conversationally. Design for the actual moment of reception. The conventions persist not because they serve their purpose well — but they should._

---

It is the summer of Mira's fourth year. The talk and poster from Chapter 10 went well. The dissertation expansion is mid-way through. And Mira has just received an email from a journal where they submitted a methodological paper four months ago.

Subject: _Decision on manuscript JPP-2025-0438._

Mira opens the email with the mixture of dread and hope every academic writer learns to recognize. The decision is **major revision**. The editor's letter is courteous but firm: the paper is interesting, the methods are mostly sound, but two of the three reviewers have raised substantial concerns that must be addressed in revision. Reviewer 1 is generally positive with minor concerns. Reviewer 2 has identified what they consider a fundamental methodological flaw. Reviewer 3 has written four single-spaced pages of detailed comments, several of which are correct, several of which Mira disagrees with, and at least one of which appears to be based on a misreading of the paper.

Mira closes the email and stares at the wall for ten minutes. Then they open it again and start reading more carefully.

This chapter is about what happens next.


### 11.1 Vignette: The Cost of Reading Reviews When You're Angry

The first thing every experienced researcher will tell a graduate student about peer review is: _do not respond when you are angry._ The second thing they will tell you is: _you will be angry._

Reviewer 3's letter has the tone of someone who is annoyed. They have written _"This is a strange choice"_ about Mira's case selection. They have written _"The author seems to be unaware of the obvious objection that…"_ about a point Mira had explicitly addressed in §3.4. They have written _"It is unclear why this paper was not framed around the more important question of…"_ about a question that is not the paper's question.

Mira's first instinct is to write a response letter that defends every choice, point out every misreading, and explain in patient detail why Reviewer 3 is wrong. They draft this response. It is 4,500 words long. It is mostly accurate. It would, if submitted, almost certainly result in the paper being rejected.

The skilled response to peer review is not the response that is _correct_. It is the response that _gets the paper accepted while preserving its core intellectual contribution_. These two goals are usually compatible — but they are compatible only when the writer manages two things their first instinct fights against:

* **Acknowledge every comment, even the dumb ones.** Politely, briefly, with grace.
* **Engage seriously where the reviewer has a real point.** Even when the reviewer's tone is hostile, the substance often contains real critique.

This chapter is about the writing craft of the **response letter** — the document that accompanies a revised manuscript and addresses each reviewer comment. It is, depending on the field, the most under-taught and most career-determining document a graduate student will write.

### 11.2 What Editors and Reviewers Look For in a Response

Editors and second-round reviewers read the response letter alongside the revised manuscript. They are asking specific questions:

**Has the author addressed every comment?** Reviewers expect their comments to be acknowledged individually. Comments that are skipped — or dismissed in a sentence — read as disrespect, regardless of the comment's substantive merit.

**Has the author actually changed the paper, where appropriate?** A response that promises changes without delivering them in the manuscript will be flagged. The response letter and the manuscript revision must be aligned.

**Where the author disagrees, do they disagree carefully?** Disagreement is allowed and sometimes necessary. The convention is to disagree with reasoning, not with affect; to acknowledge the reviewer's concern even when concluding it does not require a change.

**Is the tone professional throughout?** Defensive tone, sarcasm, or visible frustration in a response letter signals that the author is hard to work with. Editors notice.

**Does the response navigate disagreement among reviewers?** Often two reviewers will give contradictory advice. The response must acknowledge the contradiction, choose a path, and justify the choice — without taking a side that alienates either reviewer.

**Is the response letter readable?** Editors process many response letters. Clear structure, explicit references to the manuscript, and concise prose make the response easier to evaluate favorably.

A response letter that meets these six criteria gives the revised paper its best chance. A response letter that fails them — even when the manuscript revisions are excellent — can sink an otherwise viable submission.


### 11.3 The Conventional Structure of a Response Letter

Response letters have a remarkably consistent structure across fields, even though they are rarely taught explicitly. The conventional template:


#### Opening (1 paragraph)

Thank the editor and reviewers. Briefly summarize the major changes. Indicate the structure of the response.

> _"We thank the Editor and three reviewers for their careful and constructive comments on our manuscript. We have revised the paper substantially in response. The most consequential changes are: (1) we have re-analyzed the budget data using a corrected exchange-rate adjustment (Reviewer 2's principal concern); (2) we have added a new subsection (§4.5) addressing the alternative interpretation Reviewer 3 raised; and (3) we have clarified the scope of our claims throughout the discussion (multiple reviewers). Below we respond to each comment in turn, with reviewer comments in italics and our responses in plain text. Page and section numbers refer to the revised manuscript."_

This opening establishes tone (gratitude, professionalism), signals scope (substantial revision), and sets expectations for the rest of the letter (numbered, comment-by-comment).

#### Per-reviewer sections

Each reviewer gets a section. Within each section, each comment gets:

* **The reviewer's comment, quoted in full** (typically in italics).
* **Your response** , beginning with an acknowledgment of the comment, followed by what you have done about it (or why you have not), with explicit reference to where the change appears in the manuscript.

Example:

> _Reviewer 2, Comment 1: "The case-selection rationale in §3.1 is weak. The authors claim regional diversity but Da Nang and Casablanca are both coastal Asian or African cities with similar colonial-era municipal frameworks. The selection seems to be driven more by data availability than by theoretical sampling logic."_
> 
> Response: We thank Reviewer 2 for this important critique. The reviewer is right that our prior framing of "regional diversity" understated the structural similarities the cases share. We have revised §3.1 to present the case selection on a different rationale — _fiscal-regime variation under shared infrastructural baselines_ — which more accurately describes the analytical logic of our comparative design (see §3.1, paragraphs 2–3, with new Table 1 mapping the variation). We have also added explicit acknowledgment in §6.4 that the cases share a colonial-municipal-framework background, and that this constrains generalization to cities outside that historical context.

Notice the structure: acknowledge the critique; characterize what changed; point at the page/section in the manuscript; do not over-defend.


#### Navigating disagreement

Sometimes the response must disagree. This is allowed and sometimes necessary, but it must be done with care:

> _Reviewer 3, Comment 5: "The paper would be more interesting if framed around the question of climate justice rather than fiscal sequencing."_
> 
> Response: We appreciate Reviewer 3's suggestion. The framing question is one we considered carefully during the revision. Our analytical contribution is empirical-comparative — characterizing a previously undocumented pattern across mid-sized cities — rather than normatively framed around justice claims. Climate justice questions are important and adjacent to our work, but they would require different methods (interviews focused on equity perceptions; analysis of distributive outcomes by neighborhood) and different theoretical engagement. We have added a paragraph in §6.4 acknowledging the climate-justice framing as a productive direction for future work, with reference to the literature Reviewer 3 cited. We hope the reviewer will find this engagement responsive even though we have retained our original framing.

Notice: the response acknowledges the suggestion, explains why the suggested change was not made (different methods, different scope), shows that the suggestion has been engaged (a paragraph added; the cited literature acknowledged), and closes with conciliatory language. The reviewer may or may not be satisfied, but the editor can see that the suggestion was taken seriously.


#### Closing (1 paragraph)

Brief restatement of gratitude and willingness to make further revisions if needed.

> _"We are grateful for the time the editor and reviewers have invested in improving this paper. We believe the revisions have substantially strengthened the contribution, and we would welcome any further suggestions. We look forward to the editor's decision."_

#### Definition: The Response Letter

A **response letter** is the document accompanying a revised manuscript that addresses each reviewer comment, indicates how (or whether) the manuscript has been changed in response, and provides explicit references to the manuscript so editors and reviewers can verify the changes.

In plain language: the response letter is a _cross-walk_ between the reviewers' comments and your revised paper. For every comment, the letter tells the editor and reviewers exactly where the revised manuscript answers it. The structure is comment → response → location, repeated dozens of times for a heavily-reviewed manuscript.

The letter is judged separately from the manuscript. A weak response letter can sink a strongly revised manuscript; a strong response letter cannot save a weakly revised manuscript, but it can substantially improve the perception of how thoughtfully the author has engaged with feedback. Editors weight the response letter heavily because it is the most direct evidence of authorial responsiveness.


#### Common Misconception

A common misconception is that the response letter should _defend_ the manuscript against critiques the author considers wrong. New writers often produce response letters that systematically refute reviewer comments and decline to make changes.

In practice, this approach almost always fails. Even when the author is technically correct, response letters that decline most changes signal _non-responsiveness_ , and editors interpret non-responsiveness as a refusal to engage with the review process. The convention is more accommodating: make changes wherever the comment has any merit, even small merit, and decline to make changes only where the comment is genuinely wrong or where the change would compromise the paper's integrity.

The skilled response letter changes more than the author thinks necessary. The principle: _make small changes for free, save your defensive ammunition for the changes that genuinely matter, and frame your disagreements with great care._ This is the survival skill of revision.

### 11.4 The Politics of Peer Review

Reviewer 3 in Mira's example is a real type. They are not a villain. They are typically someone who has too much to do, has been asked to review another paper at an inconvenient time, has skimmed it more quickly than ideal, and has formed strong opinions partly from the skim. Their tone may be sharp; their comments may be partly correct and partly off-base; their recommendation may be tougher than the paper deserves.

Bruno Latour's framing from Chapter 7 — academic discourse as negotiation — applies to peer review with special force. Peer review is not just a check for correctness. It is also:

* **A territorial claim.** Reviewers sometimes use comments to mark intellectual ground. _"The author is unaware of the work of [Author X — often the reviewer themselves]"_ is a famously common pattern.
* **A signaling exercise.** Reviewers demonstrate their own expertise to the editor through the depth and breadth of their critique.
* **A negotiation over the field's direction.** Reviewers shape what counts as worth publishing, and they exercise that shaping through their comments.
* **A quality check.** The traditional and most-discussed function — but, in practice, only one of several.

Understanding this changes how you respond. A reviewer's tone is rarely directed at you personally; it usually reflects the reviewer's mood, time pressure, and stakes in the field. A reviewer's overly aggressive comment is often an opening move in a negotiation that the editor is monitoring. The skilled response engages the substantive critique seriously while letting the affect dissipate.

This is not cynical advice. It is descriptive of how the system actually works. Pretending peer review is purely a correctness check leads to defensive response letters that miss what's really going on. Recognizing the political layer lets you respond to both substance and affect — and editors notice the distinction.

A surprising fact, attributed to senior editors and to Ferric Fang (whom we profile in §11.8): most researchers _under-respond_ to reviewer comments and _over-defend_ their original choices. The under-response is what damages the paper's chances; the over-defense compounds the damage. Calmly addressing each comment and showing what you changed is the highest-leverage skill few researchers are taught — and the skill that most distinguishes researchers whose papers move steadily through revision from researchers whose careers stall on R&R.

### 11.5 The Six Moves Applied to Mira's Response

**Move 1 (genre/venue).** A response letter for a journal in the public-administration family. The journal's instructions specify a per-comment response format with explicit references to the revised manuscript. Length is not strictly limited but most response letters in this venue run 8–20 pages.

**Move 2 (structure).** Mira drafts the structure: opening; Reviewer 1 (3 minor comments); Reviewer 2 (1 fundamental concern + 4 secondary comments); Reviewer 3 (12 comments); closing. Each comment quoted, each response specific.

**Move 3 (calibration).** Tone is professional and grateful throughout. Disagreement is rare and carefully framed. Hedging in responses uses the matrix: _"the reviewer is right that…" / "we appreciate this concern; we have addressed it by…" / "we considered this suggestion carefully and have engaged it as follows…"_

**Move 4 (positioning).** Where reviewers have cited specific prior work, Mira engages the cited work in the response — sometimes adding citations to the paper, sometimes explaining why the cited work is adjacent rather than central. The response letter becomes a small lit-review document in its own right.

**Move 5 (anticipated reviewer).** The second-round reviewers — likely the same ones — will read the response letter looking for evidence of responsiveness. Mira anticipates this by being explicit about every change, citing every section number, and quoting back the reviewer's language to demonstrate close reading.

**Move 6 (AI).** Mira uses AI to: identify reviewer comments that look superficially difficult but are addressable through a small clarification; flag responses that read as defensive (and revise toward conciliation); produce alternative phrasings of disagreement responses that test better for tone. They do _not_ use AI to _generate_ disagreements — the substantive engagement with each comment is the writer's own.

The response letter that Mira submits is 14 pages. It addresses 19 distinct comments. It makes changes — large and small — for 17 of them; declines to make a change for 2, with careful framing in each case. The paper is accepted in the second round with minor revisions.

The pattern — major revision → careful response → second-round acceptance — is the modal trajectory for papers that ultimately succeed. Most accepted papers go through at least one round of revision, and the response letter is the document that determines whether the second round goes well.

### 11.6 Templates and Examples

**Acknowledgment phrases that work:**

* _"We thank the reviewer for this important critique."_
* _"The reviewer is right that…"_
* _"We appreciate this suggestion. We have…"_
* _"This is a useful clarification. We have revised…"_

These phrases are not empty politeness. They signal close reading and willingness to engage. Use them generously.

**Pointing at the manuscript:**

* _"See §X.Y, paragraph N, for the revised treatment."_
* _"The new Table N (page X) presents the requested breakdown."_
* _"We have added a new subsection (§X.Y) addressing this concern."_

Specificity matters. Editors and reviewers should not have to hunt for the change.

**Framing disagreement:**

* _"We considered this suggestion carefully…"_
* _"We agree with the reviewer's underlying concern but have addressed it differently…"_
* _"This suggestion would substantially change the paper's scope; we have therefore retained our original framing but have added [acknowledgment / engagement / future-work note] in §X.Y."_

Disagreement is not refusal. It is a different form of engagement, and it must read that way.

**Navigating contradictory reviewer advice:**

* _"Reviewer 1 suggested [direction A]; Reviewer 2 suggested [contradictory direction B]. We have chosen [direction] on the grounds that [reasoning]. We hope this navigates the productive tension between the two suggestions; we have acknowledged the alternative direction in §X.Y."_

This is a delicate genre. The goal: make the choice transparent, justify it briefly, and acknowledge both reviewers' contributions.

**Per-comment response template:**

> _**Reviewer N, Comment M:** "[Quote the comment in full, in italics]"_
> 
> Response: [Acknowledgment sentence]. [What was done about it, briefly]. [Explicit reference to the manuscript page/section where the change appears]. [Brief closing if the response continues the discussion].

The comment-quote-then-respond format is conventional and expected. Departing from it forces the reader to flip back and forth between the response letter and the original review; do not do this.

**Closing the response letter:**

> _"We are grateful for the time the editor and reviewers have invested in improving this paper. We believe the revisions have substantially strengthened the contribution. We would welcome any further suggestions and look forward to the editor's decision."_

Conventional. Do not innovate.

### 11.7 Common Pitfalls

**The skipped comment.** A reviewer comment is not addressed in the response. Editors notice immediately, and the skip damages the paper's chances regardless of the manuscript's quality. Fix: address every comment, even briefly.

**The under-explained change.** The response says _"We have addressed this concern,"_ without specifying how or where. Reviewers cannot find the change and assume it wasn't made. Fix: specific section/page references for every change.

**The over-defensive response.** The response refutes the reviewer's reading, declines to make changes, and reads as combative. Even when the author is correct, this signals non-responsiveness. Fix: make small changes for free; save defensive responses for genuinely consequential disagreements; frame defensive responses with great care.

**The bulk-promise opening.** The response opens with _"We have addressed all reviewer comments below,"_ then proceeds to address only some of them. Editors check. Fix: ensure the opening accurately reflects the response letter's content.

**The aggrieved tone.** The response leaks frustration — _"As we already addressed in §3.4 of the original submission…"_ This signals that the author finds the review beneath them. Fix: rewrite for neutrality; the editor cannot see your frustration as warranted, only as visible.

**The unhedged disagreement.** _"The reviewer is wrong about X."_ Sometimes the reviewer is wrong, but this phrasing is rarely productive. Fix: _"We respectfully disagree with the reviewer's characterization of X, on the grounds that Y."_

**The bait-and-switch revision.** The response promises a substantial revision; the manuscript receives only minor edits. Reviewers cross-check, and the discrepancy is held against the paper. Fix: align the response letter to the manuscript revision.

**The response that ignores contradictory advice.** Two reviewers give opposite advice; the response addresses one and ignores the other. Fix: explicitly navigate the contradiction.

**The single-paragraph response.** All comments addressed in one undifferentiated paragraph. Fix: structured per-comment format.

**The unsigned response.** Most journals expect the response to include the corresponding author's signature or formal closing. Check the journal's instructions.

### 11.8 Scholar Profile: Ferric Fang and the Calibration of Revision

Ferric Fang is a microbiologist and a longtime editor whose work on peer review and scientific publishing — including the journal _mBio_ , of which he was founding editor-in-chief — has shaped how a generation of researchers think about the social technology of publishing. Fang's writing on retraction, reproducibility, and reviewer dynamics has been widely cited; his observations about response letters, distributed across editorials and conference talks rather than in any single book, have become quiet conventional wisdom for editors in many fields.

A surprising fact, paraphrased from Fang and senior editors generally: **most researchers under-respond and over-defend.** They write response letters that decline more changes than they should, defend more choices than they should, and address fewer comments than they should. The pattern produces second-round reviews that are tougher than the manuscript deserves, because reviewers (and editors) interpret under-response as disrespect.

The skilled response letter inverts this default. It addresses _every_ comment, makes small changes for free, frames disagreements with great care, and treats the response letter as a place to demonstrate the author's engagement with the field's standards. Fang has written that the response letter is one of the most under-taught documents in scientific writing — a high-stakes, recurring genre that almost no graduate program teaches explicitly.

A second surprising fact: editors often weight the response letter more heavily than second-round reviewers do. Reviewers focus on the manuscript; editors read both, and the response letter is much of what they have to evaluate the _author_ (as distinct from the _paper_). Authors who write responsive, professional response letters develop reputations among editors as good actors — and editors remember.

A third fact: response-letter craft is a meaningful predictor of long-run academic success. Researchers whose papers move through revision steadily are not necessarily those with the strongest underlying work; they are those who navigate the revision process well. The asymmetry is uncomfortable — like Przeworski and Salomon's observation about proposal craft (Chapter 9) — but real. Explicit teaching of response-letter conventions, like the explicit teaching of CARS introductions or proposal hooks, narrows the gap between researchers who learned by osmosis and researchers who didn't.

For graduate writers entering 2026, Fang's lesson is direct: the response letter is one of the highest-leverage documents you will write. Treat it with the care it deserves. The hours you spend crafting a calm, comprehensive, professionally-toned response are some of the highest-return hours in your career. The response letter is also where the temptation to be short-tempered is highest — and where short temper is most expensive.

A fourth observation, from senior editors generally: the most damaging mistake in response-letter writing is not the substantive disagreement that fails. It is the _visible frustration_ that bleeds through across multiple responses. Frustration is human; revealing it is unprofessional; and revealing it across a 14-page response letter is career-shaping. The skill is not to suppress the frustration but to write the response letter on a different day, after the frustration has cooled.

### 11.9 Reader's Manuscript Audit Prompt

If you have a recent peer review (with comments you are revising), use it. If not, use a peer review you received in the past — even a graded paper from a course, with substantive comments — or invent one for a paper you have written.

For one substantive comment, draft a response. Apply the response template:

  1. **Quote the comment in full.** Italicize it.
  2. **Acknowledge.** Use one of the acknowledgment phrases from §11.6.
  3. **Engage.** What did the reviewer get right? What did they miss? What in the paper is at issue?
  4. **Act.** What change have you made (or will you make)? Where in the paper?
  5. **Reference.** Specific section/page.

Then read the response back. Apply three checks:

* **Tone check.** Read it aloud. Does it sound professional? Does it sound defensive? If defensive, rewrite.
* **Specificity check.** Could the editor follow your response without the manuscript open? If not, add detail.
* **Hedging check.** Are your claims about what changed calibrated to what actually changed? (The hedging matrix from Chapter 7 still applies.)

This is your ninth manuscript revision. The portfolio is now substantial: you have, by Chapter 11, nine distinct revisions across nine genres of academic writing.

(Bonus: if you have a recent peer review from a paper that has _not_ yet been revised, use this exercise to draft a complete response. The response letter is the highest-leverage document you can produce in the days after receiving an R&R, and starting it carefully is most of the work.)

**Q1.** What is the conventional structure of a response letter? Name the components.

Hint

The structure is laid out in §11.3: opening, per-reviewer sections with per-comment responses, and closing.

**Answer:** The conventional structure has three components: (1) an opening paragraph thanking the editor and reviewers, briefly summarizing the major changes, and indicating the structure of the response; (2) per-reviewer sections in which each comment is quoted in full (typically italicized) and addressed individually with an acknowledgment, a description of the change made (or why no change was made), and an explicit reference to the page/section in the revised manuscript; (3) a brief closing paragraph reiterating gratitude and willingness to make further revisions if needed.

**Q2.** Why does the chapter argue that the response letter is "one of the most under-taught documents in scientific writing"?

**Answer:** Because almost no graduate program teaches response-letter writing explicitly, even though the response letter is high-stakes (it determines whether a major-revision paper is accepted), recurring (every published paper typically requires at least one response letter), and craft-dependent (poor response letters can sink strongly revised manuscripts). Editors weight the response letter heavily, sometimes more heavily than reviewers do, because it is the most direct evidence of authorial responsiveness.

**Q3.** What is the under-respond / over-defend pattern that Ferric Fang and senior editors identify, and why does it damage a paper's chances?

**Answer:** Most researchers, in their first response letters, decline more changes than they should, defend more original choices than they should, and address fewer comments than they should. This pattern damages the paper's chances because editors and second-round reviewers interpret under-response as disrespect for the review process; even when the author is substantively correct, response letters that decline most changes signal non-responsiveness and produce second-round reviews tougher than the manuscript deserves.

**Q4.** Name three of the conventional acknowledgment phrases that effective response letters use.

Hint

The §11.3 example for Reviewer 3, Comment 5 illustrates one approach. Try producing your own version with a different acknowledgment phrasing or a different forward-looking gesture.

**Answer:** A successful response will (a) quote the comment in italics, (b) open with an acknowledgment phrase that does not concede the framing critique while showing the reviewer's suggestion has been considered, (c) explain why the suggested reframing was not adopted (different methods, different scope), (d) demonstrate engagement (a paragraph added; the cited literature acknowledged; a future-work note), and (e) close with conciliatory language. Our analytical contribution is [original framing], which differs from a [X] framing in [specific ways]. The [X] framing would require [different methods/scope]. **Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful response will (a) accurately quote each comment, (b) produce a response that acknowledges, engages, acts, and references; (c) maintain professional tone throughout; (d) calibrate the description of changes to what was actually done. **Sample Response (one of Mira's responses, abridged):** _Reviewer 2 comment, in italics: "_The case selection rationale is not adequately defended; the three cities chosen seem convenient rather than analytically justified._ " Acknowledge: "We thank Reviewer 2 for pressing us on case selection. The point is well-taken." Engage: "On re-reading, we agree that §3.2 leaves the rationale implicit. We followed a most-different design across three dimensions (regional context, fiscal regime, adaptation history), but the three dimensions and their warrant for the design were not made explicit; the reader was left to reconstruct them." Act: "We have rewritten §3.2 (pp. 8–10 in the revision) to (i) name the three case-selection dimensions, (ii) cite Hallegatte (2013) as the typology source, (iii) provide a 12-city table showing how the chosen three cases score on each dimension relative to the broader population of mid-sized coastal cities, and (iv) acknowledge the dimensions our design does not vary (notably, primary language of municipal administration). Reference: "Please see §3.2 (pp. 8–10), Table 2 (p. 11), and §5.4 (p. 22) of the revised manuscript." Reflection: drafting this response took 90 minutes, which felt long for a single comment. The time was almost entirely spent on the _engage_ step — articulating what the reviewer got right was harder than describing what changed. The response that emerged is, as a result, calmer and more responsive than a faster draft would have been._

**Q3.** Find a published paper accompanied by its review history (some journals — _eLife_ , _PLOS One_ , _Royal Society Open Science_ — publish review histories openly). (Connection: this is the diagnostic eye sharpened on a high-stakes genre.)

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A typical successful response will note that strong response letters are characterized by (a) explicit per-comment structure, (b) calibrated tone (gratitude without obsequiousness), (c) specific references to the manuscript, (d) careful framing of disagreements. Common improvement opportunities even in published response letters: occasional skipped comments, occasional defensive flashes in the prose, occasional under-specification of changes. The exercise teaches that response-letter craft is a real skill with measurable variation even among published authors.

**Q4.** Two reviewers have given contradictory advice on a paper of yours: Reviewer 1 wants you to expand a particular section; Reviewer 2 wants you to cut it. Draft a response that navigates this contradiction. (Connection to Chapter 11's templates section: this is the contradictory-advice template applied to a specific case.)

**Answer:** A successful response will (a) acknowledge both reviewers explicitly, (b) name the contradiction directly rather than ignoring it, (c) make a specific choice with brief reasoning, (d) acknowledge the alternative direction (typically by adding a brief engagement with the not-chosen path), and (e) close with conciliatory language. Example: _"Reviewer 1 suggested expanding §X to address [aspect A]; Reviewer 2 suggested cutting §X as tangential. We have chosen to retain §X with modest expansion (~200 words on aspect A, see p. Y) on the grounds that [reasoning]. We have addressed Reviewer 2's underlying concern by tightening the prose in §X and clarifying its argumentative function in §X.1. We hope this navigates the productive tension between the two suggestions."_

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The chapter argues that peer review is _partly performative_ — that reviewers are signaling territory and expertise, not only checking correctness. Some critics argue this framing is too cynical; others argue it's too forgiving of bad behavior. Where do you stand? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** Both critiques have merit. The framing is realistic: empirical surveys of reviewer behavior consistently find that comments often track reviewer interests and expertise rather than purely-substantive critique, and that reviewer tone often reflects mood and time pressure as much as the manuscript's quality. The framing is forgiving: it does not excuse abusive or hostile reviews; it only describes them. The skilled response acknowledges the partly-performative dimension without excusing reviewer misbehavior. When a reviewer has been substantively wrong or rhetorically hostile, the author can still respond professionally — partly because the editor is watching, partly because professional responses are better-aimed at the editor and second-round reviewers than defensive ones. The cynical reading ("it's all politics") and the naive reading ("it should be only correctness") both miss the point: peer review is a social system that mostly works, occasionally fails, and rewards skilled navigators. (Connection to Chapter 7's discussion of Latour: this is academic discourse as negotiation, applied to a specific high-stakes genre.)

**Q2.** Some journals and movements (post-publication peer review, registered reports, signed reviews) are reforming the peer review system. How do these reforms change the response-letter genre — or do they? Sketch your view in 250 words.

**Discussion:** Post-publication peer review largely sidesteps the response letter (comments accumulate publicly; authors respond in different formats). Registered reports change the structure: peer review of the _methods_ happens before data collection, so the response letter for the eventual paper is partly about how the executed methods compare to the registered protocol. Signed reviews change the tone: reviewers whose names appear on their reviews tend to be more measured, and authors tend to respond differently to named reviewers than to anonymous ones. The conventions of the genre — comment-quote-acknowledge-act-reference — persist across reforms. What shifts is the political dimension: signed reviews diminish (some of) the territorial dynamics; pre-registration shifts (some of) the disagreement to the methods phase. The fundamental skill — calibrated, comprehensive, professionally-toned response — transfers. (Connection forward to Chapter 17: AI-assisted peer review and AI-mediated response letters are emerging frontiers.)

**Q3.** AI tools can now read review letters and draft responses. Some writers paste the reviewer comments and ask the AI to produce per-comment responses. What are the integrity risks and acceptable uses? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** Response letters are documents in which the author makes representations to the editor about what they have done. AI-drafted responses risk: (a) misdescribing changes the author has not actually made; (b) making concessions the author would not have made; (c) declining changes the author should have made; (d) producing tone that sounds responsive but lacks the substantive engagement an editor can detect. Acceptable uses: (a) using AI to suggest tone-improvement on writer-drafted responses (rephrasing defensiveness toward conciliation); (b) using AI to flag responses that are under-specified or that miss reviewer points; (c) using AI to help structure a long response letter (per-reviewer organization, consistency of formatting); (d) using AI to play the role of a second-round reviewer reading the response. Bright line: the substantive engagement with each comment must be the author's; AI cannot stand in for the author's judgment about what the comment means and what the manuscript should do in response. The response letter is, in this sense, like the proposal: a document of commitment that must reflect what the author would defend in person. (Connection forward to Chapter 14: AI-assisted peer review responses are widely used in 2025 with varying disclosure norms; the safest practice is heavy AI assist on tone and structure, light to none on substance.)
