It is the fall of Mira's fifth year. The dissertation is in its drafting middle game. A senior economist at another university — Dr. Elena Reyes, mid-career, with prior work on municipal-finance dynamics in Latin America — has read Mira's published fiscal-sequencing paper and reached out to propose a collaboration: a co-authored paper that combines Mira's qualitative case-study evidence on adaptation sequencing with Reyes's quantitative analysis of municipal budget panel data across 200 coastal cities globally.

It would be Mira's first co-authored paper across disciplines. The intellectual fit is real — the qualitative case studies provide mechanism evidence that the quantitative panel cannot generate; the quantitative panel provides generalizability evidence the case studies cannot generate. Together they could make a much stronger paper than either could make alone.

Two weeks into the collaboration, Mira and Reyes have a problem. They have written a draft introduction together, and they cannot agree on it.

Reyes wants the introduction to lead with the panel-data finding — _across 200 coastal cities, fiscal capacity is associated with adaptation investment in patterns consistent with sequencing logic._ Mira wants the introduction to lead with the case-study mechanism — _fiscal sequencing operates through specific budget allocation pathways visible in mid-sized cities under stress._ Both leads are defensible. They imply different framings of the contribution. They will appeal to different reviewers. And they reveal something deeper: Mira and Reyes are operating in different disciplinary conventions, even though they are both working on the same data.

This chapter is about writing across disciplines — what shifts when the audience spans fields, when co-authors come from different methodological traditions, and when a paper must satisfy reviewer pools with divergent conventions.

### 13.1 Vignette: Two Disciplines, One Paper

Mira's home discipline is policy studies, with strong qualitative-comparative methods training. The conventions Mira has internalized: theory-rich introductions, case-selection rationales that emphasize comparability, methods sections that detail interview protocols and coding schemes, results sections that interleave quotation and pattern characterization, discussions that engage policy implications.

Reyes's home discipline is applied economics, with quantitative-empirical methods training. The conventions Reyes has internalized: empirical-puzzle introductions, identification strategies that defend causal interpretation, methods sections that specify regression equations and variable construction, results sections built around regression tables, discussions that engage theoretical implications and external validity.

The two sets of conventions do not flatly conflict, but they are not the same. A paper in _Mira's_ tradition would open with a problem and a gap; a paper in _Reyes's_ tradition would open with a puzzle and an empirical strategy. A paper in Mira's tradition would have a methods section organized around case selection and data triangulation; a paper in Reyes's tradition would have a methods section organized around variable construction and identification. The vocabulary diverges, the citation density diverges, the calibration diverges (economics tends toward sparser hedging than policy studies), the presentation of results diverges.

The collaboration's first task — before the science can advance — is to negotiate a shared paper. The negotiation is partly intellectual (which framing best captures the contribution) and partly social (which discipline's reviewer pool will the paper target). It is also a writing problem with no fully satisfactory solution: any choice will please one tradition more than the other, and the cross-disciplinary paper will read as slightly _foreign_ to readers in either discipline alone.

The skilled cross-disciplinary writer accepts this and works with it. The methods section in their final paper will be longer than either discipline's norm, because each tradition's conventions must be partly explained. The introduction will engage two literatures, with care to characterize each fairly. The discussion will speak to two implications strands, calibrated for each. The result will not be a paper that perfectly satisfies either discipline's purist; it will be a paper that _both_ disciplines find readable and credible. That is the cross-disciplinary writing achievement.

### 13.2 What Reviewers Look For in Cross-Disciplinary Writing

Cross-disciplinary papers face a tougher review challenge: they are typically read by reviewers from both contributing fields, and reviewers from each field bring their own conventions to the read. Editors of cross-disciplinary venues often try to assemble reviewer panels that span the contributing fields, which means the paper must satisfy two (or more) sets of expectations simultaneously.

**Is the contribution legible to _both_ fields?** A paper that requires fluency in Field A to understand it will lose Field B reviewers, and vice versa. The framing must be accessible to both.

**Are the methods explained for both audiences?** Methods sections in cross-disciplinary papers run longer because what is conventional in Field A may be unfamiliar in Field B. Both fields' readers need enough context to evaluate the methods.

**Are the citation patterns balanced?** If the paper cites Field A heavily and Field B lightly, Field B reviewers feel the paper is not serious about their tradition. Balanced citation signals respect.

**Is the calibration appropriate for both audiences?** Different fields hedge differently; the paper must navigate. Often the right calibration is the _more conservative_ of the two field norms, applied throughout.

**Are the contributions to each field articulated?** A cross-disciplinary paper typically makes related but distinct contributions to its contributing fields. The discussion should articulate both.

**Is the writing accessible without dumbing down?** Cross-disciplinary writing must avoid both extremes: the jargon-heavy prose that one discipline produces (alienating the other) and the over-simplified prose that loses precision. The middle path is harder to write than either extreme.

A cross-disciplinary paper that meets these six criteria has a fighting chance. A paper that fails any of them — particularly the first (contribution legibility) — risks being rejected by reviewers from one or both fields.


### 13.3 The Conventional Differences Across Disciplines

Some of the conventional differences across disciplines that cross-disciplinary writers must navigate:


#### Introduction conventions

* _Empirical sciences_ : CARS (Chapter 4), often with a statistical or empirical hook.
* _Theoretical sciences_ : opens with a conceptual puzzle, often with light citation, building to the new framework.
* _Humanities_ : often opens with a vivid example or scene, with the contribution emerging through extended argument rather than being announced.
* _Social sciences_ : variable; ranges from CARS-strict (quantitative subfields) to humanities-style (qualitative subfields).


#### Methods conventions

* _Lab sciences_ : detailed protocols, often with reference to standard procedures by name.
* _Computational sciences_ : data sources, code repositories, computational environment.
* _Quantitative social science_ : sample, measurement instruments, statistical models, identification strategy.
* _Qualitative social science_ : case selection, data collection, coding, reflexivity.
* _Humanities_ : typically a "sources" or "approach" section rather than a "methods" section; emphasizes the archive, corpus, or theoretical lens.

#### Results conventions

* _Lab sciences_ : figures and statistical tables; often a Results-and-Discussion combined section.
* _Computational sciences_ : benchmark tables, algorithmic comparisons.
* _Quantitative social science_ : regression tables, marginal-effects figures.
* _Qualitative social science_ : thematic narratives with quotations, often organized by finding rather than chronology.
* _Humanities_ : typically integrated into the argument rather than presented separately; the analysis _is_ the result.


#### Citation conventions

* _Lab sciences_ : dense in introduction, sparse in methods and results, dense again in discussion.
* _Quantitative social science_ : similar to lab sciences but somewhat denser overall.
* _Qualitative social science_ : dense throughout, with detailed engagement of theoretical literature.
* _Humanities_ : very dense throughout; engagement with secondary literature is part of the contribution.


#### Voice conventions

* _Lab sciences_ : third-person passive, with growing acceptance of first-person plural.
* _Computational sciences_ : first-person plural (active) is now dominant.
* _Quantitative social science_ : variable; both passive and first-person plural common.
* _Qualitative social science_ : first-person singular is increasingly common, especially for ethnographic and reflexive methods.
* _Humanities_ : first-person singular widespread; varies by subfield.


#### Length conventions

* _High-impact general science journals_ (Nature, Science): under 4,000 words main text.
* _Specialized empirical journals_ : 7,000–10,000 words.
* _Theory papers_ (across disciplines): often longer, 10,000–15,000 words.
* _Humanities articles_ : 8,000–12,000 words; some run to 15,000.
* _Working papers_ (economics, policy): often 40–60 pages including appendices.

These differences are not arbitrary. They reflect different evidentiary structures, different reading practices, and different scholarly traditions. Cross-disciplinary writers must understand them, navigate them, and sometimes compromise across them. The compromise should be deliberate, not accidental.


#### Definition: Cross-Disciplinary Writing

**Cross-disciplinary writing** is academic writing that draws on the conventions, methods, or literatures of more than one discipline, and that targets a readership spanning those disciplines.

In plain language: cross-disciplinary writing is what happens when a paper, a co-authored project, a dissertation, or a book speaks to readers from multiple fields. It is distinct from _interdisciplinary_ writing (which often implies a more thoroughly integrated theoretical synthesis) and from _transdisciplinary_ writing (which often implies engagement with non-academic stakeholders), though the terms are used inconsistently.

Cross-disciplinary writing is increasingly common. The questions that motivate much contemporary research — climate change, AI ethics, public health, economic inequality, political polarization — span disciplines, and the writing that addresses them must too. Most graduate students entering academic careers in 2026 will write at least some cross-disciplinary work; many will write predominantly cross-disciplinary work.

#### Common Misconception

A common misconception is that cross-disciplinary writing is simply "writing for a wider audience" — making the prose more accessible by removing jargon. In practice, cross-disciplinary writing is harder than that. The challenge is not just to remove field-specific jargon but to explain _the conventions_ of each contributing field without insulting the experts in those fields.

A second misconception is that cross-disciplinary writing should adopt the conventions of the _more prestigious_ contributing field — that, say, a humanities-and-economics paper should adopt economics conventions because they are more "rigorous." This view reflects disciplinary chauvinism rather than cross-disciplinary craft. Skilled cross-disciplinary writers respect both contributing fields' conventions and find a hybrid that serves the paper's contribution.

A third misconception is that the difficulty of cross-disciplinary writing is mainly logistical — coordinating with co-authors, satisfying multiple reviewer pools. The deeper difficulty is intellectual: cross-disciplinary work requires the writer to _think across_ the conventions, not just to _write across_ them. This is part of why genuinely good cross-disciplinary work is rare and prized.


### 13.4 The Methods Section as Cross-Disciplinary Crux

A surprising fact about cross-disciplinary papers: their **methods sections are typically 2–3 times longer than the methods sections of single-discipline papers** in either contributing field. The reason is that each contributing tradition's conventions must be partly explained for the other field's readers.

For Mira and Reyes's collaboration, the methods section will need to:

* Describe the qualitative case-study sample and the 12-city case selection (familiar to Mira's policy-studies audience; less familiar to Reyes's economics audience).
* Describe the panel-data construction and the 200-city sample (familiar to Reyes's audience; less familiar to Mira's).
* Explain how the two data sources relate to each other and how they jointly support the paper's contribution (familiar to neither audience as a methods convention; new explanation needed).
* Justify the integration of qualitative and quantitative evidence (familiar to mixed-methods researchers; less familiar to method-pure researchers in either tradition).
* Acknowledge the limits of the integration and the questions that remain.

A single-discipline paper would handle each of these in a paragraph; the cross-disciplinary paper needs sub-sections for each, with brief but careful explanation of the methodological choices for readers who do not share the writer's training.

The longer methods section is the price of the cross-disciplinary paper's reach. Cutting it to single-discipline length means losing one or both audiences. Skilled cross-disciplinary writers accept the length trade-off and use it well.

### 13.5 The Six Moves Applied to Mira and Reyes's Co-Authored Paper

**Move 1 (genre/venue).** The paper is targeted at a cross-disciplinary policy journal that publishes both qualitative and quantitative work and that has reviewer pools spanning several social science disciplines. Length: 9,000 words. The three-paper read of the journal shows: hybrid methods sections, cross-discipline citations, calibrated hedging.

**Move 2 (structure).** Joint structure decisions: introduction leads with a _combined_ finding (the panel-data pattern is consistent with the case-study mechanism); methods section splits into two main subsections (qualitative; quantitative) plus an integration subsection; results section presents the panel results and case studies in parallel, with a synthesis subsection; discussion integrates implications for both adaptation theory and adaptation policy.

**Move 3 (calibration).** Joint calibration choice: the more conservative tradition's hedging applied throughout — policy studies hedges more heavily than applied economics, so the paper hedges at the policy-studies level. This protects against overclaim from the reviewer pool that hedges most.

**Move 4 (positioning).** Joint citation strategy: balanced engagement of both fields' literatures. The introduction cites both qualitative case-study work (Mira's tradition) and quantitative cross-city panel work (Reyes's tradition). Reviewers from each field should see their tradition fairly represented.

**Move 5 (anticipated reviewer).** Joint anticipated objections: _"Why combine qualitative and quantitative methods at all?"_ (defended in the integration subsection); _"Aren't the qualitative cases too few to support cross-validation with the panel?"_ (defended in §3.5); _"Aren't the panel data too coarse to capture the mechanism the case studies identify?"_ (defended in §3.6); _"Isn't this two papers stapled together?"_ (defended in the integration subsection and the discussion's synthesis section). The paper must answer each of these.

**Move 6 (AI).** The collaborators use AI to: identify discipline-specific jargon that should be defined or rephrased for the cross-disciplinary audience; flag calibration inconsistencies between the two authors' drafted sections; produce alternative orderings of the methods subsections. They do _not_ use AI to navigate the substantive intellectual disagreements about framing — those require the co-authors to talk.

The paper is drafted across four months of biweekly co-author meetings, three rounds of mutual revision, and one substantial restructuring after a friendly reading by a senior cross-disciplinary scholar. It is submitted to the cross-disciplinary policy journal. It receives a major-revision decision; the response letter (Chapter 11) takes another two months. The paper is accepted on resubmission.

### 13.6 Negotiating with Co-Authors Across Disciplines

The writing problem of the cross-disciplinary paper sits inside a _collaboration_ problem: how to work productively with co-authors whose training, conventions, and intuitions differ from yours. Some practical guidance:

**Establish authorship order early.** Different fields have different conventions: in lab sciences, first-author and last-author positions carry specific meanings; in economics, alphabetical ordering is widely used; in humanities, single authorship is more common and co-authors are often listed in contribution order. Cross-disciplinary teams should explicitly agree on an authorship convention at the start, not negotiate it at the end.

**Establish convention agreements early.** Will the paper hedge at the more conservative or the more liberal calibration? Will the methods section explain each tradition's conventions for the other field, or assume readers will look up unfamiliar terms? Will citation density follow Field A or Field B norms? These choices affect dozens of writing decisions; making them once, early, prevents continual negotiation.

**Establish responsibility allocation.** Who drafts which sections? Who has final say on the introduction, the methods, the discussion? Cross-disciplinary papers benefit from explicit allocation: typically, each co-author drafts the methods subsection corresponding to their tradition; introduction and discussion are jointly drafted; results are co-drafted with the data lead taking primary authorship.

**Schedule regular meetings.** Asynchronous-only collaboration on cross-disciplinary papers tends to produce paper-thin coordination. Biweekly or monthly meetings, even brief ones, surface disagreements before they become structural.

**Read each other's traditions.** Genuinely good cross-disciplinary collaborators read substantially in the partner's discipline. This builds the mutual literacy that makes intellectual disagreements productive rather than frustrating.

**Allow the paper to be slightly foreign to both of you.** A cross-disciplinary paper cannot be perfectly comfortable for either author. Both should expect to write some passages they would not have written alone — and to be fine with that.

These are collaboration tips, not writing tips. But cross-disciplinary writing is a collaboration problem; the writing follows from how the collaboration goes.

#### Authorship Ethics in Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration

A separate concern, often quietly mishandled in cross-disciplinary work: _authorship credit_. Different fields use different conventions. Many STEM fields treat first-author and last-author positions as carrying specific signals (first = lead writer; last = senior PI). Most humanities fields use alphabetical order or treat single-authorship as the norm. Economics and many social sciences vary. Cross-disciplinary papers are written under whichever convention the contributing fields find legible — but the convention has implications for how the work counts toward each author's career, and the convention can advantage one author at the cost of another in subtle ways.

A useful framework that has gained traction across fields is the **CRediT taxonomy** (Contributor Roles Taxonomy, originally developed by CASRAI and now maintained as an ANSI/NISO standard), which specifies fourteen role categories — conceptualization, data curation, formal analysis, funding acquisition, investigation, methodology, project administration, resources, software, supervision, validation, visualization, writing (original draft), and writing (review and editing) — and asks each contributor to declare their roles. Many journals now require CRediT declarations for accepted papers; some funders use CRediT-style language in proposals. For cross-disciplinary collaborations, declaring CRediT roles explicitly — early, in writing, before drafting begins — can prevent the later disputes that authorship-order conventions alone cannot resolve.

Two related cautions: _gift authorship_ (listing senior collaborators who did not substantially contribute as authors, often as a courtesy to the lab head or department chair) and _ghost authorship_ (substantial contributors omitted from the byline, often graduate students or postdocs whose work was incorporated into the paper) are integrity violations under most journal and funder norms. Both are more common in cross-disciplinary teams than in single-discipline teams, partly because the contributing roles are harder to track when collaborators come from different lab cultures. The conversation about who is and is not an author belongs at the start of the collaboration, not at submission.

### 13.7 Templates and Examples

**Cross-disciplinary introduction (joint framing):**

> _"Across [topic], two distinct literatures have addressed the question: [Tradition A literature, with citations] using [methods of A]; and [Tradition B literature, with citations] using [methods of B]. The two literatures have rarely engaged each other directly, despite their complementary perspectives. This paper integrates the two traditions through [specific integration strategy]. We argue [contribution]. The contribution speaks to both [Tradition A's debate] and [Tradition B's debate]."_

**Methods cross-walk paragraph:**

> _"Our analysis combines [methods from Tradition A] and [methods from Tradition B]. For readers familiar with one tradition but not the other, we briefly note: [Tradition A method] involves [brief explanation]; [Tradition B method] involves [brief explanation]. The two are integrated through [integration strategy] (see §X for detail)."_

**Discussion's two-implications structure:**

> _"The findings have implications for two related debates. For [Tradition A's debate], they suggest [specific implication for A]. For [Tradition B's debate], they suggest [specific implication for B]. Together, these implications point toward [synthesis claim] — a claim neither tradition could establish alone."_

**Limitation paragraph that engages cross-disciplinary critique:**

> _"Two methodological limits warrant attention. From the perspective of [Tradition A], [A-relevant limit, with implication]. From the perspective of [Tradition B], [B-relevant limit, with implication]. Both limits indicate productive directions for future work; neither, in our view, undermines the central finding."_

These templates structure the cross-disciplinary moves; the prose around them must still be written in coherent voice across the paper.

### 13.8 Common Pitfalls

**The ventriloquism problem.** Each section reads as written by the co-author whose tradition it represents, with shifts in voice, hedging, and citation that reveal who wrote what. Fix: voice-pass on the full paper; harmonize calibration; the paper should sound like _one_ document, not two.

**The under-explained methods.** Each tradition's methods are described as if to insiders, leaving the other tradition's readers behind. Fix: cross-walk paragraphs and brief explanations for the other audience.

**The ignored contributing field.** One field's literature is engaged thoroughly; the other is engaged superficially. Reviewers from the slighted field will rightly flag this. Fix: balanced citation; substantial engagement with both fields' literatures.

**The dumbing-down problem.** In an effort to accessibility, the paper removes nuance and reads as superficial to experts in both contributing fields. Fix: explain conventions without simplifying claims; the audience can handle precision if the conventions are explained.

**The unresolved framing dispute.** The co-authors disagreed about framing and the paper reflects the disagreement — different sections frame the contribution differently. Fix: resolve framing disputes before drafting, even at the cost of difficult conversations.

**The wrong-venue paper.** A cross-disciplinary paper submitted to a discipline-pure journal whose reviewer pool will see the paper as foreign. Fix: target cross-disciplinary venues, or identify the _primary_ discipline whose reviewer pool will be most sympathetic to the paper's framing.

**The methods-section bloat.** The methods section, longer than either discipline's norm, becomes unreadable. Fix: structure the methods section carefully; use sub-headings; appendices for the most detailed material.

**The acknowledgment landmine.** Acknowledgments and authorship credits don't follow either discipline's full conventions, alienating readers from both. Fix: explicit conversation about credit conventions early; check the journal's specific guidance.

### 13.9 Scholar Profile: Suresh Canagarajah and the Translingual Frame

**Suresh Canagarajah** is a sociolinguist and writing scholar at Penn State, where he holds the Edwin Erle Sparks chair in Applied Linguistics, English, and Asian Studies. Born and educated in Sri Lanka, Canagarajah began his teaching career at the University of Jaffna during the country's civil war — an experience that shaped his attention to how academic writing's dominant conventions privilege some traditions and marginalize others. His major books — _A Geopolitics of Academic Writing_ (2002, Pittsburgh), _Critical Academic Writing and Multilingual Students_ (2002, Michigan), and _Translingual Practice_ (2013, Routledge, awarded the Modern Language Association's Mina P. Shaughnessy Prize) — have reshaped how applied linguistics, composition studies, and academic writing pedagogy think about writers who move across languages, traditions, and disciplines.

A surprising fact, central to Canagarajah's framework: **the dominant Anglophone academic writing conventions are not universal scholarly norms; they are the conventions of one tradition that has come to dominate global publication, and learners from other traditions face structural translation costs that native participants do not bear.** What Canagarajah names the _geopolitics_ of academic writing applies as forcefully to cross-disciplinary work as to cross-language work. A scholar moving from anthropology to economics performs some of the same translation work as a scholar moving from Spanish-tradition academic prose to Anglophone academic prose: each must learn the host tradition's conventions, hedging norms, citation patterns, and tacit expectations while preserving the analytical contribution carried over from their home tradition.

A second surprising fact, from Canagarajah's empirical studies of multilingual academic writers: **skilled cross-tradition writers do not "switch" between conventions cleanly; they negotiate a hybrid voice that reads as slightly foreign to readers in either tradition alone.** Canagarajah calls this _code-meshing_ — the deliberate weaving of two traditions' conventions into a single text. Code-meshing is often penalized by reviewers trained in monolingual or single-discipline norms, but it is the move that distinguishes serious cross-tradition work from mere translation. Cross-disciplinary papers, on this framework, should expect to read as somewhat foreign to readers in either contributing field; skilled cross-disciplinary writers learn to make the foreignness productive rather than alienating.

A third surprising fact, increasingly documented across applied linguistics and writing studies: **methods sections in cross-tradition papers — whether cross-language or cross-discipline — are systematically longer than methods sections in single-tradition papers in either contributing field** , often 2–3 times longer. Each tradition's conventions must be partly explained for the other tradition's readers, and the translation costs words. The pattern holds whether the "translation" is between Arabic and English academic prose or between econometrics and ethnography.

A fourth fact, on the scholarly economics: **cross-tradition papers face higher rejection rates than single-tradition equivalents at most journals** , but those that do publish often show higher citation impact, after a longer lag. Reviewer pools for cross-tradition work are harder to assemble; calibration choices that satisfy one tradition disappoint the other. Publishing cross-tradition work is slower, more iterative, and more failure-prone than publishing single-tradition work — but the work, when it does publish, reaches multiple scholarly communities and shapes them.

A fifth fact: **co-authored cross-disciplinary papers are far more common in 2026 than they were in 2010.** Funding has increasingly required cross-disciplinary teams (NSF's Convergence Research initiative; ERC's Synergy grants); the tools for cross-disciplinary collaboration have improved (shared digital infrastructure; AI-assisted translation between fields); and the questions facing scholarship continue to span fields. Most graduate students entering academic careers in 2026 will participate in at least some cross-disciplinary co-authorship.

For graduate writers entering 2026, Canagarajah's lesson is direct: cross-disciplinary writing is a specific case of a more general phenomenon — _cross-tradition_ writing — and the skills travel. Read substantially in your collaborating field's conventions. Expect the methods section to be longer than either field's norm. Write a hybrid voice with deliberate care; don't try to ventriloquize either tradition perfectly. Anticipate slower review and higher rejection rates. The skills, like all the skills in this book, are learnable, and the work, when it succeeds, contributes to a scholarship that no single tradition could produce alone.


### 13.10 Reader's Manuscript Audit Prompt

If you are working on a cross-disciplinary project, identify a co-author negotiation you have avoided.

Most cross-disciplinary collaborators have at least one — a framing dispute, a conventions disagreement, an authorship question, a journal-target divergence. The negotiations are uncomfortable, and the temptation is to draft around them rather than resolve them.

The audit:

  1. **Name the negotiation.** What is the specific point of disagreement?
  2. **Articulate both sides.** In one paragraph each, write the case for your position and the case for the co-author's position. The exercise is to see the disagreement clearly, not to win it.
  3. **Identify the cost of avoiding it.** What does the unresolved disagreement cost the paper? (Often: drift between sections, unresolved framing, wasted revision time.)
  4. **Plan a conversation.** What would you say to your co-author to surface and resolve the disagreement? Draft 3–5 sentences.

This is your eleventh manuscript revision — one per Part II chapter, accumulating toward the twelve portfolio revisions this book tracks. The portfolio completes with Chapter 14.

(If you don't have a current cross-disciplinary collaboration, do this exercise for a hypothetical case: imagine a paper you might co-author with a scholar from an adjacent field, name a likely framing disagreement, and walk through the audit. The exercise teaches the diagnostic eye for collaboration friction that even experienced co-authors find useful.)


### 13.11 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is _cross-disciplinary writing_ , and how does the chapter distinguish it from related terms like _interdisciplinary_ and _transdisciplinary_ writing?

Hint

The Definition box in §13.3 names cross-disciplinary writing and the related distinctions.

**Answer:** Cross-disciplinary writing is academic writing that draws on the conventions, methods, or literatures of more than one discipline, targeting a readership spanning those disciplines. The chapter distinguishes it from _interdisciplinary_ writing (which often implies a more thoroughly integrated theoretical synthesis) and from _transdisciplinary_ writing (which often implies engagement with non-academic stakeholders), though the terms are used inconsistently across fields.

**Q2.** Why do methods sections in cross-disciplinary papers typically run 2–3 times longer than in single-discipline papers?

**Answer:** Because each contributing tradition's conventions must be partly explained for the other field's readers. A single-discipline paper assumes its reader shares the conventions of the field; a cross-disciplinary paper has readers from multiple fields, and what is conventional in Field A may be unfamiliar in Field B. The longer methods section is the cost of cross-disciplinary reach — and skilled cross-disciplinary writers accept the trade-off and use the length well.

**Q3.** Name three of the conventional differences across disciplines that cross-disciplinary writers must navigate.

**Answer:** From §13.3: introduction conventions (CARS in empirical sciences; vivid scenes in humanities; etc.); methods conventions (lab protocols; computational pipelines; case selection; etc.); results conventions (figures and tables in lab sciences; thematic narratives in qualitative work; etc.); citation conventions (sparse in lab sciences' methods; dense throughout in humanities); voice conventions (passive in some lab sciences; first-person plural in computational sciences; first-person singular in humanities); length conventions (under 4,000 words in _Nature_ ; 8,000–12,000 in humanities). Any three are correct.

**Q4.** Why does the chapter recommend hedging at the _more conservative_ tradition's calibration when writing across disciplines?

**Answer:** Because if the paper hedges at the less conservative tradition's level, reviewers from the more conservative tradition will read it as overclaiming. If the paper hedges at the more conservative tradition's level, reviewers from the less conservative tradition may find it slightly under-claiming but will rarely reject the paper for that reason. The asymmetry favors the conservative calibration as the safer cross-disciplinary choice.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Apply the **co-author negotiation audit** from §13.10 to a current or imagined cross-disciplinary collaboration. Submit the four components (named negotiation; both sides articulated; cost of avoiding; conversation plan) and a 200-word reflection on what was hardest. (Connection to Chapter 11: this is the diagnostic eye for substantive disagreement applied to a collaboration rather than a peer review.)

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful response will (a) accurately name a real point of disagreement, (b) articulate both sides fairly (not strawmanning the co-author's position), (c) identify specific costs the unresolved disagreement creates, and (d) plan a conversation that opens the negotiation rather than pre-empting it. The most useful reflections often note that articulating the co-author's position fairly was harder than expected, and that doing so changed the writer's sense of the disagreement's stakes.

**Sample Response (Mira and Dr. Reyes's framing negotiation):** _(1) The negotiation: Mira and Reyes have not yet agreed on whether the paper's introduction should lead with the qualitative mechanism (Mira's home-discipline convention) or the quantitative pattern (Reyes's). Both have drafted their preferred opening; both leads have sat on the shared document for two weeks; neither has been edited. (2) Both sides articulated. Mira's side: a mechanism-first opening makes the contribution legible to policy-studies reviewers and accurately reflects the order of discovery (mechanism evidence motivated the panel work). Yielding cost: the paper reads as an econ paper with qualitative dressing, and the policy-studies reviewer pool is unlikely to be assembled. Reyes's side: a pattern-first opening makes the contribution legible to economics reviewers; the panel data is the wider-claim layer. Yielding cost: the paper reads as a policy-studies paper with quantitative robustness, and the economics reviewer pool is unlikely to be assembled. (3) Cost of avoiding the conversation: the paper drifts toward an "and-also" opening that satisfies neither audience; one of us writes the framing the other quietly resents; we miss the spring submission window. (4) Conversation plan: a 45-minute call on Friday with one agenda — pick the lead. Each prepares one paragraph defending their preference and one paragraph naming what they could give up. We pick by the end of the call (or schedule a second call within five days). Whoever's lead is not chosen drafts the discussion's two-implications paragraph (§13.7) so both fields' implications are articulated. Reflection: writing this audit forced Mira to notice that the negotiation had been delayed by politeness rather than substance — both knew the conversation was needed; neither wanted to start it._

**Q2.** Take a published cross-disciplinary paper in your field. Read the introduction, methods, and discussion. **Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A typical successful response will identify specific cross-disciplinary moves the paper makes (e.g., dual-tradition citation; cross-walk methods explanation; two-implications discussion structure) and characterize their execution. Common observations: well-executed cross-disciplinary papers feel slightly _foreign_ to specialists in either contributing field, but that foreignness is the cost of cross-disciplinary reach, not a failure.

**Q3.** Imagine a hypothetical cross-disciplinary collaboration in your field. The exercise teaches the explicit-conversation principle: the negotiations cross-disciplinary collaborators avoid become the conflicts that derail the paper later.

**Q4.** Take a paper you have written in your home discipline. Imagine submitting a closely related version of it to a journal in an _adjacent_ discipline. What three substantive changes would you need to make to the paper to satisfy the adjacent discipline's conventions? Write 250 words. **Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A typical successful response will identify changes such as: (a) reframing the contribution to engage the adjacent discipline's debates rather than the writer's home discipline's debates; (b) restructuring the methods section to explain the writer's home-discipline conventions for the adjacent discipline's readers; (c) shifting the citation pattern to include the adjacent discipline's literature substantively; (d) recalibrating the hedging to match the adjacent discipline's norms; (e) adjusting the voice to match the adjacent discipline's conventions. The exercise teaches that the same underlying work can yield meaningfully different papers in different disciplinary venues — and that the cross-disciplinary writer chooses among these versions deliberately.

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Cross-disciplinary papers face higher rejection rates but, when published, often have higher long-run impact. How should this asymmetry shape early-career strategy? Should graduate students lean toward cross-disciplinary work or single-discipline work? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** The honest answer is mixed. Single-discipline work is more reliable for early-career publication and tenure clocks, particularly in fields that weight first-tier disciplinary journals heavily. Cross-disciplinary work is more impactful when it succeeds but more failure-prone in submission. For most early-career researchers, a _mixed portfolio_ is the strategic answer: substantial single-discipline work to establish disciplinary credibility and clear publication track, with selective cross-disciplinary work that takes the longer-payoff bets. The mix shifts across career stages: early-career may lean single-discipline; mid-career and senior researchers can lean more cross-disciplinary as their disciplinary reputations are established. Programs that reward only single-discipline work are increasingly out of step with how research questions are organized; programs that demand cross-disciplinary work without supporting it produce stalled early careers. The reform challenge is to make tenure systems weight cross-disciplinary work fairly. (Connection to Chapter 12's dissertation discussion: cross-disciplinary dissertations carry these same trade-offs at higher stakes.)

**Q2.** Some scholars argue that the increasing prevalence of cross-disciplinary work is _eroding disciplinary depth_ — that fewer scholars develop the deep specialized expertise that has produced major breakthroughs in many fields. Others argue the opposite: that disciplinary depth in 2026 requires cross-disciplinary fluency because the questions worth pursuing now span fields. Where do you stand? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** Both positions have merit. Disciplinary depth produces certain kinds of breakthroughs (deep insights into specialized phenomena; methodological innovations within a tradition); cross-disciplinary fluency produces other kinds (integration across fields; questions visible only from multiple angles). Healthy academic ecosystems probably need both: deep disciplinary specialists _and_ cross-disciplinary integrators. The danger is monocultures — programs and incentive systems that reward only one kind of work. The deepest answer notices that the dichotomy is partly false: many of the best cross-disciplinary scholars have deep training in one field and developed adjacent-field literacy through sustained reading and collaboration. Cross-disciplinary work requires _some_ depth somewhere; it cannot be done well by writers who are shallow in every contributing field. The reform: support both deep and broad training, recognize both as legitimate scholarly contributions, and stop treating cross-disciplinary fluency as a substitute for disciplinary depth. (Connection forward to Chapter 17: AI may shift this balance further by reducing the cost of cross-disciplinary literacy.)

**Q3.** AI tools can now translate between disciplinary conventions — turning a humanities-style paper into an economics-style paper, or vice versa, with surprising fluency. What are the integrity risks and acceptable uses? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** AI translation between disciplinary conventions is a real new capability and a real new risk. Acceptable uses: (a) using AI to draft a methods cross-walk paragraph that explains your home-discipline methods for the other contributing discipline's readers; (b) using AI to flag jargon that would be unfamiliar to a cross-disciplinary audience; (c) using AI to suggest citation alternatives from the adjacent discipline's literature; (d) using AI to characterize how the adjacent discipline typically frames a topic, as input to the writer's own framing decisions. Risks: (a) AI translation often _flattens_ the conventions of both contributing fields, producing prose that satisfies neither; (b) AI may invent or misattribute citations from the adjacent field; (c) AI may introduce calibration choices that the writer would not endorse; (d) AI translation may obscure substantive intellectual work — the difficult thinking-across that cross-disciplinary writing requires. Bright line: the writer must understand _why_ a particular cross-disciplinary move makes sense, not just that AI suggested it. The skill of cross-disciplinary writing is a skill of _thinking_ across disciplines; AI can help with execution, but it cannot substitute for the thinking. (Connection forward to Chapter 14: this is one of many domains where AI assistance is increasingly accepted but where the writer's own intellectual ownership remains the standard.)

It is the spring of Mira's fifth year. The dissertation is in late drafting. The cross-disciplinary paper from Chapter 13 is in revision. Mira has been using AI tools — quietly and unevenly — throughout the dissertation: an AI to flag voice drift between chapters, an AI to draft alternative phrasings of difficult paragraphs, an AI to play the role of a hostile reviewer during defense rehearsal. None of this AI use has been disclosed in any document Mira has submitted.

In a regular meeting, Mira's advisor asks: _"How are you using AI in your writing?"_

The question is asked neutrally. It could mean _"because we should disclose it";_ it could mean _"because I'm worried about it";_ it could mean _"because I'm curious about how the kids do it these days."_ Mira, who has not thought carefully about disclosure, gives an answer that is partly true, partly evasive, and partly defensive: _"Mostly for editing. Not for writing."_

The answer is unsatisfying, and Mira knows it. The truth is that AI assistance has shaped Mira's dissertation in ways that resist a simple binary of "writing" vs. "editing." The conversation with the advisor that follows — and the personal AI policy Mira develops in response — is the subject of this chapter.

Welcome to the newest fundamental skill in academic writing. The conventions are evolving fast; the disclosure norms are still settling; and the integrity stakes are real. This chapter offers what we know in 2026.

### 14.1 Vignette: The Editing/Writing Boundary

What counts as "writing" and what counts as "editing"?

A clean case: an AI generates a complete paragraph from a bullet-point outline, and the writer pastes it in unchanged. This is _writing_. The AI did the work; the writer only described what should be done.

Another clean case: an AI suggests a single word change in a sentence the writer drafted ("perhaps _suggest_ would be more calibrated than _demonstrate_ here"). The writer accepts the suggestion. This is _editing_. The writer drafted; the AI nudged.

The interesting cases live between these poles, and there are many of them:

* An AI suggests structural reorganization of a section the writer drafted ("consider moving the limitations paragraph before the implications paragraph"). The writer agrees and reorders. _Editing or writing?_
* An AI rephrases a paragraph the writer drafted, preserving meaning but changing voice. The writer accepts most of the rephrasing. _Editing or writing?_
* An AI generates three alternative versions of a paragraph the writer drafted; the writer picks one and revises lightly. _Editing or writing?_
* An AI is asked "what's missing from this discussion section?" and identifies three alternative explanations the writer hadn't considered. The writer adds engagement of one of them in their own prose. _Editing or writing?_

These cases are not pedantically interesting. They are operationally important, because journal disclosure policies and program integrity standards in 2026 are mostly written around the editing/writing distinction, and they are not yet sharp enough to handle the in-between cases cleanly. Different journals, different programs, and different individual reviewers in 2026 draw the line in different places.

The honest writer in this environment does several things:

  1. Tracks their own AI use with enough specificity to disclose it accurately.
  2. Errs on the side of _more_ disclosure rather than less.
  3. Maintains the bright lines that almost everyone agrees on (no AI-generated citations; no AI-generated factual claims that the writer hasn't verified; no AI-generated text the writer hasn't endorsed).
  4. Defaults to discussing AI use openly with collaborators, advisors, editors.

This chapter walks through how to develop these habits in 2026, while acknowledging that the conventions will continue to evolve.

### 14.2 What Reviewers, Editors, and Programs Look For

**Has AI use been disclosed?** The dominant convention in 2026 is that AI use should be disclosed in the methods section (for substantive use) or in the acknowledgments (for editorial use). Failure to disclose is a growing integrity flag.

**Does the disclosure match the actual use?** Editors in 2026 sometimes spot disclosure-use mismatches (e.g., a disclosure that says "AI was used only for grammar checking" attached to a paper that bears the stylistic signature of AI generation). Mismatched disclosure is treated more seriously than honest disclosure of substantial use.

**Are the bright lines respected?** Across most journals, three bright lines are now widely enforced: AI is not an author; cited works must be verified; AI-generated factual claims must be checked. Violations of these lines are treated as integrity matters.

**Does the AI use align with venue policy?** Different journals (and different funders) have different specific policies. Some specify that AI may be used for editing but not for drafting; some allow drafting with disclosure; some prohibit AI use in certain document types entirely. Writers must know the specific policy of the venue they target.

**Is the AI use proportionate to the writer's contribution?** A paper in which AI did most of the substantive work is treated differently from a paper in which AI assisted on phrasing. Editors can sometimes detect the difference even when disclosure is incomplete.

**Has the writer maintained voice and originality?** AI-assisted drafts often read with a particular flatness — a generic-academic mush that lacks the writer's specific voice. Reviewers in 2026 are increasingly trained to spot this; some journals have begun deploying AI-detection tools, with mixed reliability.


### 14.3 The Current State of Journal AI Policies (as of 2026)

A surprising fact: as of 2025, **most major journals have explicit AI use policies** , and the policies cluster around a few common patterns. The specific landscape:


#### Pattern 1: AI as tool, with disclosure

The dominant pattern. Most major journals — _Nature, Science, Cell, NEJM, Lancet, PLOS, BMJ, JAMA_ , the _American Economic Review_ , _Annual Reviews_ family, most APA journals, most major society journals — accept AI use as a tool, including for substantial drafting assistance, but require disclosure. The disclosure is typically located in the methods section (for substantive use) or in a dedicated acknowledgments paragraph (for editorial use).


#### Pattern 2: AI not an author

Universal. **No major journal in 2026 lists AI as an author.** The reasoning: authors are responsible for the content they sign their names to, and AI cannot bear that responsibility. The Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) and the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) have both formalized this position.


#### Pattern 3: Specific prohibitions on certain uses

Some journals explicitly prohibit certain AI uses: AI-generated peer reviews (because reviewers are confidential and AI use risks confidentiality); AI-generated images claimed as primary data; AI-generated citations without verification. The American Mathematical Society, for instance, has specific guidance on AI in proof writing that limits the genres in which AI assistance is acceptable.

#### Pattern 4: Discipline-specific reservations

Some discipline communities — particularly in qualitative humanities and parts of theoretical mathematics — have stricter norms than the general journal landscape. Theoretical physics, by contrast, has been an early adopter and has relatively permissive norms. Discipline-by-discipline variation is large; the three-paper read of your venue tells you more than the journal's general policy page.


#### Pattern 5: Funder-level policies

Funders have begun publishing their own policies. NIH and NSF have both issued guidance allowing AI use in grant proposals with disclosure. Some private foundations have stricter rules. The funder's policy applies in addition to the journal's policy.

A surprising fact, less widely appreciated: the policies are **substantially more permissive in 2026 than they were in 2023.** The early-2023 reaction to ChatGPT was widely restrictive (some journals initially banned all AI use); by 2025, the consensus had evolved toward permissive-with-disclosure. This evolution may continue. Writers should check the _current_ policy of their target venue at the time of submission, not at the time of drafting.


### 14.4 Safe Uses, Gray-Zone Uses, Prohibited Uses

A practical taxonomy of AI uses in academic writing as of 2026:


#### Safe uses (low integrity risk, widely accepted)

* **Editing assistance.** Grammar, sentence-level revision, voice-consistency checks, identifying overlong sentences, flagging passive/active voice mixing.
* **Brainstorming.** Generating alternative phrasings, alternative structures, alternative framings — used as input to the writer's own choices.
* **Audit roles.** Asking AI to play a hostile reviewer, to identify CARS-move gaps, to apply the hedging matrix to a draft, to flag overclaim.
* **Methods boilerplate.** Translating bullet-point procedure notes into convention-appropriate prose, with the writer verifying every specific detail.
* **Tone calibration on response letters.** Identifying defensive language and suggesting more conciliatory phrasings.
* **Voice-consistency checks across long documents.** Flagging chapters whose voice diverges from others.
* **Translation.** Translating between languages, with the writer verifying technical content.
* **Reference formatting.** Converting between citation styles, formatting bibliographies.


#### Gray-zone uses (acceptable in some venues, prohibited in others, evolving)

* **First-draft generation.** Producing a full first draft from an outline, which the writer then heavily revises. Some venues accept with disclosure; some do not.
* **Substantial drafting of standard sections.** Generating the methods section from notes, generating the abstract from the paper. Acceptable with disclosure in most empirical journals; less acceptable in humanities.
* **Generating alternative interpretations.** Asking AI to suggest interpretations the writer hadn't considered. Generally acceptable as a thinking aid; problematic if the writer adopts AI-suggested interpretations without the underlying analytical work.
* **Helping with literature review searches.** Asking AI to identify relevant prior work in a field. Acceptable as a starting point; problematic if AI-identified citations are used without verification.

#### Prohibited uses (almost universally treated as integrity violations)

* **AI-generated citations.** Citing works the writer has not read, on the assumption that the AI's citation is accurate. AI hallucinates citations frequently; this is a near-universal bright-line violation.
* **AI-generated factual claims that the writer has not verified.** Putting unverified AI-generated claims in a paper, regardless of whether the AI use is disclosed.
* **Listing AI as an author.** Universally prohibited.
* **Submitting AI-generated text as the writer's own work without any disclosure.** Particularly in degree-conferring documents (theses, dissertations, qualifying exams).
* **AI-generated peer reviews.** Most journals prohibit this because peer review is confidential and AI use violates the confidentiality.
* **AI-generated grant proposals submitted without disclosure.** Most major funders treat this as a significant integrity matter.

The taxonomy will continue to evolve. Writers should treat it as a snapshot of 2026 norms, not as a fixed rule.


#### Definition: AI Disclosure

**AI disclosure** is the explicit acknowledgment in an academic document of how artificial-intelligence tools were used in producing the document, typically including which tools were used and for what purpose.

In plain language: AI disclosure is the paragraph (often in the methods section or acknowledgments) that tells the reader honestly what the writer did with AI. A typical disclosure might read: _"The authors used [AI tool] for editing assistance (grammar, sentence-level revision) on the entire manuscript, and for generating alternative phrasings of the discussion section. All substantive analytical content, citations, and claims are the authors' own. The authors take full responsibility for the accuracy of all content."_

Disclosure is the operational requirement that most journals in 2026 enforce. The standard for what to disclose is _honest description of substantive use_ — disclosure does not need to enumerate every AI suggestion the writer accepted, but it should accurately characterize the role AI played in producing the document.


#### Common Misconception

A common misconception is that AI disclosure is a _confession of inadequacy_ — that disclosing AI use signals the writer was unable to do the work themselves. In 2026, this is largely false. AI assistance is widespread, generally accepted, and increasingly normalized. Disclosure is a _professional practice_ , not a confession; it allows readers and reviewers to understand the work's provenance and to evaluate it appropriately.

A second misconception is that _no_ AI use needs to be disclosed if it falls under "editing." In practice, the editing/writing distinction is fuzzy enough that many editors prefer disclosure of any substantive AI involvement. The cost of over-disclosure is low; the cost of under-disclosure (if discovered) can be substantial.

A third misconception is that AI-detection tools can reliably distinguish AI-written from human-written prose. As of 2026, AI-detection tools have substantial false-positive and false-negative rates and are not reliable enough to be the basis of integrity findings. Most journals that have piloted AI-detection have moved away from automated tools and toward editorial judgment plus disclosure norms.

### 14.5 The Six Moves Applied to Mira's AI Use

**Move 1 (genre/venue).** Different documents have different AI conventions. Mira's dissertation has different norms than Mira's journal articles, which have different norms than Mira's grant proposals, which have different norms than Mira's peer reviews of others' work. Mira develops a separate AI policy for each document type.

**Move 2 (structure).** Mira's personal AI policy, drafted after the conversation with their advisor, has six components: (a) what AI tools they use; (b) what tasks they use AI for; (c) what tasks they do not use AI for; (d) how they verify AI suggestions; (e) how they disclose use in different document types; (f) how they reflect on their AI practice annually.

**Move 3 (calibration).** The disclosure language uses the hedging matrix: _"used for editing assistance" / "consulted for alternative phrasings" / "did not use for…"_ The disclosure is specific without overclaiming or under-claiming. It matches the actual use.

**Move 4 (positioning).** The disclosure positions the AI use within the broader practices of Mira's field. Where Mira's use is within the field's norm, the disclosure is brief; where it is more substantial, the disclosure is more detailed and may include reasoning.

**Move 5 (anticipated reviewer).** Predictable AI-related reviewer concerns: _"Did AI generate any of the substantive content?"_ (Disclosure addresses directly.) _"Did AI generate the citations?"_ (Disclosure clarifies that all citations are author-verified.) _"Did AI affect the voice?"_ (Disclosure notes editing assistance and the author's voice-consistency review.) Reviewers who see honest, specific disclosure tend to engage the substance of the paper rather than questioning AI provenance.

**Move 6 (AI on AI use).** Mira uses AI to draft alternative phrasings of their disclosure statements, then chooses among them and revises. They do not use AI to _decide_ the disclosure policy — that judgment is the writer's.

The dissertation Mira submits includes a methods-section paragraph disclosing AI use across the dissertation's preparation. The defense committee asks about it; Mira's answer is direct, specific, and unembarrassed. The committee accepts the disclosure as appropriate.

### 14.6 Templates and Examples

**Disclosure for editing-only AI use:**

> _"The author(s) used [AI tool, version] for editorial assistance, including grammar checking, sentence-level revision, and voice-consistency review. All substantive content, analyses, citations, and claims are the author(s)' own. The author(s) take full responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of the manuscript."_

**Disclosure for substantive AI use:**

> _"The author(s) used [AI tool, version] for the following purposes: (a) editorial assistance throughout the manuscript; (b) drafting alternative phrasings of the discussion section, with the author(s) selecting and revising; (c) generating an initial outline of the methods section from author-provided notes, which the author(s) substantially revised; (d) playing the role of a skeptical reviewer to identify potential weaknesses in the discussion. All citations, factual claims, and analytical interpretations were verified by the author(s). The author(s) take full responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of the manuscript."_

**Methods-section integration of AI use (where substantial):**

> _"In drafting the manuscript, the authors used [AI tool] in the roles described in §X (or in the AI Use Statement). Specifically, [tool] was used for [purposes]. The use is consistent with [journal's policy on AI assistance]. All substantive analytical work — case selection, coding, statistical analysis, interpretation — was conducted by the authors without AI generation."_

**Personal AI policy (a writer's own document, not for publication):**

> _"My AI use policy:_
> 
> _(a) Tools I use: [tools and versions]._
> 
> _(b) Tasks I use AI for: [list — e.g., grammar checking, voice-consistency review, hedging-matrix audit, alternative phrasing brainstorming, hostile-reviewer rehearsal, methods boilerplate translation]._
> 
> _(c) Tasks I do not use AI for: [list — e.g., generating substantive analytical claims, generating citations, drafting paragraphs whose ideas I have not first thought through, drafting peer reviews of others' work, generating disclosure language about my own AI use without revision]._
> 
> _(d) Verification practices: [how I check AI suggestions — e.g., I read every AI-suggested citation in the original source; I verify every AI-generated fact against my notes; I ensure every paragraph reflects my own analytical judgment]._
> 
> _(e) Disclosure practices by document type: [how I disclose in articles, in proposals, in peer reviews, in dissertation, in informal writing]._
> 
> _(f) Annual review: [when I will revisit and update this policy]."_

This is a private document, but writing one is an exercise that clarifies practice. We'll suggest writing one as the audit prompt.

**Disclosure language for non-disclosure cases (where AI was not used):**

> _"No AI tools were used in the preparation of this manuscript."_

This is rare in 2026 but still appropriate for some genres (e.g., some humanities papers, some short editorials, peer reviews under journals that prohibit AI in reviews).

### 14.7 Common Pitfalls

**The under-disclosed manuscript.** AI was used substantially, but disclosure says only "for editing." Editors increasingly detect this. Fix: disclose actual use specifically.

**The boilerplate disclosure that doesn't match.** A generic "AI was used for editing assistance" pasted into a manuscript whose AI use was much more substantial. Fix: write disclosure specific to the actual use.

**The voice-flattened paper.** AI-assisted drafting has produced prose that lacks the writer's specific voice — generic-academic-mush. Reviewers detect this. Fix: post-AI revision pass for voice; rewrite paragraphs that read flat.

**The unverified AI citation.** A citation generated by AI that the writer did not check. AI hallucinates citations frequently; this is the most common AI integrity violation in 2026. Fix: verify every cited work in the original source.

**The AI-generated peer review.** Submitting an AI-generated peer review violates most journals' policies and often violates confidentiality (since reviewer drafts are sometimes uploaded to AI tools). Fix: do not use AI to generate peer reviews; check journal policy.

**The unconsidered disclosure-policy mismatch.** Submitting to a journal whose AI policy is stricter than the writer's practice. Fix: check the policy; adapt practice or disclosure to fit.

**The dissertation AI disclosure that hides scope.** A doctoral candidate hides substantial AI use in a brief acknowledgments mention. Fix: dissertation AI use in 2026 should be disclosed candidly; programs are increasingly requiring explicit policies.

**The team without a shared AI policy.** Co-authors with different AI practices, no explicit alignment, and inconsistent disclosure. Fix: shared AI-use agreement at the start of every collaboration.

**The personal AI policy that exists only in the writer's head.** Without explicit articulation, AI practice drifts. Fix: write a personal AI policy; revisit annually.

### 14.8 Scholar Profile: Ethan Mollick and the Practical Frontier

Ethan Mollick is a management professor at the Wharton School (University of Pennsylvania) whose work since 2022 on practical AI use in education and professional work has shaped how a wide audience — including many academics — thinks about working with AI tools. His Substack newsletter _One Useful Thing_ and his 2024 book _Co-Intelligence_ have made him one of the most-cited public voices on AI integration into knowledge work.

A surprising fact, central to Mollick's work: **most major journals in 2025 allow AI as a tool but require disclosure; discipline communities differ wildly in their adoption and norms.** Theoretical physics has been a relatively early and permissive adopter; clinical medicine has been slower and more cautious; qualitative humanities has been deeply skeptical. The variation is large enough that AI policies cannot be inferred from one's home discipline; writers need to check venue-specific norms.

A second surprising fact, also documented in Mollick's surveys and others': **AI use in academic writing is far more common than disclosure rates suggest.** Many writers use AI for editing or drafting and do not disclose, either because they don't think the use rises to disclosure threshold or because they are unsure what the threshold is. This gap — substantial use, sparse disclosure — is one of the central tensions of academic AI in 2026.

A third surprising fact: **the most effective AI-assisted writers are not the writers who use AI most heavily; they are the writers who use AI most deliberately.** Mollick distinguishes between _augmented_ AI use (the writer remains intellectually in charge, AI assists at points of friction) and _replaced_ AI use (the writer outsources thinking to AI). The augmented mode produces stronger work and is more compatible with disclosure norms; the replaced mode produces hollow-sounding work that AI-detection tools (and trained reviewers) increasingly identify.

A fourth observation, from Mollick and others: **AI capabilities continue to evolve faster than the conventions can adapt.** The journal policies of 2024 are already partly out of date in 2026; the policies of 2026 will be partly out of date in 2028. Writers cannot simply learn the rules and apply them; they must continually revise their practice as both the tools and the norms shift.

For graduate writers entering 2026, Mollick's lessons are direct: develop a deliberate, documented AI practice; disclose honestly; stay current with venue policies; treat AI as augmentation rather than replacement; revisit your practice as the tools and conventions evolve. The skill of working with AI is its own academic-writing skill in 2026, and like all academic-writing skills it is learnable through deliberate attention.

A fifth observation, more philosophical: Mollick has written that the deeper question facing academic writing in the AI era is not _which tools to use_ but _what kind of intellectual contribution academic writing is for._ If AI can produce plausible-sounding academic prose at near-zero cost, the value of academic writing must increasingly come from what AI cannot do: original analytical judgment, calibrated interpretation of specific evidence, accountability to specific findings, the building of trust that comes from staking one's name on claims one has personally verified. These are the durable contributions academic writing makes; they are also the contributions writers should protect against AI-driven flattening.

We return to this larger question in Chapter 17.


### 14.9 Reader's Manuscript Audit Prompt

Write your **personal AI use disclosure statement.**

This is not a public-facing disclosure (though it may inform one). It is a private document that articulates your AI practice for your own use. The exercise:

Write 200–400 words covering:

  1. **Tools.** What AI tools do you currently use in your academic writing?
  2. **Tasks you use AI for.** What specific tasks do you delegate to AI assistance?
  3. **Tasks you do not use AI for.** What do you keep for yourself, and why?
  4. **Verification practices.** How do you check AI suggestions before incorporating them?
  5. **Disclosure practices by document type.** How do you disclose AI use in articles, proposals, peer reviews, dissertation, informal writing?
  6. **Annual review.** When will you revisit this policy?

Save the document. Revisit it in six months and again in twelve. The goal is not to lock in a fixed practice — practices should evolve as tools and norms evolve — but to make your practice _deliberate and documented_ , rather than drifting and unconsidered.

This is your twelfth manuscript revision — the final audit prompt of Part II. The exercise is more reflective than the prior audit prompts, and it is one of the highest-leverage 30 minutes you can spend on your academic writing practice in 2026.

(Bonus: share your disclosure statement with a co-author or labmate. Compare. The variation in AI practice across writers in the same field is often surprising, and the comparison sharpens both writers' practices.)

**Sample Response (Mira's personal AI-use policy, abridged):** _(a) Tools I use: Claude (latest version), ChatGPT (Plus tier), Grammarly (browser plugin). (b) Tasks I use AI for: grammar and sentence-level revision; voice-consistency review across long documents; flagging passive/active drift; alternative phrasings of difficult paragraphs; hostile-reviewer rehearsal (asking the AI to play Reviewer 3); methods boilerplate translation from bullet-point notes; brainstorming alternative framings I haven't considered. (c) Tasks I do not use AI for: generating substantive analytical claims; generating citations (every cited work is one I have read in the original); drafting paragraphs whose ideas I have not first thought through; drafting peer reviews of others' work; generating disclosure language about my own AI use without revision. (d) Verification practices: I read every AI-suggested citation in the original source before accepting it; I verify every AI-generated factual claim against my notes; I read each AI-suggested paragraph aloud to check that it matches my voice and that I would defend each sentence in person. (e) Disclosure by document type: in journal articles, methods-section paragraph naming tools and roles; in proposals, methods-section paragraph; in peer reviews, no AI use (per most journals' policies on confidentiality); in dissertation, methods-section paragraph; in informal writing (blog, talks), brief acknowledgment if substantial. (f) Annual review: every January, with my advisor, before the spring submission cycle. Reflection: writing this forced Mira to admit they had been using AI for "alternative interpretations" without consistently disclosing it. The policy now treats this as gray-zone use that requires methods-section disclosure when it materially shaped the discussion._

**Q2.** Take a recent paper of your own (drafted before this chapter) and audit it for AI involvement. For each AI use, classify per §14.4: safe, gray-zone, or prohibited. Were any uses gray-zone or prohibited? If you submitted the paper, what disclosure did you include? What disclosure should you have included? Write a 250-word reflection. (Connection to Chapter 11: this is the same diagnostic eye that sharpens response letters, applied to disclosure.)

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A successful response will (a) accurately classify the AI uses, (b) honestly assess the original disclosure (or lack thereof), (c) draft what the disclosure should have included, and (d) reflect on what the audit revealed. Many writers find the audit exposes gray-zone uses they had not flagged; the reflection on what the disclosure should have included builds the muscle for future disclosure-honest practice.

**Q3.** Find the AI use policy of two journals in your field — one general (e.g., a high-impact disciplinary journal) and one specialized (e.g., a sub-disciplinary or methodological journal). How do they differ? Write a 250-word comparison. (Connection to Chapter 2's three-paper read: this is venue research extended to AI policy.)

**Answer:** _Answers will vary._ A typical successful response will note specific differences between the two policies — disclosure threshold, allowed uses, prohibited uses, language requirements. Common findings: high-impact general journals tend to have well-developed policies; some specialized journals have brief or unclear policies; some journals have policies that have not been updated since 2023. The exercise teaches that AI policy is venue-specific and writer-current — checking the venue's most recent policy at submission time matters.

**Q4.** Imagine you have been asked to peer review a paper. The paper bears characteristics of substantial AI involvement (generic phrasings, voice flatness, occasional implausible claims). The disclosure statement says only "AI was used for editing." Draft a brief paragraph of your peer review that addresses the disclosure-use mismatch professionally. (Connection to Chapter 11: this is response-letter craft applied to a peer-review document.)

**Answer:** A successful response will (a) raise the concern professionally without accusation, (b) point to specific evidence in the paper, (c) suggest the editor consider whether disclosure was complete, and (d) avoid speculating about the writer's intentions. Example: _"The manuscript contains some passages whose voice and phrasing patterns suggest more substantial AI involvement than the brief 'AI was used for editing' disclosure indicates — particularly in §X and §Y, which read with notable register flatness compared to §Z. I do not assume bad faith on the part of the authors, but suggest the editor invite the authors to clarify their AI use practices in revision. The journal's AI policy may be relevant in evaluating the disclosure's specificity."_

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The chapter argues that the editing/writing distinction — central to most current AI policies — is fuzzy enough to be unsatisfying. What would a better distinction look like? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** Several alternatives have been proposed. _Substantive vs. cosmetic_ — does the AI affect what the paper claims, or only how the paper says it? _Generative vs. evaluative_ — does the AI produce content, or evaluate writer-produced content? _Process disclosure_ — disclose the workflow, not the output (e.g., "I drafted, used AI to suggest revisions, accepted some and rejected others"). Each has merits and weaknesses. The deeper issue is that no clean distinction will fully separate AI-as-tool from AI-as-author, because the underlying activity is on a continuum. The most useful framework may be _responsibility-centered_ : regardless of how AI was used, the writer must be able to defend every claim in the paper as one they personally believe and have personally verified. Disclosure becomes a way of showing how the writer maintained that responsibility, rather than a way of categorizing tool use into approved/disapproved buckets. (Connection forward to Chapter 17: this is part of the broader question about what academic writing is _for_ in the AI era.)

**Q2.** Some journals have piloted AI-detection tools to flag suspected AI-generated text. The tools have substantial false-positive and false-negative rates. Should journals continue to develop them, or rely on disclosure norms? Sketch your view in 250 words.

**Discussion:** Both approaches have weaknesses. AI-detection tools may falsely flag text written by ESL writers (whose register can resemble AI register), text in highly conventional genres (where formulaic prose is normal), and text that was lightly AI-edited (where AI's presence is partial and ambiguous). Disclosure norms rely on writer honesty and may be evaded. The most useful approach in 2026 combines both: disclosure as the primary signal, AI-detection as a backup that triggers editorial questions but not automatic decisions. The deepest answer notices that the question itself may shift: as AI text becomes indistinguishable from human text, the question may move from "did AI write this?" to "did the writer take responsibility for the claims?" — a question disclosure can address but detection cannot.

**Q3.** Some critics argue that widespread AI use in academic writing is producing a _flattening of voice_ across the field — that academic prose is becoming more uniform as AI suggestions converge on a generic-academic-mush. Is this critique accurate? What are its implications for the field? Develop a position in 250–400 words.

**Discussion:** The critique is partly accurate. AI tools, trained on large corpora of academic text, tend to produce convention-following prose with median register, median sentence structure, median vocabulary. Writers who outsource heavily to AI risk producing prose that reads as median; the distinctive voices of skilled academic writers (Sword, Pinker, Latour, etc.) are partly _non-median_ and would be flattened by AI-driven revision. The implications: (a) voice may become a more important distinguishing feature for skilled academic writers (since AI-flat prose is the new baseline); (b) editorial standards may shift — some venues may explicitly value distinctive voice as a sign of writer engagement; (c) the value of training in academic writing may increase, paradoxically, as the cost of producing median prose drops; (d) some discipline communities may push back against flattening through editorial conventions or explicit voice-emphasis. The deepest answer notices that flattening is not inevitable: writers who use AI as augmentation rather than replacement (per Mollick) preserve their voices. The flattening is a function of how AI is used, not of AI use per se. (Connection forward to Chapter 17: this is one of the central questions about AI's long-run impact on academic writing.)


### Chapter Summary

Writing with AI is the newest fundamental skill in academic writing, and the one whose conventions are evolving most rapidly. As of 2026, most major journals accept AI use as a tool with disclosure, three bright lines are widely enforced (no AI authorship; verify cited works; check AI-generated factual claims), and the editing/writing distinction — though fuzzy — anchors most disclosure norms.
